courses.desc: Offered spring. Students should have a working knowledge of precalculus (ie. college algebra and college trigonometry) prior to registration. Overview of recent developments in planetary system formation, stars, galaxies, and cosmology. Some astronomical observing will be required outside of normal class hours.

courses.subject: ASTR
courses.title: Galaxies and Cosmology
courses.desc: Offered spring odd-numbered years. Prereq., ASTR 132N or ASTR 142N, and PHSX 222/PHSX 223 or PHSX 207N/PHSX 208N, and M 273. The nature of the Milky Way galaxy and other galaxies, galactic evolution, the large scale structure of the universe, active galaxies and quasars, and cosmology, including the early universe.

courses.subject: ASTR
courses.title: Stellar Astronomy & Astrophysics I

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Emergency Management in Athletic Training
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Serves as an introduction to athletic training practice. Emphasis on the prevention, care, and management of acute injuries and illnesses, as well as risk management, environmental concerns, and protective taping and equipment. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Foundations of Health Care in Athletic Training
courses.desc: This course presents the overarching framework, principles, and core responsibilities of athletic training practice working in multidisciplinary healthcare teams. The course also provides the necessary foundation for athletic training practice focusing on patient-centered care, interprofessional practice, evidence-based practice, quality improvement and healthcare informatics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Foundations of Research and Evidence Based Practice in Athletic Training
courses.desc: This course explores quantitative and qualitative research methodologies used in athletic training and evaluation of published research in the field. The course will introduce evidence-based practice research, provide strategies for reading and writing critically, and offer a plan to applying evidence-based practice in daily clinical practice. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Practicum in Athletic Training I
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Builds on skills previously acquired and introduces new skills related to current coursework. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. First in the series of four practicum courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Practicum in Athletic Training II
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Expands on skills previously acquired and introduces new skills related to current coursework. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. Second in the series of four practicum courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Orthopedic Assessment I
courses.desc: Provides a study of anatomy and physiology, assessment, evaluation techniques, treatment, and management of conditions affecting the lower extremities and lumbar spine. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Diagnosis and Management of Sports Related Concussion
courses.desc: This course discusses assessment techniques commonly used in the clinical evaluation of sport related concussion. The course also provides the necessary foundation for establishing inter-professional care teams to treat sport related concussion. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: General Medical Assessment
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Examines the recognition, assessment, and management of general medical conditions and illnesses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Orthopedic Assessment II
courses.desc: Provides a study of anatomy and physiology, assessment, evaluation techniques, treatment, and management of conditions affecting the upper extremities, head, and thoracic and cervical spine. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Practicum in Athletic Training III
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Broadens skills previously acquired and introduces new skills related to current coursework. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. Third in the series of four practicum courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Practicum in Athletic Training IV
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Reviews and refines skills previously acquired and evaluated in previous coursework. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. Fourth in the series of four practicum courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Clinical Immersion in Athletic Training I
courses.desc: Practice intensive experience that allows the student to experience the totality of care provided by athletic trainers. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. This is the first in the series of three immersion courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Clinical Immersion in Athletic Training II
courses.desc: Practice intensive experience that allows the student to experience the totality of care provided by athletic trainers. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. This is the second in the series of three immersion courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Clinical Immersion in Athletic Training III
courses.desc: Practice intensive experience that allows the student to experience the totality of care provided by athletic trainers. Students will be assigned to a clinical education rotation under the direct supervision of a clinical preceptor. This is the third in the series of three immersion courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Clinical Anatomy Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered Summer. Restricted to students in the Master of Athletic Training program. Clinical applications of anatomy in Athletic Training. Laboratory time for practical applications including prosected cadavers, surface anatomy, osteology, radiology, functional analysis of movement, applied clinical anatomy and sports application. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Performance and Technology in Athletic Training
courses.desc: Grounded in return-to-competition decision making, the course material covers all aspects of sport performance including nutrition and methods of physical training. Technologies are integrated in movement analyses to help quantify athletic movements and support clinical decisions. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Pharmacology for Sports Medicine
courses.desc: Explores the pharmaceutical and chemical processes of therapeutic interventions and therapies. This course examines the constraints placed on patients in the performance environment as well management, protocols, and legal issues. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions I
courses.desc: Theories and application methods of comprehensive therapeutic treatment, modalities and rehabilitation programs for injuries commonly sustained by the physically active to the lower extremity. The first course in a series of three courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions II
courses.desc: Theories and application methods of comprehensive therapeutic treatment, modalities and rehabilitation programs for injuries commonly sustained by the physically active to the upper extremity. The second in a series of three courses. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions III
courses.desc: Theories and application of methods of comprehensive manual therapy and joint manipulation techniques for the treatment of athletic injuries. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Healthcare Administration and Leadership in Athletic Training
courses.desc: Exploration of the aspects of athletic training leadership styles, organization and administration. This course focuses on program leadership, risk management, policy and procedure development, and organizational operations. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Research
courses.desc: This course explores quantitative and qualitative research methodologies used in athletic training and evaluation of published research in the field, including but not limited to: quality improvement projects, novel research, case studies, and systematic reviews. The first course of this series involves developing and completing a practice-based research project, culminating in the creation and submission of research abstracts. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Seminar in Athletic Training
courses.desc: This course provides an opportunity for students to engage in conversations with clinical experts focused on transition to clinical practice. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ATEP
courses.title: Research Capstone in Athletic Training
courses.desc: This course explores quantitative and qualitative research methodologies used in athletic training and evaluation of published research in the field, including but not limited to: quality improvement projects, novel research, case studies, and systematic reviews. The second course of this series involves disseminating a practice-based research project, culminating in the creation of a final written document and presentations. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Seminar/Workshop
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., CHMY 143N. An introduction to important advances in biochemistry through readings from the primary literature and discussion of this literature. Faculty members will also make presentations on their research. Graded credit/no credit.

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Biochemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., CHMY 223 or BIOB 260. Fundamental biochemistry; chemistry and metabolism of biomolecules, energy relationships in metabolism; storage, transmission, and expression of genetic information. Credit not allowed for both BCH 380 and 480-482.

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Advanced Biochemistry I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 223. Primarily for science majors. The chemistry of biomolecules, with emphasis on the structure and function of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids. The chemistry and regulation of the transfer and expression of genetic information, protein synthesis. Credit not allowed for both BCH 380 and 480-482. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Advanced Biochemistry II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BCH 480. Continuation of BCH 480. Enzyme kinetics, metabolism, especially macromolecule biosynthesis and energy acquisition pathways, and the associated energetics and molecular physiology. Credit not allowed for both BCH 380 and BCH 480-482. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Biochemistry Research Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BCH 380 or BCH 480. Restricted to students in the Biochemistry or Chemistry majors or minors. Other students will be allowed to enroll on a space-available basis with the consent of the instructor. Applications of biochemical principles to modern protein biochemistry. Basic micro- and molecular-biology techniques are used to produce mutant proteins; then students learn basic and advanced biophysical techniques to characterize the mutant proteins. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-10) Offered every term. Independent research under the direction of a faculty member. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BCH

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Internship/Cooperative Ed
courses.desc: (R-15) Extended non-classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Senior Thesis/Capstone
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Restricted to students with senior standing. Preparation of a thesis or manuscript based on undergraduate research for presentation and/or publication. Student must give an oral or poster presentation at the Undergraduate Research Symposium or a scientific meeting. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Graduate Student Data Club: Molecular & Biomedical Science
courses.desc: (R-14) Focus on experimental design, methods, and presentation of experimental results for graduate students in laboratories with a molecular, cellular or chemical biological focus. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: RNA Structure & Function
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered every semester. Prereq., BCH 482 & BIOB 260. Exploration of current scientific literature and new data that focuses on RNA biochemistry. Emphasis on literature relevant to research on RNA viruses and ribosomes and protein synthesis. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Intro to Research
courses.desc: (R-2) Offered autumn and spring. Required course for Biochemistry and Biophysics graduate students. Students are acquainted with faculty research projects. Instruction in basic research techniques, research equipment. Introduction to relevant scientific research literature. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Physical Biochemistry
courses.desc: Offered spring odd-numbered years. Techniques of physical chemistry used in studying biological structure and function of macromolecules. Emphasis is on spectroscopic methods, hydrodynamic methods and x-ray and other scattering and diffraction techniques. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Proteins and Enzymes
courses.desc: Offered autumn even-numbered years. Prereq., BCH 482. An investigation into the structure/function relationship in proteins and a detailed exploration of enzyme kinetics, using examples from current literature. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Nucleic Acids
courses.desc: Offered autumn odd-numbered years. Prereq., BCH 482. Emphasis on critical reading of current literature that investigates structure, chemistry, and function of nucleic acids. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Research
courses.desc: (R-40) Offered autumn and spring. Directed individual research and study appropriate to the background and objectives of the student. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-24) Offered intermittently. Requires graduate standing and consent of instructor. Experimental offerings of new courses by resident or visiting faculty. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Thesis
courses.desc: (R-10) Offered intermittently. Restricted to students in the Biochemistry and Biophysics M.S. program. Laboratory research for and preparation of a master's thesis. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Cell Organization & Mechanisms
courses.desc: Offered spring even-numbered years. Prereq., BCH 480. Primary literature exploration of the regulation of structure, function, and dynamics of eukaryotic cells. Topics include membranes, cytoskeleton, transcription, translation, signal transduction, cell motility, cell proliferation, and programmed cell death. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Biochemistry & Biophysics Seminar
courses.desc: (R-14) Credit/No credit only. Presentation of current research in Structural Biology, Biochemistry, Biophysics, or related fields by invited outside speakers, UM faculty, and senior graduate students. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BCH
courses.title: Dissertation
courses.desc: (R-20) Offered intermittently. Restricted to doctoral students in Biochemistry & Biophysics. Laboratory research for and preparation of a doctoral dissertation. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Introductory Ecology
courses.desc: Offered spring. An introduction to ecological principles, stressing the structure and function of natural communities and examining human's role in these ecosystems.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Field Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed one semester of college-level biology, chemistry, and mathematics. The principles and practices of the study of animals and plants in their natural environments, including human influences, with focus on the Crown of the Continent area of the Rocky Mountains and taught entirely outdoors.
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: General Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 272. Analysis of the distribution and abundance of plants and animals. Includes individual, population and community-level processes (e.g., population growth and regulation, competition, predation, succession, nutrient cycling, energy flow and community organization).

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: General Ecology Lab (equivalent to 271)
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 161N, WRIT 101, and either STAT 216 or WILD 245. Prereq. or coreq., BIOE 370. Methods of describing and testing alternative explanations for patterns in nature. The use of scientific methodology in ecology.
courses.prereq: BIOB 161N, WRIT 101, and either STAT 216 or WILD 245

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Seminar/Workshop
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Preparatory readings and attendance at seminars on a wide variety of ecological and wildlife management topics followed by critiques.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Aquatic Microbial Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summer only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed one semester of college-level biology and chemistry and two semesters of college-level mathematics. This course is an immersive (2 week) summer class offered to both undergraduate and graduate students with interests in microbiology and ecology. The course includes lectures, laboratories, and several field-based sampling trips. The course provides conceptual foundation and hands-on field and laboratory training in modern methods in aquatic microbial ecology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summer only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BIOB 260 or BIOB 272. Comparative study of vertebrate morphology using evolutionary transitions among species to explore design and function. Laboratory includes systematic study of organ systems and workshops in the dynamics of biomechanics and functional morphology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Behavior & Evolution
courses.desc: Offered autumn, odd-numbered years. Prereq., BIOB 272. Diversity of animal behavior in an evolutionary context including inheritance of behavior, diets, avoidance responses, mating systems and sexual selection, parental care, and evolution of animal groups and societies. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Alpine Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed one semester of college-level biology, chemistry, mathematics, and ecology. Distribution, abundance and life cycles of plants and animals and their unique ecophysiological adaptations to life in the rigorous environments of the high mountains above the timberline, with emphasis on the Crown of the Continent area. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Freshwater Ecology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 160. Physical and chemical dynamics of lakes and streams. Diversity, distribution and dynamics of freshwater organisms. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Stream Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed two semesters of college-level biology and one semester of college-level mathematics, chemistry, and ecology. The biota and biogeochemical processes of running waters with unifying principles and contemporary research approaches. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Conservation Biology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed one semester of college-level biology and ecology. Concepts and approaches for sustaining biodiversity and other natural goods and services provided by terrestrial and aquatic systems. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Ecosystem Ecology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOO 105N or BIOE 172N. Introduction to systems thinking and the ecosystem concept, review of water and energy balances, carbon cycling, nutrient cycling, trophic dynamics, and species effects on ecosystem function across terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOO 105N or BIOE 172N

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Terrestrial Plant Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn, even-numbered years. Prereq., BIOE 172N or BIOE 342 or BIOE 370 or FORS 330. The interrelationships between plants and plant communities and their natural environment. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: BIOE 172N or BIOE 342 or BIOE 370 or FORS 330

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Landscape Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed two semesters of college-level biology and mathematics and one semester of college-level ecology and chemistry. Biophysical processes that determine landscape and ecosystem structure and function using remote sensing tools, geographic information systems and dynamic models to demonstrate landscape change. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Lake Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed two semesters of college-level biology and one semester of college-level chemistry, mathematics, and ecology. The physical, chemical and biological characteristics of lake ecosystems with an emphasis on nutrient cycling, food web interactions and water quality. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Forest and Fire Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Students taking this course should have completed two semesters of college-level coursework (sophomore standing). Patterns, processes, and disturbances of northern Rocky Mountain forests in the context of principles of population, community, landscape, and ecosystem ecology with particular emphasis given to ecology of wildfire. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summers only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Plant Evolution
courses.desc: Offered autumn, odd-numbered years. Prereq., BIOB 272 and either BIOO 335 (preferred ) or BIOO 320. Lecture, reading and discussion on the evolutionary processes that shape major patterns of plant diversity. Topics include but are not restricted to: local adaptation, floral and mating system evolution, polyploidy, genome evolution, and speciation. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: BIOB 272 and either BIOO 335 (preferred ) or BIOO 320

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Advanced Undergrad Research
courses.desc: (R-10) Offered every term. Restricted to students with junior or senior standing. Independent research under the direction of a faculty member. Graded credit/no credit. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered intermittently. Presentations by student, faculty, and associates on issues and topics in their field. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Discover Biology
courses.desc: Offered every term. Offered on Mountain Campus and at Missoula College. Contemporary exploration of the organization and complexity of living organisms and the systems in which they live. The central questions of biology -- the relationship between form and function, acquisition and use of energy, and continuity between generations will be addressed through lectures and laboratory investigations.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Montana Ecosystems
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. An introduction to the landscapes and ecosystem diversity of Montana, with an emphasis on exploring the dominant habitats of western Montana. Required, integrated laboratory includes field trip investigations, classroom lab exercises, and presentations.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Apprentice-Level Beekeeping
courses.desc: This course aims to teach the basic beekeeping of honey bees. Participants will gain a general knowledge of honey bee biology and how to care for honey bees throughout the year. Students will be taught how to recognize common honey bee ailments and pests and the methods for treating them. After completion, students will know how to manage honey bee colonies for maximum bee health and honey production as well as a general understanding of basic insect biology.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Principles of Living Systems
courses.desc: Offered every term. Non-science majors are encouraged to take either BIOB 101N (Discover Biology) or BIOB 170N (Principles of Biological Diversity) instead of BIOB 160. Unifying principles of biological structure-function relationships at different levels of organization and complexity. Consideration of reproduction, genetics, development, evolution, ecosystems, as well as the inter-relationships of the human species to the rest of life. Students requiring a laboratory should also register for BIOB 161N.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Principles of Living Systems Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn and summer. Coreq. or prereq., BIOB 160. Lab experiences illustrate biological principles underlying growth, reproduction, development, genetics and physiology, and are designed to give students practice in scientific methods of description, development of hypotheses, and testing.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Principles of Biological Diversity
courses.desc: Offered spring. Survey of the diversity, evolution and ecology of life including prokaryotes, viruses, protista, fungi, plants and animals.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Principles of Biological Diversity Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or Coreq., BIOB 170N. The diversity of life including prokaryotes, viruses, protista, fungi, plants and animals including structure and evolutionary relationships.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Your Future in Biology
courses.desc: Your Future in Biology is a one-credit seminar that will introduce students to the diverse set of careers that are available with a biology degree. Interactions with the instructor and visiting speakers will highlight the suite of skills that a degree in biology provides and that are required to tackle crucial challenges in healthcare, genomics, biotechnology, environmental science, conservation, and other biology-focused careers. Students will directly engage with world-class researchers and successful professionals using their training in biology to solve important problems and to provide essential services to society. Along the way, speakers will share their personal stories and academic journeys to help students better understand the many pathways to success with a degree in biology. Students will also interact regularly with members of the Division of Biological and Biomedical Sciences, including the Associate Dean, to help them establish meaningful and lasting connections at UM. Graded credit/no-credit only.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of learning during placement off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Communicating Biology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Offered at Missoula College. An examination of modern methods for sharing scientific discovery with an emphasis on biological issues related to the human experience.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Our Environment & Us
courses.desc: This course approaches the topic of environmental ethics from a biology perspective. We will discuss the specific environmental consequences of human behavior as well as their potential ethical implications. It is largely a readings and writings class, although some lecture material will be presented, and assigned readings and thoughtful written responses will constitute a significant portion of the coursework. The class is divided into four units. In the first unit, we will explore concepts related to the value of the natural world: anthropocentrism, instrumental and intrinsic value, moral importance of species, environmental stewardship, and ecological sabotage. The second unit will delve into the ethics involved in our interaction with animals: animal moral worth, well-being, and the morality of animal use in research, meat consumption, factory farming, and animal captivity for conservation and education. The third unit centers on climate change topics: the grave complexity of biological consequences, strategies such as the polluter-pays approach, personal responsibility, indigenous viewpoints, technological solutions, and rejection of climate science. In the last unit, we will cover issues related to future human generations: ethical considerations of having kids, excess consumption, population growth, and what is the moral value of unborn generations.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Journeyman-Level Beekeeping
courses.desc: Prereq., BIOB 125. This course will cover topics such as the honeybees’ interaction and relation to native pollinators and the plants they work with as well as a look into pesticide uses and truths. The student will be given detailed instruction on the honeybees’ internal anatomy and structures and the uses of their unique external anatomy. Students will learn to use the microscope and understand how it is used in diagnosing insect diseases and pests. By the end of the course, students will understand the honeybees’ place in the ecosystem and how their unique anatomy contributes to their interactions with the world both inside and outside the hive.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: General Science: Chemical & Life Sciences
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or coreq., M 132. Integrated lectures, laboratory exercises, and field trips on topics in chemical and biological science for prospective elementary school teachers and the non-scientist. Two two-hour laboratory sessions are required each week.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Cellular and Molecular Biology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and summer. Prereq., BIOB 160 (preferred) or BCH 110/BCH 111 (preferred) or B- or higher in BIOH 112; and either CHMY 123 or CHMY 143N. Analytical exploration of the structure and function of the cell, the fundamental unit of life, with an emphasis on energy transformations and information flow. Topics include molecular building blocks, membranes, organelles, and mechanisms of replication, gene expression, metabolism, signal transduction, cell birth, cell death, and cell differentiation.
courses.prereq: BIOB 160 (preferred) or BCH 110/BCH 111 (preferred) or B- or higher in BIOH 112; and either CHMY 123 or CHMY 143N

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Genetics and Evolution
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., either BIOB 260; OR both BIOB 160 and BIOB 170N; OR just BIOB 160 with a B- or better; AND one of M 121, 122, 151, 162, or 171; OR Maplesoft Pre-Calculus>=10; OR Maplesoft Algebra>=17; OR EdReady Math placement level 4. Principles and mechanisms of inheritance and evolution. Population genetics, fossil record, macroevolution, speciation, extinction, systematics, molecular evolution.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Natural Beekeeping: Integrating Honey Bee Ecology into Modern Beekeeping
courses.desc: Prereq., BIOB 125. This course introduces a method of beekeeping that, as best we can, emulates how bees naturally occur in nature while promoting the practices that qualify us as beekeepers, not just people with a hive in the backyard. This course is designed to introduce the beekeeper to a method of beekeeping that incorporates the behaviors and preferences of naturally nesting colonies into managed beekeeping practices.

courses.title: Developmental Biology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 260. BIOB 272 is recommended. An analysis of the origin and development of form and patterns in organisms, stressing the processes of growth and differentiation in plants and animals. Graded traditional letter grade only.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Master-Level Beekeeping
courses.desc: Prereq., BIOB 225. The Master course is the third and final level in the Master Beekeeping curriculum. It offers a more detailed look into bee flight, anatomy, and reproduction, discusses bee pheromones and genetics, and provides templates for record-keeping for improved bee management. The course also covers hive products, bee nutrition, selection of apiary locations, and basic principles for conducting your own experiments. By the end of the course, students will have a better understanding of advanced bee management and an introduction to the beekeeping business. They should be ready to develop and maintain healthy hives for hobbyists and larger-scale endeavors.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: General Genetics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 260 and 272. This course will focus on the molecular genetics of eukaryotes, with special emphasis on transmission genetics and gene structure and regulation.

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Immunology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 260. Current concepts and methods in Immunology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Immunology Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq. or coreq., BIOB 410. Modern techniques for analysis of immune responses. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Advanced Cellular & Molecular Biology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 260 and BIOB 272. BCH 380 or BCH 480 is strongly recommended. Cell structure and function, cell cycle, cellular signaling, molecular basis of cancer, regulated cell death, membrane transport, organelle dynamics, cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, and the molecular basis of learning and memory. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Comparative Animal Physiology
courses.desc: Offered Spring. Prereq., BIOB 260. Animal physiology with emphasis on diversity of functional processes, with strong links to broader ecological and evolutionary contexts. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Molecular Analysis of Development
courses.desc: Offered alternate spring semesters. This course covers key topics in developmental biology through the detailed study of the primary literature. Seminar topics are updated for each year the course is offered and listed in syllabus. With help of the instructor, the students present each topic and lead a discussion each class period based on the assigned research paper and one or two review articles to provide background on the topic. CR/NCR only (no letter grade). Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Endocrinology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BIOB 260 and BIOB 272. Integration of fundamental concepts of endocrinology (such as hormone release, hormone transport and receptor activation) into complex systems (such as reproduction). Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Conservation Genetics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 272. Genetic basis for solving biological problems in conservation including the genetics of small populations, the application of molecular genetic techniques to conservation biology and case studies of the application of genetics to conservation problems. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Phylogenetics and Evolution
courses.desc: Offered autumn semester, odd-numbered years. Prereq., BIOB 260 and BIOB 272. Phylogenies, or evolutionary trees, provide insights into the history of life on Earth, including our own origins. This course focuses on the theoretical foundations of popular methods of reconstructing phylogenies from molecular sequence data and how to implement these methods with computational software for real data sets. Other current methods for testing evolutionary hypotheses with sequence data will also be introduced. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Genomics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 272. Principles and mechanisms of genome biology of animals and microbes, including genome function, evolution, and basic molecular and computational methodology used in genome biology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.title: OBE Core Course - Genetics and Evolution
courses.desc: Offered every other autumn. Exploration of the fundamental concepts and approaches in evolutionary biology, functional biology and evolutionary genetics with evolutionary ecology woven throughout. Lectures and discussions, with an emphasis on primary literature, classic and contemporary. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: OBE Core Course - Ecology
courses.desc: Offered alternate years. Broad overview of population and community ecology. Lectures and discussions, introducing theoretic foundations and exploring classic and more recent empirical tests of ecological theory with relevant topics in evolutionary ecology and functional biology woven throughout. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Plant-Consumer Interactions
courses.desc: Offered alternate years. Prereq., BIOE 370. Ecology and evolution of plant-consumer interactions. Review of classic and contemporary literature on plant-consumer interactions. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Readings in Morphology, Physiology, and Zoology
courses.desc: (R-8) Review and discussion of current literature in the fields of morphology, physiology, and ecology. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Physiological Plant Ecology
courses.desc: Offered alternate years. Prereq., BIOE 370 and BIOO 433. The physiological basis of plant adaptation and response to the environment. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOB
courses.title: Electron Microscopy Lab
courses.desc: (R-6) Practical laboratory experience in the preparation of various samples and hands-on operation of the transmission and/or scanning electron microscopes. Level: Graduate

Seminar topics are updated for each year the course is offered and listed in syllabus. With help of the instructor, the students present each topic and lead a discussion each class period based on the assigned research paper and one or two review articles to provide background on the topic. Graded CR/NCR only. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Basic Human Biology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Missoula College. A one semester course with laboratory focusing on learning scientific principles and a general understanding of human functional anatomy and physiological processes.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Basic Human Biology Laboratory
courses.desc: Missoula College. Basic human biology lab is required laboratory for students enrolled in BIOH 104N. Lab activities provide hands-on, investigative instruction in the fundamentals of anatomy and physiology of the human body. Exploration of anatomy using models, preserved materials and demonstrations reinforces principals taught in accompanying lecture.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Form and Function I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Explores the fundamentals of structure and function at basic cellular and tissue levels, in addition to the anatomy and physiology of the integumentary, musculoskeletal, and nervous systems.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Form and Function II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Explores the fundamental structures and functions of the endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy & Physiology I
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Restricted to students in the following majors: Missoula College Health Professions and Pre-Health Professions majors, Medical Information Technology, Pre-Physical Therapy, Athletic Training, Integrative Physiology, and Health & Human Performance. Introductory science course or college-prep high school biology course recommended. Comprehensive knowledge of human form and function necessary for students preparing for health-related professions. Emphasis on structure, function and homeostatic regulation of body systems with presentation of basic concepts in chemistry and microbiology as they relate to human anatomy and physiology. Covers tissues through nervous system. Required, integrated laboratory includes some dissection.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Coreq., BIOH 201N. Restricted to students in the following majors: Missoula College Health Professions and Pre-Health Professions majors, Medical Information Technology, Pre-Physical Therapy, Athletic Training, Integrative Physiology, and Health & Human Performance. Gen Ed Attributes: Natural Science Lab Course (N)Required companion laboratory for BIOH 201N. Comprehensive study of tissues and gross human anatomy necessary for students in health-related programs. Emphasis on typical structure and function as they relate to health. Topics include tissues through nervous system. Laboratory activities include some dissection and study of human cadaver.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., BIOH 201N. Coreq., BIOH 212N. Restricted to students in the following majors: Missoula College Health Professions and Pre-Health Professions majors, Medical Information Technology, Pre-Physical Therapy, Athletic Training, and Health & Human Performance. Comprehensive knowledge of human form and function necessary for students in health-related programs. Emphasis on structure function and homeostatic regulation of body systems with presentation of basic concepts in chemistry and microbiology as they relate to human anatomy and physiology. Covers endocrine through reproductive systems. Required integrated laboratory includes frequent dissection.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Coreq., BIOH 211N. Restricted to students in the following majors: Missoula College Health Professions and Pre-Health Professions majors, Medical Information Technology, Pre-Physical Therapy, Athletic Training, and Health & Human Performance. Required companion laboratory for BIOH 211N. Basic knowledge necessary for students in health-related programs. Emphasis on normal anatomy and physiology with presentation of basic concepts in chemistry and microbiology as they relate to human anatomy and physiology. Covers endocrine through reproductive systems. A cadaver lab is included.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Health Professions I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 121N or CHMY 141N; BIOB 160 or BIOH 112 or 113. Introduction to basic cellular structure and function. The fundamental facts and concepts of the anatomy and physiology of cells and tissues, the integumentary, musculoskeletal, nervous and special senses with an emphasis on clinical application for students preparing for careers in health care. Laboratory component includes presentation of cadaver prosections and models.
courses.prereq: CHMY 121N or CHMY 141N; BIOB 160 or BIOH 112 or 113

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Health Professions I Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq. or coreq., BIOH 365. Laboratory-based instruction in the fundamental facts and concepts of the anatomy and physiology of cells and tissues, the integumentary, musculoskeletal, nervous and special senses with an emphasis on clinical application for students preparing for careers in health care. The laboratory uses cadavers and models.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Health Professions II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOH 365. The fundamental facts and concepts of the anatomy and physiology of the endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems with an emphasis on clinical application for students preparing for careers in health care.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Health Professions II Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or coreq., BIOH 370. Laboratory-based instruction in the fundamental facts and concepts of the anatomy and physiology of the endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems with an emphasis on clinical application for students preparing for careers in health care. The laboratory uses cadaver prosections and models.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of learning during placement off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Hematology
courses.desc: Offered spring, odd numbered years. Prereq., BIOH 365 or BIOH 201N. This course is intended to introduce the student to normal and pathologic hematology, with emphasis on blood cell development, cellular components, and normal vs. abnormal morphology. Clinical laboratory testing will be presented as a way to diagnose and monitor disease progression. Normal and pathologic coagulation will likewise be addressed. Treatment options for disease states will also be covered. Laboratory exercises will instruct the student in proper specimen collection, preparation of peripheral blood smears, microscopic examination of blood smears, and other manual tests associated with blood and coagulation studies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Genes and Development Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring semester odd years. Prereq., BIOB 260. BIOB 272, BIOB 301, and BIOB 375 are recommended. This is a laboratory course that will introduce the students to the tools and methods for investigating how genetic information drives animal development and to using model organisms for studying genes associated with human disease. Students will gain practical experience in experimental design, data collection, results analysis, and scientific communication. Students will perform research independently or in a small group as well as attend formal classroom presentations and discussion. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I Tutor
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOH 365 with a minimum grade of B. This select group of students performs tutoring for students enrolled in BIOH 365 and assists in preparation and grading of lecture and laboratory course teaching materials. Students enrolled in BIOH 461 have the option of co-enrolling in the cadaver dissection course. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: BIOH 365 with a minimum grade of B

courses.subject: BIOH
courses.title: Principles of Medical Physiology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., WRIT 101; and BIOH 365, 370, and either CHMY 123 or 143N with a minimum grade of C. An advanced course in human physiology for students preparing for careers in health care. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: WRIT 101; and BIOH 365, 370, and either CHMY 123 or 143N with a minimum grade of C

Students enrolled in BIOH 463 have the option of co-enrolling in the cadaver dissection course. Level: Undergraduate

Students enrolling for the 4 credit option will also provide occasional comparable assistance for BIOH 112. Level: Undergraduate

Students enrolling for the 4 credit option will also provide occasional comparable assistance for BIOH 113. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbiology for Health Sciences
courses.desc: Offered spring and summer. Infectious diseases, including concepts of virulence, resistance, prevention and control of microbial diseases in the individual and in the community. If laboratory experience is desired, the student may enroll concurrently in BIOM 251. Credit not allowed toward a major in microbiology.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbiology Health Sciences Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 250N. Observation of live microorganisms, their characteristics and activities. Experience with microbiological techniques. Credit not allowed toward a major in microbiology.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Vector-Borne Diseases: Public Health Perspectives
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. An exploration of major vector-borne diseases including Lyme disease, malaria, dengue fever, yellow fever, Zika, etc. Lectures will cover disease history, biology and transmission dynamics, geographic and demographic trends, intervention strategies, and relationships to climate change. Students will be encouraged to bring perspectives from any major field of study to discussions of the public health challenges of vector-borne diseases in the 21st century.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: General Microbiology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and summer. Prereq., CHMY 123 or 143N. Prereq. or coreq., BIOB 260. Microbial structure and function, growth and reproduction, physiology, ecology, genetics, environmental factors, control of microorganisms and sterility, antimicrobial agents, microbial diversity.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: General Microbiology Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 360. Basic microbiology procedures and techniques.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered every term. Independent research under the direction of a faculty member. Graded credit/no credit.

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Pathogenic Microbes
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOM 360. A study of the pathogenic bacteria and fungi and the diseases they produce. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Pathogenic Microbes Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOM 361. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 402. Laboratory study of pathogenic bacteria and fungi. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Clinical Diagnosis
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOM 360 & BIOM 361; or BIOH 365 & BIOH 366; or BIOM 402 & BIOM 403 (may concur). Principles of blood chemistry, urinalysis, blood banking, serology and other clinical parameters of disease and health. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: BIOM 360 & BIOM 361; or BIOH 365 & BIOH 366; or BIOM 402 & BIOM 403 (may concur)

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Clinical Diagnosis Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 407. Clinical diagnostic methods. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbial Genetics
courses.desc: Offered spring even-numbered years. Prereq., BIOM 360 and BIOM 361. The molecular genetics of prokaryotic organisms including: structure and replication of the prokaryotic chromosome; gene expression; mutagenesis and DNA repair; plasmids and other tools of genetic engineering; transmission of genetic material and recombination in prokaryotes; regulation of gene expression in prokaryotes; recombinant DNA and biotechnology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Experimental Microbial Genetics Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring even-numbered years. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 410. Experiments in microbial genetics: Analysis of genes and genomes. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbial Diversity Ecology & Evolution
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 260. BIOB 272 and BIOM 360 are recommended. A broad overview of the physiological, phylogenetic and genomic diversity and ecology of microorganisms within a framework of general ecological principles. Focuses on microbial interactions with their environment at the level of the individual, population and community, including intimate associations with plants and animals. Surveys current methods for studying microbial ecology and diversity in the environment. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Host-Microbe Interactions
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BIOB 260 and BIOB 272. Many organisms on the planet are hosts that interact with a diversity of microbes. Understanding these interactions is crucial to explain patterns of biodiversity and to improve the quality of human life. This course explores the diversity of host-microbe interactions in nature using the primary scientific literature as our guide. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: General Parasitology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 272. Parasitism as a biological phenomenon, origin of parasitism, adaptations and life cycles, parasite morphology, fine structure, physiology, parasites and their environment. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: General Parasitology Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Coreq., BIOM 427. Taxonomy, morphology and identification of parasitic protozoa, helminths and arthropods. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Virology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOB 260. The general nature of viruses, with emphasis on the molecular biology of animal and human viruses. Co-convenes with BIOM 535. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbial Physiology
courses.desc: Offered autumn, odd-numbered years. Prereq., BIOM 360. Microbial structure and function, physiological diversity, microbial metabolism, role of microbial activity in the environment. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbial Physiology Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn, odd-numbered years. Prereq., BIOM 361. Prereq. or coreq., BIOM 450. Experimental approaches to analysis of microbial structure, composition and metabolism. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Ecology of Infectious Diseases
courses.desc: Offered spring. In this course, we will take an ecological approach to understand infectious diseases. We will examine how diseases spread through time and space, and examine mathematical models of disease spread and their usefulness in control strategies. We will discuss case studies of both human and animal diseases, and the ecological concepts that apply to a wide range of systems. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

Student must give an oral or poster presentation at the Biological Sciences Undergraduate Research Symposium or a scientific meeting. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Advanced Immunology
courses.desc: Offered autumn even-numbered years. Advanced topics and immunological techniques used in modern immunology. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Advanced Virology
courses.desc: Coreq., BIOB 592. A “principles-based” discussion of virology, focusing on the molecular processes and events that must be completed by all viruses for successful replication within an individual host, and spread through host populations. The molecular basis of alternative replication strategies, the interactions of viruses with hosts organisms, and how these interactions lead to disease will be presented with examples drawn from a representative set of more well-understood animal viruses. BIOM 535 emphasizes independent, creative, critical thought. Co-convenes with BIOM 435. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Microbial Pathogenesis
courses.desc: Offered fall. Current concepts in pathogenesis at the molecular and cellular levels. Focus is on microbial (virla, bacterial) and genetic factors leading to disease and the host's involvement in the process. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOM
courses.title: Experimental Microbial Ecology
courses.desc: Offered every term. Focus on experimental design, methods, and presentation of experimental results in the area of microbial ecology. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Introduction to Botany
courses.desc: Offered spring. Introduction to the plant kingdom including anatomy, physiology and ecology.

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: General Botany
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BIOB 260 and BIOB 272. Anatomy, morphology, ecology and physiology of photosynthetic organisms.

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Rocky Mountain Flora
courses.desc: Offered spring. A prior college-level course in biology is recommended. Systematics of vascular plants with primary focus on flowering plant diversity and regionally important taxonomic groups. This integrated lecture and laboratory emphasizes applying general botanical terminology, characterizing major plant groups to recognize them without keying and understanding their functions (ecology) and origins (evolution), and the use of dichotomous keys for plant identification down the species level.

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Biology and Management of Fishes
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 272 and either STAT 216 or WILD 240. Diversity, adaptations and ecology of fishes. Analysis and management of fish populations and communities.
courses.prereq: BIOB 272 and either STAT 216 or WILD 240

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Field Work/Clinical/Practicum
courses.desc: (R-12) Field work, clinical, or practicum experience in the biological sciences.

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Plant Physiology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BIOB 260. The molecular, biochemical and biophysical basis of plant function, from the subcellular to the whole organism level. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Plant Physiology Lab
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq. or coreq., BIOO 433. Laboratory exercises designed to familiarize students with concepts and techniques in plant physiology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Entomology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq. or coreq., BIOB 272. The classification, morphology, anatomy, development, life-history, behavior and ecology of insects. Labs include identification of major insect groups, internal and external anatomy and student collections. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Ornithology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., or corequisite BIOB 272. The classification, structure, evolution, behavior and ecology of birds. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Mammalogy
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 272. The evolution, systematics, anatomy, physiology and ecology of mammals. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOO
courses.title: Advanced Undergrad Research

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Ecosystem Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn every other year. This course includes the fundamentals of an ecosystem approach to ecological research by emphasizing relationships among physical, chemical, and biotic elements of interactive systems. It will provide a fundamental basis for more advanced Systems Ecology courses (e.g., Limnology, Integrated Systems Ecology, Landscape Genetics, etc.). Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Integrated Systems Ecology
courses.desc: Offered spring semester alternate years. Principles, theories and empirical studies that describe the complex attributes and processes of coupled natural and human systems. Landscape, climate, economic and social change dynamics and processes emphasized. Flagship course of the UM-DBS Systems Ecology Program. Students strongly advised but not required to take BIOS 532 Fundamentals of Ecosystem Ecology prior to this course. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BFIN
courses.title: Financial Management
courses.desc: Restricted to students in College of Business Graduate Programs. This MBA course in Corporate Finance provides a comprehensive foundation in the principles and practices essential to financial decision-making within a corporation. Students begin with an overview of financial statements and cash flow analysis, progressing to performance evaluation using financial models. Core topics include discounted cash flow valuation, net present value, and investment decision rules. The course also covers equity valuation techniques and the relationship between risk and return. Advanced modules explore the cost of capital, capital structure decisions, and the strategic use of debt. Students will develop an understanding of short-term financial planning, capital raising, and the broader implications of financing choices on firm value. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on applying theory to real-world corporate finance problems.

Business majors are advised to register for this course their freshman year.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Issues in Sustainability
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. This literature-intensive course is intended to expose the student to a variety of essays addressing the balance of economic development with the principles of sustainability and social equity. The student is offered an introduction to sustainability concepts, natural systems/cycles, and environmental economics. Natural capitalism and triple bottom line maximization are explored along with the role of corporations and small businesses in sustainable development. A survey of issues surrounding corporate social responsibility and sustainability-driven innovation will be conducted.

It also addresses organizations and their relationship to the external environment, the law, and various stakeholders.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Business Models and Operations
courses.desc: Offered all semesters. Prereq., or corequisite one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. Operations are the activities of a business where products in the form of goods or services are produced. Inputs in the form of material, labor, capital, energy, and ideas are transformed by these activities into products to serve the needs of customers. This course will foster understanding of how operations integrate with finance, marketing, management, accounting, and management information systems to produce goods and services. This end-to-end conception of a business will focus on different models of the business to achieve this productive integration. Students will learn various means of production, methods of integration with other business functions like finance and marketing, and explore in depth specific topics like the management of projects, supply chains, inventory, and quality. Team projects will be assigned where students develop an integrated production system.

We cover a range of topics including building value-added relationships, sales techniques, managing objections, servicing customers, account management, and negotiating contracts, among others. The Situation-Problem-Implication-Need Payoff (SPIN) consultative sales method is taught.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: People, Process and Technology I
courses.desc: Offered all semesters. Prereq., ACTG 201, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. The course is designed to prepare College of Business students for the future of work that is characterized by automation, artificial intelligence, technology and innovation, creative disruptions, and the necessary human mindset and behaviors required to be successful in that environment. Specifically, this course focuses on 1) the process of data-driven decision-making 2) the practice of individual human behaviors influencing the data-driven decision-making 3) to understand how business leaders can leverage people, processes, and technology to facilitate organizational change, and 4) to analyze data and communicate results to business leaders 5) the importance of a growth mindset.
courses.prereq: ACTG 201, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: People, Process and Technology II
courses.desc: Offered all semesters. Prereq., ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, BGEN 341, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. This course is the second in the People, Process, and Technology sequence. Our goals are to explore and develop our understanding of how business leaders can foster an agile organization, identify tools and techniques to effectively lead organizational change, and equip ourselves to be confident, ethical technology users and decision makers.
courses.prereq: ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, BGEN 341, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201

courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. Analysis of business in diverse parts of the globe. Examines the impact of socio-economic, political, legal, educational, and cultural factors on management.

Topics include the nature and sources of law, courts and procedure, contracts, employment, the Uniform Commercial Code, property, environmental law, business organizations, tort liability, insurance, consumer and creditor protection, bankruptcy, criminal law, and agency law.

courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Restricted to students in College of Business graduate programs. This course provides an overview of the functional areas of business and how the functional areas connect to professional careers in business analytics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Foundations of Accounting and Finance
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course covers both accounting and finance. The accounting portion introduces key financial statements—income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements—along with accruals and revenue recognition principles, equipping students to assess an organization’s financial health. The finance portion builds on basic economics, covering financial markets, ratios, capital structure, and budgeting, helping students make informed decisions on investments and financial resource management. The course also explores financial assets, markets, and interest rates, providing a comprehensive foundation in accounting and finance.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Graduate Sustainable Business Practices
courses.desc: In today’s business environment, managers are expected not only to generate profits and jobs but also to create social and environmental value. This course explores how companies balance profitability with sustainability, examining strategies and practices that align business value creation with societal and environmental expectations. Students will gain insight into sustainable business practices, ethical frameworks, and emerging opportunities in socially responsible enterprise. Professionals with sustainability expertise are in high demand, offering both personal and career advancement potential. Co-convenes with BMGT 410. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Applied Business Statistics
courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course is a three-hour graduate level offering covering introductory topics in statistical methods. Students will learn topics from descriptive analytics, hypothesis testing, data visualization, unsupervised analytical methods, categorical data analysis, and linear and non-linear regression models. The class will be taught in the statistical software package R, using RStudio as the user-friendly interface. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Graduate Introduction to Business Analytics
courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course introduces the terminology and application of big data and data analytics. Students will complete cases in a variety of disciplines as they become acquainted with some of the software, tools, and techniques of data analytics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Management Foundations
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course introduces basic management principles, covering key concepts such as strategic planning, goal-setting, leadership, motivation, giving feedback, and reward systems. Drawing on insights from both theory and practice, the course explores how and why people think, feel, and act within organizational settings, equipping students with the tools to effectively manage and lead teams.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Data Literacy
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course explores the fundamental role of data in organizations, emphasizing how accurate, accessible, and well-organized data drives decision-making. Students will gain a broad understanding of data literacy, including management information systems, cloud computing, data security, and reliable access. The course also covers data analytics, focusing on transforming data into actionable information using tools like Excel. Additionally, students will explore the applications and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence (AI) in business.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Marketing & Operations: An Integrated Supply Chain Perspective
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course provides an integrated introduction to marketing and operations management principles with a focus on how organizations manage their supply chains. Students will explore key concepts in business strategy, operations management, supply chain management, and marketing, gaining a comprehensive understanding of how these areas work together to drive organizational success.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Business Communication
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course emphasizes the planning, writing, and revising of written correspondence. After completing the course, students will know how to collect information, focus on a topic, adapt voice for different purposes and audiences, and revise for clarity, brevity, and accuracy. The course will explore the topics of verbal, non-verbal, and visual communication, AI applications, and frequently used communication technologies.

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Introduction to SQL
courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course lays a technical foundation for work as an analyst or data scientist, teaching you the fundamentals of Structured Query Language (SQL). SQL is, simply, the way people interface with regular data. Being good at SQL is a pre-requisite for getting an analytics job and succeeding in a data-intensive job. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Graduate Introduction to Python
courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This is a graduate course covering Python fundamentals, including how to do basic programming for manipulating, analyzing, and visualizing a variety of datasets. In addition, the course explores modern workflows and tools for version control of code, leveraging open-source libraries, and using tools like Jupyter notebooks on local machines. The course assumes students have no prior programming experience and will start with fundamentals of the Python language and coding principles. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BGEN
courses.title: Sales and Negotiations
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. This course provides an integrated overview of personal selling, sales management, and negotiation. Students will learn practical sales techniques, explore sales force management, and develop negotiation strategies for a range of scenarios. Emphasis is placed on real-world application through exercises and simulations.

Human resource topics of selection, training, assessment, and compensation tools and strategies will be addressed heavily in this course.
