courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Entertainment and Sports Event Management
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., ACTG 202, BGEN 105S, and BMKT 325. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Open to non-business majors. Students are introduced to skills that are necessary for managing sports & entertainment events. Planning, marketing, sponsorship, budgeting, management, risk management, impacts, and evaluation of events are discussed. Students will participate in several live events.

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Principles of Entertainment & Sport Business
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., ACTG 202, BGEN 105S, and BMKT 325. This course introduces students to the fundamental aspects of the entertainment & sports industries in terms of functional areas of business, industry segments, and career readiness. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Entertainment & Sport Business
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BMGT 401 and BMGT 402. Students will participate in case studies and experiential learning projects with sport and entertainment industry partners on advanced entertainment topics. Topics include: artificial intelligence in sport & entertainment business, sustainability, labor relations, branding, agency relations and responsibilities, ticketing, and contracts. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Sustainable Business Practices
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. This course explores how changing perceptions around environmental and social issues influence current business practices. Through this exploration, we discuss the impact these influences have on business and how adept firms can gain competitive advantage through embracing and integrating them into their core strategies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Leadership and Motivation
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., BGEN 341. Study of fundamental concepts, theories, and models of leadership and motivation. Selected topics include: trait and behavioral theories of leadership, charismatic and transformational leadership, power and influence, emotions and justice perceptions in motivation, expectancy, and equity theories. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Leading Teams & Conflict Management
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., BMGT 341. This course teaches students essential skills in written, verbal, non-verbal, visual, and persuasive communication, building and equipping effective teams, providing coaching and feedback, relationship building and conflict management, mediation, and negotiation. There is an emphasis on skills practice through role play, simulations, and real life applications. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. This course focuses on starting and managing a growing business. Topics include recognizing business opportunities, setting strategy for the firm, raising capital, marketing new products, and organizing the managerial team. Students develop a business model canvas and/or write a business plan for themselves or for a local entrepreneur. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Advanced Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: (R-3) Offered spring. Prereq., or corequisite BMGT 448. Focus on managing and marketing a growing business, legal and technology issues for entrepreneurs, and financing new ventures. Students refine an existing or write a new business plan and participate in a business plan competition or write case analyses. UM instructors supervise course content delivered by local and regional experts in entrepreneurship. Four separate one credit weekend seminars are offered. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Global Operations and Supply Chain Management
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BGEN 222 and BMKT 325. The course introduces students to the challenges and opportunities companies face and how they manage the risk associated with the global supply chain. It provides an overview of global supply chain operations management as a field and describes the strategic role it has in today's intensely competitive business environment. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Cross-Cultural Management
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201. Study of issues related to cultural diversity within the workforce and the problems inherent in the management of a firm's activities on an international scale. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Global Operations and Supply Chain Management
courses.desc: Restricted to student in College of Business graduate programs. This course provides an understanding of how global supply chains (GSCs) impact national economies, businesses, and consumers. It covers the flow of materials and information across firms worldwide, from raw materials to end customers, integrating logistics, information systems, marketing, and operations management. Topics range from inventory management and sourcing decisions to the latest trends in GSCs driven by emerging technologies and shifting geopolitics. The course includes lectures, case studies, discussions, and guest speakers, with an emphasis on active participation and real-world applications. Co-convenes with BMGT 467. Level: Graduate

courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in the Master of Business Administration and Master of Accountancy programs. An introduction to strategic management with a focus on the analysis of the firm and its environment as the basis for strategic decision making. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Organizational Behavior
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in the Master of Business Administration or Master of Accountancy programs. Professionally oriented strategic overview of intrapersonal, interpersonal, and leadership skills for employees, management, and organizational designers. Topics include diversity, communication, motivation, groups/teams, culture and structure. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Human Resource Management
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in the College of Business. The role of human resource management is a crucial (and often misunderstood) part of an overall organizational strategy. Human resource management affects every employee in an organization, and a better understanding of this area will prepare students for success in their professional ambitions. This course is designed to help unravel the complexities of human resources within an organization and to help students understand the environment within which HRM occurs. A working knowledge of job design, recruitment, selection, training, development, and performance management are of relevance to the job seeker and will be addressed heavily in this course.

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Business Ethics
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Master of Business Administration program. This course is designed to acquaint students with the ethical implications of business decisions, policy, strategy, and operations. Students will learn how to (1) develop a system of ethics that will form the foundation for future ethical practices in business; (2) analyze specific contemporary issues in business for their ethical implications and content; and (3) challenge conventional thinking about ethics by introducing broad-based ethical principles and systems to enlighten and inform ethical thinking. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMGT
courses.title: Strategic Management Seminar
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered spring. Prereq., ACTG 605, BFIN 681, BMIS 674, BMGT 604, and BMGT 640. Coreq., MBA 603. Restricted to students in the Master of Business Administration or Master of Accountancy programs. Analysis of the firm within its industry and the structure of the industry; competitive positioning and competitor analysis; decision-making under conditions of uncertainty; developing a competitive advantage in international markets. Level: Graduate
courses.prereq: ACTG 605, BFIN 681, BMIS 674, BMGT 604, and BMGT 640

courses.subject: BMIS
courses.title: Linux Network Security
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., ITS 150, ITS 212 & ITS 222. This course requires students to have a basic knowledge of computers and networks that can come from courses offered in the Computer Science Department, the Management Information Systems Department, Missoula College, or through work experience. Business & MIS students should have completed the lower core. Knowledge of Linux in general is indispensable for students aspiring for careers in cyber security, information technology, and related fields. In today's business landscape, where technology underpins operations, secure and efficient network infrastructure is paramount. Linux, being widely used in enterprise environments and renowned for its reliability and flexibility serves as a robust platform for network management and security in enterprise environments. Mastery of Linux network administration not only enhances students' technical capabilities but also increases their employability and effectiveness in addressing the evolving challenges of cybersecurity and IT infrastructure management.

courses.title: Enterprise Systems and Emerging Technologies

Explores the evolution of technological infrastructures with an emphasis on strategic implications. Students develop an enterprise infrastructure and then examine innovations that allow for the design and development of products and services in a global business environment.

courses.subject: BMIS
courses.title: Ethical Hacking
courses.desc: Prereq., BMIS 364 or BMIS 471. This course is designed to prepare students for the mindset and skillset of an ethical hacker. Students will practice skills of scoping, executing, reporting on vulnerability assessments, recommending mitigation strategies, cleaning up the offense traces, and restore systems back to the original state. Students will be familiar with a variety of commonly used hacking tools with lots of hands-on labs and assignments/projects to learn how to effectively secure an organization against security attacks.

courses.title: Cybersecurity Operation Center
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BMIS 364 and BMIS 374. The purpose of this course is to introduce skills required to operate in a security operations center (SOC). Cyber operations specialists aid organizations to prevent, mitigate, identify, protect against, respond to, and analyze network anomalies and intrusions through transformative processes. This requires the development of two skillsets: 1) technical abilities related to the cyber infrastructure, and 2) interpersonal communication abilities within organizations through a writing component referred to as Writing in the Disciplines.

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Digitial Marketing & CRM
courses.desc: Offered spring. Offered at Missoula College. In today’s digital world, marketing isn’t just about reaching people; it is about guiding them through a journey. This course will explore how different digital marketing channels work together to attract, engage, and convert leads into customers. By the end of this course, students will have a strong understanding of the digital marketing ecosystem -- how SEO, paid ads, social media, email marketing, and other channels fit together; lead generation and nurturing -- how to attract potential customers and move them through the sales funnel; data-driven decision making -- using analytics to refine strategies and maximize ROI; customer journeys -- how people discover, consider, and decide to buy; marketing and sales interaction -- pptimizing the "warm handoff" of a lead from marketing to sales in an organization as well as the technologies that enable said tranasition. Key Topics include search engine optimization, paid advertising, social media marketing, affiliate and influencer marketing, content marketing, and CRM optimization. The course will include a mix of lectures, discussions, and hands-on projects and students will get real-world examples, case studies, and practical assignments that simulate actual marketing campaigns. Students should expect to analyze brands, create marketing strategies, and track digital performance.

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Sports Marketing
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. This course examines the marketing of sports products and non-sports products using sports as a platform. Topics include the use of traditional marketing strategies as well as the use of sponsorship strategies, including endorsements, venue naming rights, and licensing. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Integrated Online Marketing
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., BMKT 325. This course is and exploration and application of marketing communications principles to the internet environment. Students develop individual WordPress websites/blogs, learn about online marketing techniques, and complete online marketing and social media projects. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Marketing Analytics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BMKT 325. The purpose of this course is to learn about the importance and value of using new measurement tools in marketing and using related research and data to create compelling content. Students in this course are also challenged to bring actual ideas to life. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Logistics and Transportation
courses.desc: This course provides a practical managerial perspective on the main logistics areas, including transportation, distribution, inventory and order management, key operational and financial performance indicators, sustainable logistics practices, and an introduction to logistics technology. Students engage with logistics firms in practical applications and discuss current events. Co-convenes with BMKT 550. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Marketing Hi-Tech Production and Innovation
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., BMKT 325. This course explores the concepts and practices related to marketing in fast-paced environment; draws from a range and diversity of industries and contexts including the Internet. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Telling Stories with Data
courses.desc: Restricted to students with at least junior standing. This course explores how we turn data into stories that can be understood by a nontechnical audience. Students will work with both raw and summarized data from several industries. Co-convenes with BMKT 582. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Digital Media Execution
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BMKT 325. This course will provide students with a solid understanding of the digital marketing landscape and can help them differentiate themselves as digital marketers. Course will cover online marketing channels such as display ads, search engine marketing, Over-the-top (OTT), Native, media services, email marketing, video advertising, paid social media advertising, and mobile ads. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Prereq., BMKT 325. An experiential course in the strategy, research, and execution of an integrated marketing communications plan. Students’ work culminates in the American Association of Advertising's National Student Advertising Competition. Level: Undergraduate

Field-based, experiential courses that focus on international business topics, incl. the culture and business environment of important U.S. trading partners, such as China, Germany, or Italy. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: ACTG 201, ACTG 202, ECNS 201S, BGEN 222, BMIS 270, and one of STAT 216, SOCI 202, PSYX 222, or FORS 201

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Advanced Marketing Research
courses.desc: Prereq., BMKT 325 and STAT 216; or BMKT 560 and BMIS 326. Restricted to students in College of Business graduate programs. The purpose of the course is to learn how to provide information for better business decision making. Students study the different aspects of marketing research as it relates to business problems and develop a mindset that continually relies on information-based decisions. Level: Graduate
courses.prereq: BMKT 325 and STAT 216; or BMKT 560 and BMIS 326

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Marketing Management
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in the Master of Business Administration or Master of Accountancy programs. Marketing decisions faced by managers in a variety of business settings including large corporations, small businesses and not-for-profit organizations. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Applied Data Analytics
courses.desc: Prereq., BMKT 325 and STAT 216; or BMKT 560 and BMIS 326. This course applies statistical skills and technical expertise to real-world big-data business applications. Students will work with the tools of data science and hone their ability to answer business questions through the analysis of data. Level: Graduate
courses.prereq: BMKT 325 and STAT 216; or BMKT 560 and BMIS 326

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Advanced Applied Modeling
courses.desc: Prereq., BGEN 516. This course focuses on applied statistics, improving students' statistical fluency and modeling. We cover resampling statistics to solidify our basic statistical understanding, improve our programming, and learn this vital technique to understanding uncertainty. We cover linear regression modeling extensively in the next section of the course. The final half of the course covers applied predictive and explanatory modeling using cutting-edge tools from our statistical software package. This course has weekly programming assignments. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Big Data and Innovation
courses.desc: Prereq., BGEN 526, BGEN 516, and BGEN 505. An integration of Data Science theory and the actual practice of searching, sorting, relating, and deriving results from textual data. Students will be exposed to machine learning, natural language processing, as well as other computer assisted data mining techniques and then gain hands-on proficiency in the practice of data science using the software from data mining and document analysis vendors. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: MSBA Capstone Prep
courses.desc: Prereq., BGEN 505, BGEN 516, and BGEN 526. Restricted to graduate students. This course is the prequel to the capstone class that culminates the MS in Business Analytics. To set yourself up for success, you will spend five weeks finalizing your capstone topic, sourcing data, preparing the data for analysis, determining your research questions, and building an analysis plan. Additionally, this class will force you to produce multiple low-stakes writing assignments, building the habits that will propel you through the capstone.

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Topic vary. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: BMKT
courses.title: Capstone
courses.desc: Prereq., BGEN 516, BGEN 526, BGEN 631, BGEN 632, BMIS 625, BMKT 582, BMKT 670, and BMKT 689. Coreq., BMIS 601, BMKT 673, and BMKT 680. Using a project-based approach, the course enables students to synthesize domain knowledge, apply their technical skills, and convey results of their data analysis through data visualizations and clear written and oral communication skills to achieve an integrative perspective of business analytics. Level: Graduate
courses.prereq: BGEN 516, BGEN 526, BGEN 631, BGEN 632, BMIS 625, BMKT 582, BMKT 670, and BMKT 689

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Addictions and Diversity
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. This course required for students seeking to obtain their Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical and Addiction Studies and who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. Introduction to multicultural competencies where students will be exposed to the fundamentals of working with substance abusing and dependent individuals from the cultural impact of race, nationality, gender, age, sexual orientation, religion, and socio-economic status on the development and progression of alcohol/drug problems. Appropriate for students of Social Work, Psychology, community health, Business and Counseling students, Education, and those with an interest in diversity and addictions.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Field Work/Clinical/Practicum
courses.desc: (R-3) Offered intermittently. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., CAS 242. This field work placement focuses on prevention and will provide Chemical Addiction Studies students with direct experience working in community organizations where they will create and implement alcohol and drug prevention activities. May also be appropriate for students of Social Work, Psychology, Sociology, Community Health or those with an interest in learning about prevention practices with direct experience in community organizations.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Theories of Counseling
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Offered at Missoula College. This is an entry level survey course of various approaches to counseling and psychotherapy. The course is a mixture of lecture, discussion, experiential learning, demonstrations, role playing, viewing counseling sessions, and practice of the major contemporary models of counseling. Ethical and professional issues are also addressed.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Pharmacology and Addictions
courses.desc: Offered autumn semester through Missoula College. This online course will provide students with an understanding of the pharmacology involved in addiction, with emphasis on addiction behavior and counseling.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Fundamentals of Substance Abuse and Addiction
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. This course is for students seeking to obtain their Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical and Addiction Studies and who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. May also be appropriate for Students of Social Work, Psychology, Sociology, or Community Health.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Substance Abuse Counseling I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. This course is required for students seeking to obtain their Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical and Addiction Studies and who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. This course is created to provide students specific knowledge regarding the theories, research, and evidenced-based literature in the provision of addiction counseling services. Students will be introduced to the overall scope of the problems of addictions, professional characteristics and principles of addiction counselors, ethical and legal responsibilities of professional behavior, addiction counseling skills and competencies required to be addiction counselors.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Substance Abuse Counseling II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., CAS 243. This course is required for students seeking to obtain their Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical and Addiction Studies and who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. Meets specific State of Montana educational requirements associated with individual and group counseling for addiction, as well as ethics for addiction counselors. The course requires the student to draw upon the resources provided by experts. The course work significant amount of experiential application and counseling practice techniques.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Gambling and Gaming Disorders in Addiction Counseling
courses.desc: Offered spring at Missoula College. This course is part of a suite of courses leading to Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical Addiction Studies.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Co-Occurring Disorders-Assessment & Treatment Planning
courses.desc: Offered spring. Introduces students to Substance Use Disorders and co-occurring mental illness. Students will learn treatment protocols, and will learn how to work with individuals experiencing addiction and also have some other mental health issues. This is a Course that is part of a suite of courses that students can take to qualify for application to the Board of Behavioral Health for their ACLC (Addiction Counselor License Candidacy.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Addiction Assessment/Documentation/Treatment Planning
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. This course is required for students who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. Intended to provide a comprehensive education to meet State of Montana education requirements for Licensure in Addiction Counseling. Students will be trained in clinical assessment diagnosis, treatment planning and patient record documentation with the client who has substance use disorders. Students will complete experiential application of the materials.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Advanced Addiction Assessment/Treatment Planning and Documentation
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., or corequisite CAS 260. This course includes lectures, group work, applied activities, and written demonstration of addiction assessment skills, including addiction treatment planning and documentation. It is designed to provide advanced assessment, treatment planning and documentation education to those wishing to apply to become a Licensed Addiction Counselor.

courses.subject: CAS
courses.title: Field Work/Clinical/Practicum
courses.desc: (R-4) Offered intermittently. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., CAS 242. This course is offered for students seeking to obtain their Certificate of Technical Studies in Chemical and Addiction Studies and who wish to become Licensed Addiction Counselors in the State of Montana. This Field Work Placement focuses on addiction treatment and counseling activities. The student will work in the community under the supervision of an addiction treatment professional and be given the opportunity to witness and participate in alcohol and drug treatment counseling activities.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Preparation for Chemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., EdReady placement level 2; or SAT 530; or ACT 21; or Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 16; or Maplesoft Algebra score >=14; or M 090 (Introductory Algebra) w/ C+ or better. An introduction to concepts and calculations in chemistry that provides preparation for CHMY 141N. Not appropriate toward chemistry requirement in any major.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Introduction to Brewing Science
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., or corequisite BIOB 160 and CHMY 121N. Introduction and review of chemistry, biochemistry and microbiology fundamentals needed to complete CHMY 314.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Introduction to General Chemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., EdReady placement level 2.5; or SAT >= 540; or ACT >= 22; or UM Math Placement score >= 25; or M 121 (may be taken simultaneously) or a higher level mathematics course. This is the first semester of an introduction to the general, inorganic, organic, and biological chemistry series. It is intended for majors and programs that do not intend to take more than one year of chemistry or for students who require additional preparation before taking CHMY 141N.
courses.prereq: EdReady placement level 2.5; or SAT >= 540; or ACT >= 22; or UM Math Placement score >= 25; or M 121 (may be taken simultaneously) or a higher level mathematics course

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Introduction to General Chemistry Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq. or coreq., CHMY 121N. Restricted to students in the Missoula College Nursing program. A laboratory course emphasizing inorganic chemistry, quantitative relations and synthesis of inorganic and organic compounds.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Introduction to Organic and Biochemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., CHMY 121N or CHMY 141N. Second semester of an introduction to general, inorganic, organic and biological chemistry.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Introduction to Organic and Biochemistry Lab
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq. or coreq., CHMY 123. Laboratory to accompany CHMY 123.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: College Chemistry I
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., EdReady placement level 3; or SAT 560; or ACT 23; or Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14 ; or M 095 with a C+ or better and Chemistry Placement Exam score >= 13; or either CHMY 104 or CHMY 121N. Coreq. or prereq. CHMY 142N. For science majors and other students intending to take more than one year of chemistry. Properties of elements, inorganic compounds, liquid solutions, chemical equilibria and chemical kinetics.
courses.prereq: EdReady placement level 3; or SAT 560; or ACT 23; or Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14 ; or M 095 with a C+ or better and Chemistry Placement Exam score >= 13; or either CHMY 104 or CHMY 121N

courses.title: College Chemistry I Lab
courses.desc: Offered Autumn and Spring. Prereq. or coreq., CHMY 141N. Use of experimental methodologies, scientific questioning and hypothesis driven guided inquiry experiments to explore and understand important fundamental chemical and laboratory concepts including stoichiometry, measurements, molecular structure, and thermodynamics.

courses.title: Analytical Chemistry-Quantitative Analysis
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 143N and CHMY 144N. Classroom and laboratory work in gravimetric, volumetric, colorimetric and electrochemical methods of analysis; theory of errors; ionic equilibria in aqueous solutions.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Brewing Science
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 114; or BIOM 360, CHMY 311, and BCH 380 or BCH 480. Advanced malting and brewing chemistry, biochemistry, and microbiology, including lecture, laboratory, and practical components.

courses.title: Physical Chemistry-Quantum Chemistry & Spectroscopy
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., CHMY 373. Systematic treatment of the laws and theories relating to chemical phenomena.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Physical Chemistry-Kinetics & Thermodynamics
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 143N, M 172, and PHSX 222. Systematic treatment of the laws and theories relating to chemical phenomena.

Review of concepts from general chemistry. Student leaders mentor a team of general chemistry students in working toward constructing chemistry knowledge and developing problem-solving skills.

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 223. Theory and principles of inorganic chemistry and a systematic coverage of descriptive inorganic chemistry in the context of the periodic table. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., CHMY 224 and CHMY 373. Preparation of inorganic and coordination compounds. Isolation and characterization by ion exchange, column chromatography, IR, UV-VIS, derivatives, MP, and BP. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Advanced Organic Chemistry
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CHMY 221 and CHMY 223. In this course, students will study organic chemistry, including chemoinformatics, structure and conformation, acid-base properties, kinetics/thermodynamics, mechanisms and reactivity, and synthetic strategy and key reactions. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Chemoinformatics
courses.desc: Offered Spring in even years. Demonstration of the wide possibilities of chemical computer modeling through a series of lectures and guided programming/simulation projects. The course will cover structure representations, representation interconversions, structure/reaction database searching, and structure similarity searching, followed by methods for the prediction of bulk properties, structures, reaction mechanisms, biological activity predictions and the design of drugs. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Advanced Instrument Analysis
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., CHMY 311. Theory and use of instrumental methods in the study of analytical and physical chemistry. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Aquatic Chemistry
courses.desc: Offered autumn odd-numbered years. Prereq., CHMY 311. Application of chemical equilibria theory for understanding and modeling chemical processes in natural waters with an emphasis on spreadsheet computations. In depth examination of concepts such as pH, alkalinity, buffering, and solubility as they apply to natural waters. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Organic Spectroscopy
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Theory and interpretation of the NMR, IR, UV, and mass spectra of organic compounds with the goal of structure identification. Enrollment is capped at 16 for this course. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: FT-NMR Option for Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CHMY 221 and CHMY 222. Operation of the FT-NMR spectrometer and brief background of NMR spectroscopy. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Laboratory Safety
courses.desc: Offered autumn. This course is for students who plan to teach high school and middle school science. Legal responsibilities of teachers, awareness of laboratory hazards and how to manage those hazards, resources for information regarding laboratory hazards. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Forensic Research
courses.desc: Offered autumn, spring and summer. Laboratory investigations and research on forensic chemistry topics under the direction of a faculty member. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Forensic Research Seminar
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CHMY 421. Seminar speakers on forensic science topics in the areas of ethics, law, anthropology and criminology; tours of the Montana State Crime Laboratory. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered autumn, spring, and summer. Laboratory investigations and research in the laboratory of a faculty member. Level: Undergraduate

courses.title: Teaching Laboratory Chemistry
courses.desc: (R-3) Offered every semester. Prereq., CHMY 143N and CHMY 144N. Methods of peer-led learning as applied to general chemistry laboratory instruction. Review of concepts from general chemistry along with instruction in laboratory techniques, instrumentation, and data analysis. Student leaders mentor a group of general chemistry students in working toward constructing "hands-on" chemistry laboratory skills and developing data collection and problem-solving skills. Level: Undergraduate

courses.title: Internship/Cooperative Education

courses.subject: CHMY
courses.title: Senior Thesis/capstone
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., CHMY 490. Restricted to students with senior standing. Students complete and report on undergraduate research initiated in CHMY 490 or equivalent research experience. Reports are both oral and written. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Health Misinformation
courses.desc: We live in an amazing era in which it’s easier than ever to gather information. But what is accurate, what is misleading, and how can we tell the difference when it comes to health and illness? Health-related myths, assumptions, and flat-out lies not only trick people out of money but lead them to make bad healthcare decisions, which can lead to negative outcomes such as prolonged sickness and even premature death. This course will help students become a better healthcare consumers by exploring how health topics are properly, and improperly, communicated, and asking them to think critically about what we know, what we assume, and what we completely fabricate regarding health and illness. Throughout the semester, students will learn to identify misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation in several specific contexts, such as a) public health, including government regulations, oversight, and policies; b) corporate health communication, including the rise of the “Wellness” industry; c) misrepresentation of research results and health-related statistics; and e) interpersonal miscommunication about health. Case studies and true examples are used often to illustrate the idea that misinformation takes many forms. Along the way, students will learn new things about health, nutrition, healing, illness, and science, and will boost their health communication savviness by developing the critical thinking skills that will protect them from health-related myths, false assumptions, and flat-out lies. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify biased and inaccurate health-related information and critically analyze what makes it misleading; understand why health misinformation is out there and how it spreads; express ideas and academic knowledge in a coherent, complete way; have respectful, intelligent conversations about misunderstood health-related topics; and effectively work with others on a multiple-member team to complete a final project, which includes practicing team conflict management skills.

courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Communication principles and processes in cross-cultural environments. Non-Western cultures are emphasized by contrasting them to Western communication norms. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Communication in Nonprofit Organizations
courses.desc: Offered yearly. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Focuses on issues in nonprofit organizational communication at macro and micro levels. Topics include: organizational identity, change processes, public relations, fund-raising, advocacy, socialization, stress and burnout, board management and professionalization. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Communication and Technology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. This course takes a critical look at the influence of communication technologies on organizational communication. Students will examine how the world of work is changing due to new technologies and explore the social and ethical implications of technical innovation, adoption and use. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Risk, Crisis, and Communication
courses.desc: Offered every other year. This course explores the communicative dynamics that both prevent and cause organizational crisis. Through case studies, the class examines how people plan, communicate and make good decisions in high-risk situations, as well as how to manage crisis public relations effectively. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Organizations and Identity
courses.desc: Course explores a communication perspective on identity and investigates foundational questions relevant to all humans: “Who am I?” and “How should I act?” in the context of organizations. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: New Media Skills
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Students examine the role of social media in many high-profile case studies and apply key learnings from these examples to develop their own social media skills. Students will learn to use industry-standard tools to complete assignments that can become portfolio pieces that demonstrate their knowledge of using social media strategically. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Rhetorical Criticism and Theory
courses.desc: Offered yearly. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Introduction to study of rhetorical criticism and theory. Current theoretical and methodological issues and approaches explored. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Feminisms and Film
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Hollywood films are cultural artifacts that speak to the times in which they are made. In this class, we explore the intersection between US feminisms and films, focusing on films made during the second wave of feminisms as well as films that depict this history of the feminist movement. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Rhetoric of Women's Activism
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Explores the rhetoric surrounding contemporary women's social activism in the U.S. Topics include women's rights, women's liberation, consciousness raising as a rhetorical form, reproductive rights, sexuality, and intersections between gender, race, and class. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Research Methods
courses.desc: Offered once each year. Restricted to students in the Communication Studies major. Students are encouraged to take COMX 461 in conjunction with this course when it is offered. Introduction to the major types of communication research and the foundations of quantitative research methods. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Communication Research Seminar
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. This course should be taken in conjunction with COMX 460 or COMX 462. Application of quantitative and qualitative research methods to specialized contexts. Emphasis on direct student involvement in research activities. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Qualitative Research Methods
courses.desc: Students are encouraged to take COMX 461 in conjunction with this course when it is offered. Students will explore qualitative research methods commonly used in Communication Studies, including data collections like ethnography, focus groups and interviews, and analysis methods like grounded theory coding and content analysis. Working in small groups, they will plan, develop, conduct, write, and present an original qualitative research project. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Health Communication
courses.desc: Offered yearly. This course explores key findings in health communication research and practice, focusing on a wide range of media. As a survey course, it provides an overview of the field of health communication with attention to analysis and practice of health communication relationships and messages. It examines the literature and key health communication campaigns, messages and target audiences. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Communication for Social and Behavior Change
courses.desc: Aims to equip students with skills for using the power of communication to bring about positive change locally and globally in areas such as public health, sustainable development, and social justice. The course connects theory to practice in social and behavior change communication and introduces a wide array of implementation models and tool kits. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Social Interaction and Human Well-Being
courses.desc: Offered yearly. Examines theory and research on the health correlates of human interaction across the lifespan. Students learn how and why specific types of communicative activity relate to health and well-being outcomes. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Health and Family Communication
courses.desc: Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. This course will explore the intersection of communication, family, and health. Using communication theories, models and concepts, we will address the following questions: How does the family's health and illness impact the way they communicate? How does family communication influence health behavior and beliefs? Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-9) Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Study Abroad/Tours
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Organized faculty-led study abroad tours. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Practicum
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. Supervised, practical experience in a professional setting relevant to the student's field of study. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Seminar in Personal Relationships
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered yearly. Examines theory and research on the process and functions of communication in personal relationship contexts. Interdisciplinary readings illuminates the dynamics of communication in the development, maintenance, and deterioration of romantic relationships, friendships, and family relationships. Discussion and assignments center around theoretical, methodological, and practical issues in research on communicative activities and events in personal relationships. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Survey of Interpersonal Communication
courses.desc: Offered every other year. Survey of theories and research in interpersonal communication including definitions of interpersonal communication, its place in the field of communication, and methodological issues. Overall emphasis on foundational readings and recent research developments. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Seminar in Organizational Communication
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every other year. Introduction to theories and research in organizational communication. Topics include culture, networks, structure, technology, identity, power, resistance, gender, and globalization. Overall emphasis on foundational readings and recent research developments. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Seminar in Rhetoric, Criticism, & Theory
courses.desc: Offered yearly. Exploration of contemporary issues in rhetorical criticism and theory. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Qualitative Research Methods
courses.desc: Offered every year. An emphasis on the philosophy and practice of qualitative inquiry, the development and use of descriptive frameworks, and gathering and testing qualitative data to develop human communication theory. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Seminar: Rhetoric & Environmental Controversy
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. The study of how advocates use symbols to influence meaning and action in environmental controversies. Rhetorical theory is used to identify, analyze, and evaluate persuasive strategies and tactics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-9) Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Topical Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to graduate students in Communication Studies. Professional development seminar. Offered credit/no-credit only Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Communication Studies Teaching Methods
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to graduate students in Communication Studies. This course cover teaching methods in Communication Studies. Offered CR/NCR only. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: COMX
courses.title: Thesis/Professional Paper
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered every term. Preparation of a thesis, manuscript, or professional paper based on research for presentation and/or publication. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Foundations of Clinical Practice in Speech-Language Pathology & Audiology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Introduction to the scientific study of human communi­cation and its disorders and to the professions of Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology. Overview of biological systems of speech, language, and hearing and the nature and treatment of communication disorders.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Signed Communication for Health & Ed Professionals: Foundational Skills & Ethical Considerations
courses.desc: Prereq., CSD 110 or CSD 210. Students will be introduced to the foundations of signed communication for health and education professionals and topics impacting members of a linguistic and cultural minority and the healthcare and educational models that guide ethical decision-making. This course examines the moral dimensions of the health and education professions in select issues, including models of disability, communication as a basic human right, and contemporary issues intersecting with the Deaf community.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Clinical Application and Observations in Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology
courses.desc: Students will learn roles and responsibilities of being a speech-language pathologist and audiologist HIPAA regulations, and health and safety guidelines. This course is designed as an orientation and observation class which will prepare you for your future work in the area of Communicative Disorders.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Speech & Language Development
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to students with at least sophomore standing. Topics include typical speech and language development, phonology, semantic, morphological, syntax, and pragmatics, along with individual differences, second language acquisition and literacy.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Signed Communication for Health and Education Professionals: Foundational Skills II
courses.desc: This course introduces the fundamentals of Signed Communication used by the Deaf Community, including basic vocabulary, syntax, fingerspelling, and grammatical non-manual signals. It also focuses on basic expressive and receptive communicative competence. In addition, this course provides a survey of various issues surrounding Signed Communication and the Deaf community.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Introduction to Sound and Hearing
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Introduction to the principles of sound from the perspective of production and perception; the physical properties of sound (pitch, intensity, duration/phase) and their perceptual correlates and differential sensitivities; the concepts of dB and threshold measurements; and the anatomy and physiology of the hearing (and vestibular) system.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Foundations of Scientific Writing
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Students learn to use library resources and research databases/search engines to develop research questions and explore a scientific topic. Students develop their topic, develop scientific questions, write summaries of peer-reviewed scientific journal articles, and develop an annotated bibliography. Students orally present their findings at the end of the semester and engage in self-reflection about their writing.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Clinical Applications of Language Science
courses.desc: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to language as a science and the application of language science in clinical contexts. Students will investigate the domains of human language including phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics. Each language domain will be analyzed in clinical applications and contexts. This course also explores how linguistic structures are situated within psychological and social contexts, examining how psychological or social breakdowns can result in language disorders or processing difficulties.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Clinical Phonetics
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Exploration of the sounds and sound structure of American English and some of its dialects. Introduction to the theory and practice of phonetic and phonological analysis and trained in the transcription of speech into the International Phonetic Alphabet.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Diagnostic Audiology
courses.desc: Prereq., CSD 222. Introduction to the principles of acoustics as a basis for understanding hearing assessment. Development of the ability to interpret audiograms as well as the results from a hearing evaluation. Includes pure tone audiometry, speech audiometry, acoustic immittance, and acoustic reflex testing, as well as electrophysiological tests. Hearing screening procedures are also included.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Speech and Swallowing Mechanism
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Introduction to anat­omy and physiology of the speech and swallowing mechanisms including the anatomical orientation and embryological devel­opment, the breathing mechanism, structures of phonation and swallowing, articulators, and the nervous system.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Neurological Bases of Communication and Swallowing
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 330. Focused study on the anatomy of the nervous system and how the nervous system supports behaviors inherent to communication and swallowing. Students will be introduced to anatomical terms, structures, and functions. Clinical implications will be linked to class with a focus across the lifespan. Level: Undergraduate.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Developmental Communication Disorders
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., CSD 210. Nature of developmental speech and language disorders and basic understanding of principles underlying assessment and treatment of these disorders.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Acquired Communication and Swallowing Disorders
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 210. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Identification, assessment, and intervention for a variety of acquired speech, language, cognitive, and swallowing disorders. Introduction to potential psychosocial impacts and educational concerns, utilizing the WHO-ICF, multicultural considerations, and incorporation of family members. Introduction to clinical documentation for acquired disorders.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Inclusive Campus-Based Practices for Neurodiverse Persons
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Application required. This course educates students about neurodiversity in adults. The two-credit instance of this course includes a didactic portion that addresses topics aligned with the specialized consideration for people with autism and neurodiversity and a service-learning portion that allows direct mentorship and support to neurodiverse adults on and off campus. The one-credit instance is offered as a service learning opportunity for students enrolled in CSD 445.

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: The Clinical Process
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 210, CSD 222, CSD 320, and CSD 365. The underlying principles of clinical methods and practice including: the observation of human behavior and clinical processes, assessment of communication differences, clinical management of these differences, delays and disorders, behavior, interviewing/counseling, lesson planning, and writing skills. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Speech Science
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 222, CSD 320, and CSD 330. Physiologic, neurologic, and acoustic aspects of human communication, theoretical framework for speech science, and principles of acoustics applied to speech language pathology across the lifespan. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Senior Capstone
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., WRIT 101. Restricted to students with senior standing. Part one of a two course sequence where the student completes an independent project. Students will prepare a literature review, and ethics application, and a proposal in preparation for a major research project of their design. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Social Communication Skills, Behavior, and Neurodiversity
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. This course explores and integrates social aspects of communication (e.g., behavioral and social understanding/competence), communication accommodations, adaptations, and strategies for functional communication and independent living skills. Topics include foundational information on autism as well as assessment and treatment using evidence-based practices for autism spectrum disorder and related disorders. Co-convened with SLP 545. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Rehabilitative Audiology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 210 and CSD 222. Fundamental skills in speech reading and knowledge of various types of hearing aids, implantable devices, and the tools necessary to assess and implement auditory training. Management of the clients across the lifespan with hearing impairment including psycho-social development and educational intervention. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Multicultural Issues
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 210, CSD 222, and CSD 320. Topics include: dynamics of community and culture; strategies to communicate with people from a variety of backgrounds; learning English as a second language; phonological and linguistic analysis of differences between Standard English speakers and culturally diverse populations and international differences in service delivery. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Multicultural Issues
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSD 210, CSD 222, and CSD 320. Topics include: dynamics of community and culture; strategies to communicate with people from a variety of backgrounds; learning English as a second language; phonological and linguistic analysis of differences between Standard English speakers and culturally diverse populations and international differences in service delivery. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.desc: (R-6) Independent research under the direction of a faculty member. Level: Undergraduate

courses.title: Practicum
courses.desc: (R-5) A maximum of 5 credits of clinical practicum may count toward graduation. Allows the advanced student an opportunity to pursue independent or small group clinical practicum. Students will be directly supervised by a certified speech and language pathologist or audiologist. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CSD
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: CHTH
courses.title: Health and Culture: A Global Perspective
courses.desc: This course will provide students with an interdisciplinary perspective on global health. Students will assess health beliefs, health-related behavior, sickness distribution, treatment and experience in a range of socio-cultural contexts. There is an emphasis on applied research in health promotion and disease prevention programs. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: CHTH
courses.title: Principles of Epidemiology
courses.desc: Epidemiology is the basic science of public health. Specifically, epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of disease and of health in human populations as well as the application of epidemiologic methods to promote health. This course is designed to introduce students to the foundational principles and methods of epidemiology. Topics covered in this course include: basic principles of epidemiology; causality; health data sources; measures of disease frequency and excess risk; and epidemiologic study designs. Students will develop skills to interpret and critically evaluate epidemiologic information. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: CHTH
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-6) Directed individual research and study appropriate to the background and objectives of the student. Level: Undergraduate

A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: CAPP
courses.title: Introduction to Computers
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Introduction to computer terminology, hardware, and software, including wire/wireless communications and multimedia devices. Students utilize word processing, spread sheet, database, and presentation applications to create projects common to business and industry in a networked computing environment. Internet research, email usage, and keyboarding proficiency are integrated.

courses.subject: CAPP
courses.title: MS Word
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Preparation of business forms, correspondence, mail merges, columnar projects, and reports using up-to-date software. Business related application projects, graphics, and printer operation are included.

courses.subject: CAPP
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered at Missoula College. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Computer Fluency
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Introduces the skills and concepts of information technology, both from practical and a more theoretical point of view. During lectures and interactive computer labs, students will explore a wide range of digital and information technologies, including common PC applications, networking, databases, privacy, and security.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Careers in Computer Science
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Exploration of various careers available in the general area of Computer Science. Includes discussion of strategies for success in the major. Computer Science faculty members also will discuss possible undergraduate research opportunities and motivation for graduate education.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: The Joy and Beauty of Computing
courses.desc: This course examines the computing field and how it impacts the human condition, introduces exciting ideas and influential people, and provides a gentle introduction to computational thinking using the Python programming language.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. This course covers basic programming concepts such as variables, data types, iteration, flow of control, input/output, functions, and objects. The course will also cover programming ideas such as libraries, files, modularity, where to turn to for help, and debugging. Students will learn about the role computation can play in solving problems by writing programs to address practical problems. No prior programming experience is expected. Includes two hours of independent lab per week.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Interdisciplinary Computer Science I
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered on both Mountain Campus and at Missoula College. Prereq., CSCI 150. This course will introduce students to fundamental computer science concepts including functions, libraries and APIs, recursion, data types, optimization, searching and sorting, all while using a high level structured programming language.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Interdisciplinary Computer Science II
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at both Mountain Campus and Missoula College. Prereq., CSCI 151 and M 162 or M 171 or M 172 or M 273. Prereq. or coreq., M 151. Survey of computer science topics including recursion, basic data structures, algorithms, computational theory, computing architecture, and modern software development practices.
courses.prereq: CSCI 151 and M 162 or M 171 or M 172 or M 273

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Intro to Computer Modeling
courses.desc: Offered fall and spring. Offered on the Mountain Campus and at Missoula College. Problem solving and data modeling using computer productivity software. Emphasis using spreadsheets and database for data analysis.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Web Design and Programming
courses.desc: Offered spring. Students will learn how to critically analyze the usability of web sites and create their own by understanding and applying universal principles of design. Programming and other key concepts covered include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Web Graphics. Students will complete many different types of Web projects throughout the semester, culminating in an online portfolio used to showcase work completed in this class and others. No prior programming experience is expected.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Programming with C/C++
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., CSCI 152. Concepts and principles of programming languages with an emphasis on C, C++, and object-oriented programming. Syntax and semantics of object-oriented languages. Principles and implementation of memory allocation and de-allocation, type-checking, scope, polymorphism, inheritance.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Social & Ethical Issues in CS
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., WRIT 101. Exploration of ethical issues in the field of computing. Skills needed to identify and analyze various ethical concerns. Standard ethical concepts and theories, methods of ethical analysis. Strong emphasis on practical application of the ethical process.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Intermediate Data Structures and Algorithms
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., CSCI 152 with a minimum grade of B-. Abstract data types, analysis of algorithms, stacks, queues, lists, recursion, trees, hashing, graphs, and applications of data structures in algorithm development. Course is offered in the Java programming language.
courses.prereq: CSCI 152 with a minimum grade of B-

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Databases and SQL
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. Relational database design including: requirements analysis, data structure, entity relationships, normalization, relational algebra and integrity. Physical implementation focuses on data storage, retrieval and modification, concurrency, optimization, security, SQL, and XML.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Web Application Development
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., CSCI 152. This class is designed to give students introductory exposure to client-server web development. Students will be exposed to modern web/software development principles, practices and systems.

courses.subject: CSCI
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-10) Independent research under the direction of a faculty member.
