courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to graduate students in Environmental Studies. Preparation of a thesis, manuscript, or professional paper based on research for presentation and/or publication. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Getting to Know Environmental Studies
courses.desc: Course is designed to introduce entering EVST majors to the EVST program, the PEAS Farm and UM FLAT, and the broader Missoula environmental community, as well as internship opportunities. Offered CR/NCR only.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Info Resources
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to majors in Environmental Studies. Students learn how to find, evaluate, and use existing information to understand environmental issues. Students will learn research methods; research a question using a variety of sources; evaluate sources critically; and write and give an audio/video presentation on their question. Focus is on critical thinking and dealing with the information explosion.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Sustainable Communities
courses.desc: Offered spring. Exploration of ways that communities promote sustainability and environmental health. Introduction of relevant social science concepts.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Nature and Society
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered on Mountain Campus. Explores the relationship between ideas about nature and the development of political and social ideas, institutions, and practices, primarily in western (Euro-American) society. Complements ethics offerings in philosophy aimed at environmental studies majors.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Nature and Society
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., WRIT 101. Offered at Missoula College. Explores the relationship between ideas about nature and the development of political and social ideas, institutions, and practices in primarily western (Euro-American) society. Course is an elective for students in the 2-year AA and AAS degree programs.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Special Topics/Experimental Courses
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environment Montana: A to Z
courses.desc: Offered spring. The environment of Montana has changed dramatically since its founding 150 years ago. The purpose of this course is to provide an introduction to the land, people and places of Montana as viewed through the lens of environmental change. It will explore environmental change in relation to the actions of human beings. It will also explore how federal policies intersect with Montana environmental stories. Through a combination of lectures, readings, focused in-class discussions, and a research project students will learn the environmental stories of Montana.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Earth Ethics
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., ENST 230H or PHL 112E. We often think of environmental issues primarily as issues of science and politics: what does science tell us about problems facing the environment, and how can politics help us respond? But environmental issues are simultaneously ethical issues with several moral dimensions: because each issue raises questions of how we should respond, exploring the moral dimensions of environmental issues can help us to discern better or worse responses, and to understand why we choose to respond as we do. In this course we will develop broad familiarity with different approaches within the field of environmental ethics in order to use a case study approach to examine a range of contemporary environmental issues. Students will have the opportunity to develop their own responses within a moral framework. By the end of the course students will have learned how to examine the moral dimensions of a range of environmental issues and how to ground their own perspectives within an ethical framework.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Literature of the Earth
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., WRIT 101. Provides interpretations and understanding of forms and themes in American nonfiction, fiction, poetry, and film that interrogate nature, the relationship between humanity and non-human life, ecological-racial justice, and the movement of environmental dissent and activism.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Energy and Climate
courses.desc: Energy and Climate takes an interdisciplinary look at the electrical grid and energy transition in the context of climate change. Students explore energy issues through technical, economic, environmental, and political lenses by tracing energy from its end-use back through the grid to its ultimate source, touching on every step along the way. Class time is dedicated to discussion, role-playing games, simulations, and occasional lectures.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Politics & Policies
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., WRIT 101. Foundation in public lands history, bedrock environmental laws, policy processes and institutions. Research and analysis of current environmental and natural resource policy issues. Focus is domestic illustrated by case studies.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Writing the Earth: Workshop on Nature, Environment & Justice
courses.desc: Offered spring. Writing workshop for the creation, critique, and revision of essays about the environment to include natural history, personal narrative, science interpretation, advocacy/editorial, place-based essay, and others. Examination of concepts, forms, and approaches to writing about environmental concerns, activism, and justice. Reading and responding to published work, primarily from the perspective of technique and approach.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Law
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., WRIT 101. Introduction to the history, law and theory of environmental regulation in the United States using public and private land regulation mechanisms as case studies. Basic principles of constitutional and administrative law relevant to environmental regulation, substantive public and private land use law and the history of environmental problems and their regulation.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Special Topics/Experimental Courses
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Field Studies: Environmental Studies
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered every term. Via extended backcountry travel, experiential examination of cultural history and public lands management, and how those affect ecosystem integrity. Investigation of personal roles in and relationships with human and ecological communities. Offered by the Wild Rockies Field Institute and Swan Valley Connections.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: TEK of Indigenous Peoples
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Examines traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) of Indigenous peoples of North America and the world. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: US Environmental Movement
courses.desc: Offered Intermittently. Study of the environmental movement as a social movement. Examination of different approaches to environmental protection and restoration in view of the movement’s historical roots and contemporary debates. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Social Issues: The Mekong Delta
courses.desc: Offered intermittently in fall. This on-campus course focuses on the history, culture, economy and environment of Vietnam, with particular emphasis on the Mekong Delta region. This is achieved through various media, class discussions, personal and group projects, and activities with the instructor and guest experts. As a prerequisite for the study abroad course to Vietnam (ENST 437), the goal of the course is to provide an understanding of the unique environments and the socio-economy of the Mekong Delta region to facilitate learning about the effects of climate change on these complex natural and anthropogenic systems. Co-convenes with ENST 514. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Climate Change: Mekong Delta
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., ENST 427. This study abroad course focuses on the threats posed by climate change in Vietnam, with particular emphasis on the Mekong Delta region. This is achieved through lectures from Can Tho University professors, active participation in field trips, the homestay, course readings, and synthesis through questions sets and discussions provided by University of Montana instructor. The goal of this course is to provide an understanding of the potential impacts of climate change on the ecosystems and people of the Mekong Delta, and explore opportunities for people to adapt to and mitigate these impacts. Co-convenes with ENST 516. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: General Science: Conservation Education
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. A study of the foundations of environmental science and conservation education with applications to community service and teaching. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Community Sustainability in Practice
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students with at least junior status. Project-based, capstone-like course that develops student sustainability practice, leadership and environmental citizenship competencies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Food Justice and Sustainability
courses.desc: Offered spring. Seminar course that examines the social justice, economic, and sustainability dimensions of the contemporary food system with a focus on the United States. Develops student understanding of the dominant food system and emerging alternatives. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Globalization, Justice & Environment
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., WRIT 101. Study of current trends in economic globalization and its effects on efforts to work for social justice and environmental sustainability, particularly in the Global South. Examination of different models and theories of globalization, analysis of ethical issues raised, and assessment of alternatives proposed. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Justice Issues & Solutions
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Examination of evidence, causes and consequences of social inequality in the distribution of environmental risks and in access to natural resources and environmental amenities. Community, government and industry responses and service approaches for addressing environmental inequities. Course co-convenes with ENST 589. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-15) Independent undergraduate research in forest management, wood science, soils, wildlife management, silviculture, recreation and other topic areas. Level: Undergraduate

courses.title: Field Work/Practicum
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Organized field experience or practicum in Environmental Studies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Senior Thesis/Capstone
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to majors in Environmental Studies with senior standing. For seniors who want to design and perform a significant capstone project involving research and/or service. Students have responsibility for designing their projects which are subject to faculty approval. A final report and public presentation are required. Honors credit available. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Earth Storytelling: Nature, Climate, Resistance
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This seminar considers works of environmental literature, from the perspective of both creators and critics. We will examine works of fiction, essay, memoir, literary journalism, science fiction, poetry, and film that interrogate the human relationship with nature, climate change, and racial justice. We will look both at the writer’s craft as well as overarching thematic concerns. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Issues of Indigenous Peoples
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This graduate seminar provides an overview of environmental issues of Indigenous peoples from the 19th to 21st centuries. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Natural Resource Conflict Resolution
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Examines the basic framework for preventing and resolving natural resource and environmental conflicts in America. Reviews the history of alternative approaches, emphasizes the theory and practice of collaboration, and considers future trends. This highly interactive course uses lectures, guest speakers, case studies, and simulations. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Social Issues:The Mekong Delta
courses.desc: Offered intermittently in spring. This on-campus course focuses on the history, culture, economy and environment of Vietnam, with particular emphasis on the Mekong Delta region. This is achieved through various media, class discussions, personal and group projects, and activities with the instructor and guest experts. As a prerequisite for the study abroad course to Vietnam (ENST 516), the goal of the course is to provide an understanding of the unique environments and the socio-economy of the Mekong Delta region to facilitate learning about the effects of climate change on these complex natural and anthropogenic systems. Co-convenes with ENST 427. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Negotiation Mediation
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This course prepares students to effectively engage in multiparty negotiation on natural resource and environmental issues. It is grounded in theory and provides an opportunity to develop practical skills in both negotiation and facilitation/mediation. Guest speakers, case studies, and simulations allow students to develop, test, and refine best practices. The course is fast-paced, highly interactive, and serves as the second of three required courses in the Natural Resources Conflict Resolution Program. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Climate Change: Mekong Delta
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., ENST 514. This study abroad course focuses on the threats posed by climate change in Vietnam, with particular emphasis on the Mekong Delta region. This is achieved through lectures from Can Tho University professors, active participation in field trips, field data collection, analysis and interpretation, the homestay, course readings, independent graduate research, and synthesis provided by University of Montana professors. The goal of this course is to provide an understanding of the potential impacts of climate change on the ecosystems and people of the Mekong Delta, and explore opportunities for people to adapt to and mitigate these impacts. Co-convenes with ENST 437. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Foundations of Change
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to graduate students in Environmental Studies. Designed for the first-year graduate cohort in Environmental Studies, this foundational course aims to strengthen participants’ capacities to effectively meet today’s environmental and social justice challenges. Participants explore their own sense of personal purpose, plan their degrees, and develop leadership skills and community. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Foundation in Environmental Education
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to graduate students in Environmental Studies. Problem-solving approaches to environmental education; problem identification, research and design and implementation of an educational approach to selected environmental issues. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: The Greening of Religion
courses.desc: Offered yearly. A critical examination of different religious traditions' views on nature and society, and contemporary religious traditions' responses to environmental issues. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Local Climate Solutions
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This course seeks to develop students’ understanding and skills for participating in local solutions to climate change that can also support broader conservation, efficiency and sustainability efforts. This will be accomplished by engaging in planning and carrying out group projects that further advance existing climate change mitigation or adaptation efforts. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Building Effective Environment Organizations
courses.desc: (R-3) Offered intermittently. Focus on the tasks and skills necessary to building and managing effective environmental organizations, particularly non-profit. Budgeting, fund-raising, grant-writing, attracting and utilizing volunteers, working with the media. Strategic approaches and how they are shaped by issue, context, and structure. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Conservation Without Borders
courses.desc: Offered intermittently in autumn. Restricted to graduate students in Environmental Studies. Review of the political systems and administrative systems of each country relevant to natural resource policy decision-making and ecological systems. Study theory of integration of conservation with management such as common pool resource management, transboundary protected areas and international agreements. Review pertinent literature, interact with stakeholders, and produce group reports. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Supervision and Teaching Environmental Education
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Design, selection and evaluation of materials for the teaching of environmental education. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Qualitative Research Methods & Analysis
courses.desc: This graduate seminar introduces students to qualitative research methods and analysis through an experiential, co-created learning approach focused on social-ecological systems. Rather than treating methods as mere tools, the course examines how qualitative approaches are inherently theoretical, carrying epistemological and ethical implications that shape research purpose, process, and outcomes. Students will gain hands-on experience with diverse methods—including participant observation, interviews, photovoice, and archival research—while building a portfolio of work throughout the semester that connects research questions, study design, analytical tools, and deliverables. Central to the course is critical examination of participant engagement approaches, reflexive consideration of researcher positioning, and exploration of how qualitative research can build theory and facilitate social change. Through collaborative learning that emphasizes community and inclusion, students will develop both methodological competencies and career readiness skills, including ethical research practices, critical analysis, and the thoughtful integration of emerging technologies like AI. The course is particularly valuable for students conducting research on environmental and social issues, offering a supportive environment to experiment with methods while engaging deeply with the theoretical foundations that make qualitative research a powerful tool for understanding and transforming complex social and environmental relationships. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Impact Analysis
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Covers legal and scientific aspects of the Environmental Impact Analysis (EIA) including: What is required by international, national and state law and regulations? How does one organize an effective interdisciplinary team research effort and public participation program? What scientific tools are used in EIA? How could EIA process be improved? Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Land Use Planning Law
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Basic overview of the law of land use planning including background in the traditional governmental regulatory, proprietary, and fiscal land use tools. Examination of modern techniques for land use planning; consideration of constitutional limits of authority of state and local governments. Focus on skills in interpreting, drafting and applying state legislation and local ordinances. Co-convenes with LAW 687. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Introduction to Environmental Law
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Philosophy and values underlying environmental regulation, basic introduction to administrative law, in-depth study of air and water pollution and the environmental policy acts. Co-convenes with LAW 650. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Public Land & Resources Law
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to graduate students in Environmental Studies. Historical development of United States public land law, state-federal relations, and the roles of Congress, the executive and the courts; the law applying to specific public land resources: water, minerals, timber, range, and preservation. Co-convenes with LAW 654. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Water Law
courses.desc: Offered spring. Interstate water problems; federal/state powers; federal/Indian water rights/Montana water law. Co-convenes with LAW 663. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Ethics & Restoration
courses.desc: Offered autumn. A critical examination of the ethical issues that emerge in the field of ecological restoration, and decisions to manipulate nature intentionally for social and ecological goals. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Writing
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn. Writing workshop designed to improve skills in writing on environmental topics for general audiences. Approaches include personal narrative, natural history, science interpretation, advocacy/argument, place-based essays. Includes analysis of published work from the perspective of technique and craft. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Practicum in Collaborative Conservation
courses.desc: (R-4) Offered every semester. Prereq., ENST 513. Designed as the capstone experience of the Natural Resources Conflict Resolution Program. Provides practical experience in multi-party collaboration and conflict resolution. Students may design their own project in consultation with the director of the NRCR Program, or participate in a project organized and convened by faculty. Projects may be conducted year-round. Co-convenes with LAW 679. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: The Politics of Food
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This seminar explores social, economic, and ecological issues related to the contemporary food and agricultural system and alternatives to that system. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: Environmental Justice Issues and Solutions
courses.desc: Course examines how and why environmental burdens, amenities, and services are inequitably distributed among various segments of society and approaches to addressing environmental inequalities and discrimination in environmental decision making. Co-convenes with ENST 489S. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: ENST
courses.title: PEAS Farm Practicum
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered Spring and autumn for 2 credit and as a summer intensive course for 3 credit. Restricted to graduate students. Students learn small scale sustainable vegetable farming in a hands-on work environment at the PEAS farm (a 15 minute bike ride from campus). Lectures, readings, and reflection inform the work. Summer students also visit local farms on once-a week field trips. This course is repeatable as the curriculum changes across the season, and students can attend any semester, though the 3-credit graduate level summer intensive course is the heart of the program. Level: Graduate

courses.title: Wildlife & People
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Intended for non-wildlife biology majors. Interactions of wildlife and people in todays society.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Fish & Wildlife Interest Group
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Discussion section for incoming students.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Careers in Wildlife Biology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Subject matter and fields of study within wildlife biology conservation and management. Topics to include wildlife ecology, aquatic ecology, human dimensions, conservation and management, and other opportunities for careers in wildlife biology.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Conservation Science
courses.desc: Prereq., BIOO 105N or BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOE 172N. The goal of this course is to introduce students to major issues related to the conservation of biodiversity. Lectures will illustrate how science can be used to identify and solve conservation problems. Lectures will cover current threats to biodiversity (human population growth, extinctions, habitat destruction, degradation and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, global climate change) and discuss how science can be used to help ameliorate these impacts.
courses.prereq: BIOO 105N or BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOE 172N

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Intro to Biostatistics
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Introduction to statistical ecology: distributions, hypothesis testing, and fitting models to data with emphasis on problems in ecological sampling.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Data, Inference, and Statistics
courses.desc: Prereq., M 115 (preferred) or M 121 or M 132 or M 140 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171. Students will gain familiarity with wildlife data management, probability, R, statistics, and the different types of models used to make inference from wildlife data. Students will think about the relationships between and among ecological questions, predictions, data collection, statistics, inference, and public communication.
courses.prereq: M 115 (preferred) or M 121 or M 132 or M 140 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Techniques
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Wildlife Biology major or minor with at least sophomore standing. This course tntroduces techniques and field skills used by wildlife professionals, with emphasis on survey methods, animal welfare standards, and research design. Students gain hands-on experience through multiple field trips, a required weekend-long field trip, and a wildlife research paper based on real-world data.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Human Dimensions of Wildlife
courses.desc: Offered spring. This course provides a foundation for students to understand the human dimensions of fish and wildlife management. Successful resource management requires an understanding of how people value and interact with wildlife populations. We use contemporary wildlife challenges facing Montana as focal points for learning.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Fisheries Techniques
courses.desc: This course provides an overview of fisheries techniques as they are applied in Montana. Students learn a wide variety of fisheries methods. Case studies and guest lectures expose students to current issues faced by fisheries managers in Montana. Field trips provide hands-on experience.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wild Sustenance
courses.desc: This course introduces hunting to college students at the University of Montana. The course is intended for students who have not had the opportunity to hunt. There are two components to the course: on campus class meetings and a 3-day immersive workshop at the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial Ranch owned by the Boone and Crockett Club in Dupuyer, MT. Students from a diversity of majors are encouraged to participate. On campus we discuss the role of hunting in wildlife management, the history of wildlife conservation, hunter ethics, and human dimensions of hunting. The 3-day field activity provides students time in the field, on the shooting range, and in the kitchen to understand the entire hunting process from field to table. While at the ranch, we discuss motivations for hunting, concerns of first-time hunters, firearm safety, selection, and many other topics. Open dialogue and respectful discourse is encouraged. Food is an important part of the program. We harvest a deer on the ranch and a professional butcher demonstrates how to process the deer and students complete the process. A professional chef prepares wild game every meal, and spends time with students on cooking game.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Physiological Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., BIOB 272. Restricted to majors in Wildlife Biology. How physiological and biochemical processes in animals influence behavior and ecology. Application of physiological approaches to wildlife conservation such as assessment of animal health, nutritional condition, and physiological performance.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Habitat Conservation & Management
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., BIOB 272 and either WILD 240 or WILD 245. Restricted to majors in Wildlife Biology with at least junior standing. Application of principles of wildlife biology to conservation and management of wild bird and mammal habitats including statistical and field applications. Lab and lecture material will include vegetation, habitat, and habitat use sampling.
courses.prereq: BIOB 272 and either WILD 240 or WILD 245

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Hunter Check Station
courses.desc: (R-2) Offered autumn. Students learn techniques for determining species, age and sex of game animals, then work 3-5 days as volunteers at hunter check stations operated by management agencies.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Aquatic Habitat Conservation & Restoration
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., STAT 216 or WILD 240 or WILD 245 or FORS 201; and BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOO 105N or BIOE 172N. Application of principles of animal physiology, entomology, freshwater and fish ecology, and zoology to conservation and restoration of aquatic habitats including statistical and field applications. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: STAT 216 or WILD 240 or WILD 245 or FORS 201; and BIOB 160 or BIOB 170N or BIOO 105N or BIOE 172N

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Policy
courses.desc: Offered spring odd years. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Overview of the laws affecting wildlife and how those laws are initiated, implemented, and enforced; impact of politics, interest groups, and agency jurisdictions. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Conservation of Wildlife Populations
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., WRIT 101; BIOE 370; M 162 or M 171; WILD 245. Restricted to students with senior standing in Biology, Forestry, Recreation Management, or Wildlife Biology. Application of population ecology principles and theory to the conservation and management of wildlife populations. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: WRIT 101; BIOE 370; M 162 or M 171; WILD 245

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Handling & Chemical Immobilization
courses.desc: Offered spring. Principles of wildlife chemical immobilization for researchers and managers. Ethical and legal issues, field organization, animal care and handling, immobilizing drugs, drug delivery systems, animal monitoring and veterinary emergencies. No labs. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Conservation of Fish Populations
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., WRIT 101; BIOE 370; M 162 or M 171; and WILD 245. Restricted to students with senior standing in Wildlife Biology, Biology, or Environmental Science and Sustainability. Application of population ecology principles and theory to the conservation and management of fish populations. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: WRIT 101; BIOE 370; M 162 or M 171; and WILD 245

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: The Upshot--Applied Wildlife Management
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq/Coreq.,WILD 370, WILD 408 or WILD 470. Designed for students to apply their knowledge in the development of wildlife management planning. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Aquatic Invertebrate Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. This course is designed to provide students an understanding of the life histories, ecology and importance of macroinvertebrates in freshwater aquatic systems. The primary focus will be on insects, although an introduction to other invertebrates will also be included. The lab portion will involve identification of major groups of aquatic macroinvertebrates and participation in an environmental assessment using invertebrates as indicators of stream condition and restoration efficacy. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-15) Independent undergraduate research in forest management, wood science, soils, wildlife management, silviculture, recreation and other topic areas. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-10) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Senior Wildlife Seminar
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to majors in Wildlife Biology with at least senior standing. Analysis and discussion led by students of current topics in wildlife biology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Undergraduate Thesis
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students with at least senior standing. Preparation of major paper based on study or research of a topic selected with an advisor according to needs and objectives of student. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Research Design
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Students registering should have taken an introductory statistics course. Examination of study designs for experiments, quasi-experiments, observational studies, and sampling surveys with an emphasis on application. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Research Design Lab
courses.desc: (R-3) Coreq., WILD 540. Students will be expected to learn R programming skills, R data management and R graphing functions as well an introduction to statistical analysis in R.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Statistical Applications in Wildlife Biology
courses.desc: (R-5) Offered autumn odd-numbered years. Explores statistical problems encountered by wildlife biology and ecology graduate students. Students will bring statistical problems of interest to class where, as a group, we will explore analysis options, assumptions, pitfalls, and alternative solutions. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Strong Inference Science
courses.desc: (R-7) Offered fall. This course teaches the principles and philosophy of conducting strong inference science with practical application to students own thesis research. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Wildlife Habitat Modeling
courses.desc: Offered spring, odd years. A survey of theory and applications in the study of resource selection by animals. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Topics in Habitat Ecology
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered every term. Discussion of recent scientific papers on advances in ecology, conservation, and population dynamics as related to habitat ecology and conservation. Prior to registering for this course, WILD 562 is strongly recommended. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Topics in Aquatic Ecology
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered every term. Review and synthesis of the scientific literature current issues and analyses in aquatic ecology. We assume a general understanding of fish biology, aquatic ecology, as well as a background in population, community and ecosystem ecological concepts. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Estimation of Demographic Parameters
courses.desc: Offered autumn of even years. Examines methods for estimating demographic parameters of wildlife populations including survival, fecundity, abundance, and movement. Considers theory of capture-recapture and count-based modeling. Includes maximum likelihood and Bayesian treatments of the problems.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Theoretical Ecology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This class provides a general toolbox of ecological modeling approaches. It will be more about how to model than about models themselves, but in illustration we will cover a variety of commonly used ecological and evolutionary models, ranging from behavior of individuals (optimality, game theory) to populations (structured and unstructured, logistic growth, matrix models) to communities (competition, predation, parasitism). The focus will be on formalizing conceptual ideas into a mathematical framework and will not deal heavily with data. (Of course, data is important, but other courses here concentrate on data and model fitting.) Most weeks, sessions will each cover a new theoretical model, including derivation of the equations from ecological theory, and students will complete an assignment that includes coding the model in R and exploring its dynamics. Other sessions will be discussion of a journal article that includes the model(s), so students can become comfortable with seeing and comprehending mathematical notation and theoretical literature. The course will culminate with a project in which students will design a model for some aspect of their study system that could potentially be published.

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Research
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered every term. Restricted to graduate students in Wildlife Biology. Directed individual research and study appropriate to the background and objectives of the student. Level: Graduate

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Graduate Seminar in Wildlife Biology
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to graduate students in Wildlife Biology or Fish and Wildlife Biology. Analysis of selected problems in wildlife biology and conservation. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Professional Paper
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered every term. Restricted to graduate students in Wildlife Biology. Professional paper written in the area of the student's major interest based on either primary or secondary research. Subject matter must be approved by graduate committee. Graded credit/no-credit only. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: WILD
courses.title: Thesis
courses.desc: (R-20) Offered every term. Restricted to graduate students in Wildlife Biology. Preparation of thesis. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Introduction to Forestry Field Skills
courses.desc: Offered autumn. This course is focused on developing introductory forestry field skills through experiential learning at the Colleges Lubrecht Experimental Forest. Classroom lecture and experiences that introduce students to orienteering, map reading, GPS, tree measurements, fire and fuels management, recreation, human dimensions, hydrology, wood products, and the careers possible with a Forestry degree.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Urban Forestry
courses.desc: Offered spring. An introduction to urban forestry principles and practices. Benefits of the urban forest. Topics covered include plant species selection, site design, site assessment, planting, watering, fertilization, insects and diseases, pruning and tree care, inventory of property values, and community forestry development.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Biometrics
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., M 115 or M 121 or M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172. Introduction to probability and statistical methods for forestry and environmental sciences covering natural resource applications of common probability distributions, data analysis, hypothesis testing, and regression.
courses.prereq: M 115 or M 121 or M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Mensuration
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., M 121 and M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172; and either prereq. or coreq. FORS 201 or STAT 216 or SOCI 202 or WILD 240. The theory and practice of timber inventory and growth projection, including field measurements, sampling procedures, statistical methods, inventory compilation, and stand growth simulation under specified management prescriptions. Stand growth under specified management prescriptions.
courses.prereq: M 121 and M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172; and either prereq. or coreq

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Fire Management & Environmental Change
courses.desc: Offered Spring. Introduction to wildland fire and its role as a transformative process in the environment. Topics include pyrogeography, fire behavior, fire ecology, fire policy, and fire management. Examines the role of fire in shaping ecological and social systems, with a focus on societal issues of natural resources, human health, land use, climate change, and economics. Provides foundational understanding of first principles. Serves as a stepping off point for further study of fire.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Insects & Diseases
courses.desc: Offered spring. Identification, ecology and management of insects and pathogens affecting western North American forest.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Tree Biology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Exploration of the biological processes that allow trees to capture, convert, and allocate energy and water, ultimately shaping forest ecosystems. Beginning with light absorption in the chloroplast, students will trace the paths of energy, water and nutrients as they fuel photosynthesis, respiration, and carbon transport, leading to growth, reproduction, and adaptation. Topics include primary and secondary growth, xylem and phloem function, wood formation and anatomy, water transport, and the influence of environmental stressors such as drought, temperature extremes, herbivory, and pathogens. The course also examines the role of trees in carbon sequestration, nutrient cycling, and ecosystem function, with applications in forestry and forest management. Through hands-on laboratory exercises and field-based observations, students will gain a functional understanding of tree physiology and its relevance to silviculture, tree health assessment, and sustainable forest management.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Dendrology
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., BIOO 105N or BIOB 272 or FORS 240. Methods and techniques for identifying the major families of North American trees, based on gross morphological and anatomical features. Building and use of identification keys.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Intro to GIS for Forest Mgt
courses.desc: Offered every term. This course is designed as a practical introduction to the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for storing, retrieving, analyzing and displaying spatial data. It will also cover the history of cartography and the conventions of the modern map-making process. Students need to register for a required lab section. Credit cannot be earned for both FORS 250 and GPHY 284.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors; new courses or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered every term. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered fall. Restricted to majors in Forestry. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Field Methods in Forest Ecology
courses.desc: This course introduces students to all aspects of forest demography and forest community ecology in the field. Particular attention is given to the agents of woody plant mortality, including beetle gallery identification, pathogenic fungi, spatially explicit density-dependent mortality, fire, and the effects of landscape position. Students learn how data are collected to maximize information used to answer scientific questions, including the relationships between accuracy, precision, uncertainty, and cost (in time and money). Students then collect tree demography data within the Yosemite Forest Dynamics Plot. Students learn how to measure fuel loading at landscape scales according to federal standards. In addition to specific measurements in one forest type (white fir/sugar pine), students visit and compare the other principal forest types of the Sierra Nevada and White Mountains (ponderosa pine, red fir, Jeffrey pine, lodgepole pine, whitebark pine, pinyon/juniper, and bristlecone pine).

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Environmental Economics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. M 121 and M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172. Economic techniques to support decision making about the allocation of scarce resources in relation to the management of forests for timber and other ecosystem services.
courses.prereq: M 121 and M 122 or M 151 or M 162 or M 171 or M 172

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., one of BIOO 105N, BIOB 170N, BIOE 172N, BIOB 160, or BIOB 101N ; and either prereq. or coreq. one of ENSC 245N, FORS 241N, NRSM 211N, or GPHY111N. Examination of physical and biological factors affecting forest structure, composition, and function, including biodiversity and species interactions, succession, disturbance, and nutrient cycling. Introduces foundational ecological theory and terminology, illustrated with examples from local, regional, and global forest ecosystems.
courses.prereq: one of BIOO 105N, BIOB 170N, BIOE 172N, BIOB 160, or BIOB 101N ; and either prereq. or coreq. one of ENSC 245N, FORS 241N, NRSM 211N, or GPHY111N

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Wildland Fuel Management
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., FORS 230. The fire ecology of some western vegetation types is discussed. Elements of the principles of wildland fuel management are presented. Prescribed fire use and mechanical manipulation are matched to historic ecosystem processes. Smoke management considerations and health issues are also presented.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Fire Ecology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., FORS 230 or FORS 330 or BIOE 370 or BIOE 342 or NRSM 462. A detailed analysis of fire ecology in terrestrial ecosystems with a focus on the Rocky Mountains, including fire history, fire effects, landscape patterns, land use legacies, management implications, and current topics. Includes at least one required all-day field trip.
courses.prereq: FORS 230 or FORS 330 or BIOE 370 or BIOE 342 or NRSM 462

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Ecology Field Laboratory
courses.desc: Prereq., FORS 130 or FORS 202. Prereq. or coreq., FORS 330. Field course with overnight camping. Must be able to safely travel off trail on steep, forested terrain. Introduces field techniques for measuring forest ecosystem attributes and illustrates foundational forest ecology theory and concepts with field visits to local and regional forests.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Sustainable Forest Products
courses.desc: Offered spring. Survey of forest products, including manufacture, use, markets, and impact on forest management. Life cycle analysis of wood products is compared to common alternatives. Labs include visits to area forest product manufacturing facilities including an all-day field trip.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Timber Harvesting & Roads
courses.desc: Offered spring. An overview of harvesting system capabilities and selection for multiple resource objectives. Fundamentals of forest road management. Best management practices as they apply to forest operations in Montana and the western United States.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Wood Anatomy, Properties, & Identification
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., BIOO 105N or FORS 241N. Lecture and laboratory investigation of the structure, identification, and physical and mechanical properties of the commercial tree species of North America.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Multiple Resource Silviculture
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., FORS 330 or BIOE 370. Credit not allowed for both FORS 347 and 349. An introduction to the concepts and application of silvicultural techniques to forest ecosystems to meet multiple resource objectives.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Practice of Silviculture
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., FORS 202 and FORS 241N. Prereq. or coreq., FORS 330. Practice of Silviculture is designed primarily for Forestry majors (open to others with appropriate prerequisites), and will consider the conceptual foundations behind various silvicultural practices and techniques, as well as and their application in forest ecosystems to meet multiple resource objectives. The course will cover natural stand dynamics, stand assessment and site classification schemes, even- and uneven-aged silvicultural systems, thinning/stand density concepts, regeneration practices, stand diagnosis and prescription development, vegetative management strategies for diverse objectives, along with quantitative assessment and modeling of alternative prescriptions.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forestry Apps of GIS
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., FORS 250 or GPHY 284. Introduction to the basic concepts and techniques of computerized spatial data management and analysis systems and application to natural resource management.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Env Remote Sensing
courses.desc: Offered spring. The theory and application of photo- and electro-optical remote sensing for mapping resources and developing information systems.

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Community Ecology
courses.desc: Prereq., FORS 330 with a minimum grade of B. This course provides a foundation in ecological theory as well as an introduction to current findings and recent advances in vegetation community ecology, stand structure dynamics, and forest disturbance process. Co-convenes with FORS 531. Level: Undergraduate
courses.prereq: FORS 330 with a minimum grade of B

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Advanced Forest Roads
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., FORS 341. The purpose of this course is to help students understand the principles and skills of forest road design and the concepts of forest transportation planning. The course will cover the basic topics of road location, design, construction, and maintenance and provide students with techniques to identify the combination of roads, facilities and transport systems which minimize costs and negative environmental impacts. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Advaced Timber Harvesting
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., FORS 341. This course covers the fundamentals of logging feasibility and cost analyses of various timber harvesting systems including the characteristics and performance of ground vehicles, cable and aerial systems; cost factors and cost analysis procedures; safety issues; and environmental impacts of harvesting systems. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Statistical Models for Ecological Data Analysis
courses.desc: Prereq., FORS 201. This is an applied course covering statistical modeling techniques using examples from forestry, ecology, and the environmental sciences. I will cover data management, visualization, and scripting with R, an open source data analysis and statistics platform which is the standard in many scientific disciplines. After reviewing the linear regression model and associated diagnostics, I will explore various parametric and non-parametric modeling strategies that relax the linear model assumptions and allow for non-linear response functions and/or non-Gaussian response distributions. Estimation and inference in the context of generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and classification and regression trees will be discussed using examples from the scientific literature. Co-convenes with FORS 538. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Stand Management
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., FORS 202 and FORS 341 and FORS 347 or FORS 349. The management and manipulation of forest stands to reach multiple objectives, with a focus on the planning of forest operations for a community partner. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: FORS 202 and FORS 341 and FORS 347 or FORS 349

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Applied Methods in Forest Restoration and Utilization
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered every term. Meeting all day on Saturdays, and some Sundays, this course involves training students to safely and efficiently identify forest stands to be restored through appropriately-planned management activities including both live and dead timber felling operations, manufacture of sawlogs and pulpwood, proper management of slash and residuals, grapple skidding and the production of lumber using both circular sawmill and bandsaw mill. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Planning
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., FORS 320; and FORS 347 or FORS 349. Integrated multiple use planning at the forest-wide level: defining multi-resource management goals, generating management alternatives, projecting outcomes, assessing environmental impacts, and implementing preferred option. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Honors Forest Planning
courses.desc: Coreq., FORS 481. This course is the honors increment for FORS 481, providing honors students with greater insight into the complexities of forest management in Montana and the Norther Rocky Mountain region through in-depth small group conversations with forest management leaders. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Wildland RxFire Practicum
courses.desc: Students should have prior fire experience. An intensive field course providing students with technical training, practical applications, and theoretical foundations in ecological burning for restoration purposes. Class is typically held in southeastern United States. Co-convened with FORS 544. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Senior Thesis
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students with senior standing. Preparation of a major paper based on study or research in a field selected according to the needs and objectives of the student. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Sampling Methods
courses.desc: Offered spring. Fundamentals of statistical sampling emphasizing natural and environmental resource applications. Principles of inferences and alternative estimators are studied in the context of simple random, systematic, unequal probability, stratified, and 3P/Poisson designs. Variable radius plot sampling, line intersect sampling, and other probability proportional to size designs used in forest and ecological inventories are also covered. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Forest Community Ecology
courses.desc: Prior coursework or experience in ecology, botany, or forestry is strongly recommended. This course provides a foundation in ecological theory as well as an introduction to current findings and recent advances in forest community ecology, stand structure dynamics, and forest disturbance process. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Applied Forest Ecology
courses.desc: This course covers the use of ecological theory and data in the design of silvicultural treatments to achieve multiple management objectives, with particular emphasis on forest restoration and climate change adaptation. We examine methods of silvicultural design, including use of historical and contemporary reference conditions, and climate adaptation strategies. Analysis exercises use the open source statistical program and language R for data analysis, visualization, and modeling, especially of spatial point pattern data. Introduction to monitoring and adaptive management of silvicultural treatments. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Ecological Statistics
courses.desc: Offered autumn. This is an applied course covering advanced statistical modeling techniques using examples from forestry, ecology, and the environmental sciences. Covers data management, visualization, and scripting with R, an open source data analysis and statistics platform. Explores various parametric and semi-parametric modeling strategies that allow for non-linear response functions and/or non-Gaussian response distributions. Estimation and inference in the context of generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and classification and regression trees are discussed using examples from the scientific literature. Lays the foundation for subsequent graduate-level analytic coursework. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Fire and Disturbance Ecology
courses.desc: This course covers foundational concepts in disturbance ecology and fire ecology, examines important and influential theories in both fields, and focuses on currently literature at the cutting-edge of fire ecology research. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Adv. Wildland RXFire Practicum
courses.desc: An intensive field course providing students with technical training, practical applications, and theoretical foundations in ecological burning for restoration purposes. Students will practice leadership skills by supervising and training fire personnel in application of prescribed fire. Class typically held in southeastern United States. Co-convened with FORS 495. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FORS
courses.title: Landscape Ecology
courses.desc: Offered Spring semester even years. Prereq., FORS 538. The purpose of this course is to provide students with an introduction to the discipline of landscape ecology with a focus on applications within ecology and natural resource management. In addition to studying the fundamentals of landscape ecology through reading primary literature, students will gain exposure to a range of tools used in the analysis of geo-spatial data including raster analysis, environmental remote sensing, state transition models and species distribution models. Another objective is to engage students in student-directed learning within an inter-disciplinary environment to improve and refine students oral and written communication skills. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: FRCH

courses.desc: Prereq., FRCH 301. Survey of literature and culture of the diverse Francophone World with a focus on the significance of plural cultural identities.

courses.title: The French Cinema
courses.desc: (R–6) Offered intermittently. An historical, aesthetic, and critical survey of the French cinema, from its beginnings in 1895 through the contemporary cinema (Muet, classical, Realism, Nouvelle Vogue, etc.) With an introduction to contemporary film criticism. Students taking the course for French credits are required to do research, reading, and writing in the French language.

courses.desc: (R-6) Offered spring. Prereq., FRCH 301. Chronological/topical study of French culture.

courses.subject: EGEN
courses.title: Intro to Engineering Calculation & Problem Solving
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq. or coreq., M 151, or M 121 and M 122, or M 171 or M 172 or ALEX score of 5, or M03-Maplesoft Calculus score >= 15. An introduction to engineering calculations, problem solving, and design. Students are taught to solve and present engineering problems on computers using spreadsheet and graphic software (AutoCAD). In addition, there will be discussions on engineering failures and engineering ethics.
courses.prereq: or coreq., M 151, or M 121 and M 122, or M 171 or M 172 or ALEX score of 5, or M03-Maplesoft Calculus score >= 15

courses.subject: EGEN
courses.title: Engineering Statics
courses.desc: Prereq., PHSX 220 and M 171. Prereq. or coreq., M 172. Equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies; addition and resolution of forces, vector algebra, moments and couples, resultants and static equilibrium, equivalent force systems, centroids, center of gravity, free body method of analysis, two and three dimensional equilibrium, trusses, frames, friction, and method of virtual work.

courses.subject: EGEN
courses.title: Engineering Mechanics - Dynamics
courses.desc: Prereq., EGEN 201 and M 172. Particle and rigid body kinematics and kinetics; rectilinear, curvilinear, and relative motion, equations of motion, work and energy, impulse and momentum, systems of particles, rotation, rotating axes, rigid body analysis, angular momentum, vibration, and time response.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Intro to Physical Geography: Climate, Landforms, and Vegetation
courses.desc: Offered spring. Introduction to earth system science, the study of the earth’s climate, surface processes, and ecosystems, and their distributions, functions, and interactions.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Intro to Physical Geography Laboratory: Climate, Landforms, and Vegetation Lab
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq. or coreq., GPHY 111N. Introduction to techniques and methods needed to understand and analyze data, graphs, maps, and images of the earth’s climate, surface processes, and ecosystems, and their interactions.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Human Geography
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Introduction to Human Geography focuses upon the linkages between geography and society including analysis of regions, ethnic groups, urban landscapes, migration and population change, geopolitics, economics, and cultural differences.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Geography of World Regions
courses.desc: Offered autumn and/or spring. An overall view of how the lands and peoples of the world are organized into coherent geographical regions, how landscapes differ from region to region, and how the people differ in terms of their traits, beliefs, ways of life, and economic livelihood.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Montana
courses.desc: Offered autumn. The physical, cultural, economic, political, and historical geography of the state including Montana’s mountains and the prairies.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: The Middle East
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. A survey of the biophysical and cultural geography of Southwest Asia and North Africa. Emphasis on environmental change; prehistory; patterns of cultural and historical change; issues of socio-economic, religious, and political diversity; and the broader political significance of the region.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Intro to GIS and Cartography
courses.desc: Offered every term. This course is designed as a practical introduction to the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for storing, retrieving, analyzing and displaying spatial data. It will also cover the history of cartography and the conventions of the modern map-making process. Students need to register for a required lab section. Credit cannot be earned for both FORS 250 and GPHY 284.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Mountain Field Studies
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring as a series of one-credit courses with a maximum of three-credits per semester. Field studies of Montana's Rocky Mountain Front, Crown of the Continent, or Yellowstone. Students prepare to conduct field work, spend time in the field observing wildlife, physical landscapes and cultural aspects of these landscapes, and follow up their observations in written reports.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Geomorphology
courses.desc: Offered autumn even-numbered years. Prereq., GPHY 111N or GEO 101N. Important landforms and landscapes, their biophysical processes, and their formative elements.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Economic Geography of Rural Areas
courses.desc: Offered spring odd-numbered years. Study of the location of economic activities, including agriculture, industry, and services. Focus on the changing nature of rural areas.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Water and Sustainability
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Geographical perspective on water resource issues and challenges facing the public, resource managers, and water users in the western United States. Examines concepts, terms, and regulatory environment which provide the foundation for sustainable water management and policy.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Mountains and Society
courses.desc: Offered spring. Physical and cultural aspects of the mountains of North and South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia. Emphasis on combining the physical landscape with an overview of the indigenous people who inhabit the worlds’ heights.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Field Studies in Geography
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Through extended backcountry travel, experiential examination of regional landforms, climate, hydrology, soils, and patterns of vegetation and wildlife. Local landscapes, natural-resource endowment, and societies with particular emphasis on human-environmental interaction. Geographical skills and techniques, including map reading and navigational skills. Offered by the Wild Rockies Field Institute as part of a semester-long, 12-credit field experience with corequisite courses in allied fields.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Preceptorship in Geography
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Assisting a faculty member by tutoring, conducting review sessions, helping students with research projects, and carrying out other class-related responsibilities.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Field Techniques
courses.desc: Offered autumn and intermittently in spring. Field techniques used by geographers and planners in making field observations and in collecting data.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: GPHY

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary.

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Field Studies
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered fall and/or spring. Field experience in the region. Includes geographically relevant field courses offered as part of Swan Valley Connections' Landscape and Livelihood Field Semester, focusing on natural and human communities and on conservation solutions of the Southwest Crown of the Continent Region: Sustainability and Agriculture (3 cr), and Biogeography of Northwest Montana (4 cr).

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Geography Capstone
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students with senior standing. Exploration of current research, projects, and programs of geographers and scientists/practitioners in allied disciplines and fields, and preparation of a professional portfolio. Student preparation for post-graduate professional and academic careers is emphasized. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Sustainable Cities
courses.desc: Offered spring even-numbered years. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. A discussion of sustainability efforts in cities around the world. Topics include, for example, urban sprawl and smart growth, alternative energy, public transportation, integrated waste management, integrated water management, green architecture, and urban agriculture. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Community Resilience
courses.desc: Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. Examines human-environment relations and interactions. Topics include: human geographic perspectives on landscape, cultural ecology, political ecology, community resilience in relation to complex adaptive systems, and planning applications. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Planning Principles & Processes
courses.desc: Offered autumn even-numbered years. Restricted to students with at least junior standing. Surveys planning principles, practices and issues in urban and rural environments. Attention is devoted to Montana, state planning programs in the United States., and federal programs and policies that influence land-use planning. Emphasizes skills and techniques used in plan development and implementation. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Environmental Planning
courses.desc: Offered autumn odd-numbered years. Introduction to practice of environmental planning which includes elements of physical planning, planning design at the landscape scale, and conservation planning. Includes field visits and project-based work. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Community & Regional Analysis
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Coreq., GPHY 469. Socio-demographic analysis of communities and regions: population, employment, and spatial interaction. Hands-on course designed for future planners, GIS analysts, and others interested in socio-demographic change. To succeed in this course students should have comfort with basic algebra. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Planning & Analysis Laboratory
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Coreq., GPHY 468. Laboratory to accompany GPHY 468. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: UAV Remote Sensing for Field Ecology
courses.desc: Offered summer only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station. Prereq., FORS 250 or GPHY 284. This course will introduce students to field-based methods of close-range remote sensing in freshwater ecosystems. Students will gain knowledge of basic spatial analysis through GIS and remote sensing techniques. Students will learn basic applications of UAVs and Acoustic Doppler Profilers, two remote sensing instruments of fast-growing interest in ecological research and application. Students will learn about essentials to operate UAVs and ADPs, initial post-processing of data products and integrating these data into ecological research and application. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.offered: summer only at the Flathead Lake Biological Station

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Advanced Cartographic Design
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., GPHY 284 or FORS 250. This course concentrates on the presentation of spatial data and the construction of cartographic products that have clear communication and excellent aesthetic design. The class meets the University's service learning course objectives through a semester long project where students consult with a client, design and construct a map, and deliver a final product. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Spatial Analysis & GIS
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., GPHY 284 or FORS 250. Coreq., GPHY 489. Quantitative analysis of spatial data, including techniques for pattern analysis, classification, and interpolation within a GIS environment. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Internet GIS
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., GPHY 284 or FORS 250. Principles and techniques for distributing GIS and mapping applications through the Internet. Students need to register for a required linked lab section. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Transport, Planning & GIS. 2,3 Credits
courses.desc: Coreq., GPHY 489. A project-oriented course focusing on patterns and trends in urban passenger transportation, principles of transport planning, and modeling in GIS-T. To succeed in this course students should have comfort with basic algebra and statistics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Remote Sensing/Raster GIS
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq. or coreq., GPHY 284 or FORS 250. Coreq., GPHY 489. Basic principles of remote sensing and analyzing images within a raster GIS. Review current data sources. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Applications of GIS
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., GPHY 284 or FORS 250. Application of GIS for managing natural and cultural resources. Covers choropleth maps, dot maps, proportional figure maps, isarithmic maps, and others. Includes computer mapping and GIS exercises. Students need to register for a required linked lab section. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: GPHY
courses.title: Cartography/GIS Laboratory
courses.desc: (R-4) Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., or coreq., GPHY 482, 486 or 487. Lab to accompany cartography and GIS courses. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Concepts and techniques in geography, with emphasis on their use in teaching geography in Montana schools. Students are required to prepare and present a teaching unit project. Designed for pre-service or in-service teachers. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
