courses.subject: M
courses.title: Prealgebra
courses.desc: Offered every term. Offered at Missoula College. Arithmetic and basic algebra skills needed for Introductory Algebra. Topics include integers and rational numbers, decimals and percentages with applications, ratios and proportions with applications, single variable linear equations with applications, introduction to graphing, exponents, factoring, and an introduction to polynomials. Credit does not count toward a certificate or degree. Credit does not count toward Associate of Arts, Associate of Applied Science, or Baccalaureate degrees.

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Introductory Algebra
courses.desc: Offered every term. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., M 065 or appropriate math placement score. Review of arithmetic principles of integers and rational numbers, linear equations in one or two unknowns, systems of linear equations and operations with polynomials and rational expressions. Credit does not count toward an Associate of Arts, Associate of Applied Science, or Baccalaureate degree.
courses.prereq: M 065 or appropriate math placement score

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Intermediate Algebra
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Prereq., M 090 or appropriate math placement score. Topics include linear equations, inequalities, applications and graphing; polynomials; radicals, rational exponents and complex numbers; quadratic equations. Graphing calculator required. Credit does not count toward Associate of Arts or Baccalaureate degrees.
courses.prereq: M 090 or appropriate math placement score

courses.subject: M
courses.title: STEM Algebra Prep
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., M 065 with a grade of C or better; or EdReady placement level 1.5; or ACT score of 18; or SAT score of 460 (with the new test); or ACT score of 15 and HS GPA 3.0; or SAT score of 400 and HS GPA 3.0. Intended for students heading into STEM fields who took high-school Algebra II or an equivalent course but did not place into M 121 College Algebra with co-requisite support. Students engage with functions from four complementary perspectives—geometric (graphs), numeric (tables), symbolic (formulas), and written (verbal descriptions and interpretations)—to develop conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. Students will model real-world situations using linear, quadratic, polynomial, rational, and exponential functions, and interpret functions and their parameters in practical contexts. Through practice, group-work, and application, students strengthen their algebra skills while building confidence in their mathematical abilities.
courses.prereq: M 065 with a grade of C or better; or EdReady placement level 1.5; or ACT score of 18; or SAT score of 460 (with the new test); or ACT score of 15 and HS GPA 3.0; or SAT score of 400 and HS GPA 3.0

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Contemporary Mathematics
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., M 090 or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 16; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2. An introduction to mathematical ideas and their impact on society. Intended for students wishing to satisfy the general education mathematics requirement. Co-Requisite Support sections of M 105 are 4 credits; they are offered autumn and spring. Co-requisite support section prerequisites as follows: EdReady placement level 1 or consent of instructor.
courses.prereq: M 090 or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 16; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Indigenous Ways of Knowing in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics
courses.desc: Offered fall. Over hundreds of generations, indigenous communities have developed sophisticated practices and ways of knowing in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). Understanding these practices and ways of knowing leads all students to have a a richer understanding of all STEM disciplines. This course introduces indigenous ways of knowing in STEM, including traditional ecological knowledge and indigenous perspectives on the relationships between human and other-than-human communities. The course also explores the connections between indigenous and western ways of knowing. The course is offered in collaboration with Montana American Indian Nations and may include guest lectures from elders and other knowledge keepers and place-based learning on community homelands.

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Probability and Linear Mathematics
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., M 090 or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 16; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2. Systems of linear equations and matrix algebra. Introduction to probability with emphasis on models and probabilistic reasoning. Examples of applications of the material in many fields. Co-Requisite Support sections of M 115 are 4 credits; they are offered autumn and spring. Co-requisite support section prerequisites as follows: EdReady placement level 1.5; or ACT score of 18; or SAT score of 460 (with the new test); or ACT score of 15 and HS GPA 3.0; or SAT score of 400 and HS GPA 3.0; or consent of instructor.
courses.prereq: M 090 or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 16; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Mathematics for Music Enthusiasts
courses.desc: Offered autumn and/or spring. Prereq. M 090 with a grade of B- or better; or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 18; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2; and elementary music background. An introduction to the interplay between mathematics and music. Course intended for Music majors/minors, and others with musical backgrounds/interests, who wish to satisfy the general education mathematics requirement.
courses.prereq: M 090 with a grade of B- or better; or M 095 with a grade of C- or better; or EdReady placement level 2; or M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >= 18; or ACT score of 21; or SAT score of 530 (with the new test); or ACT score of 20 and HS GPA 3.2; or SAT score of 510 and HS GPA 3.2; and elementary music background

courses.subject: M
courses.title: College Algebra. 3,4 Credits
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., M 095; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.4; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.4. The central theme of College Algebra is functions as models of change. This course fulfills the prerequisites for M 122 (College Trigonometry) and for M 162 (Applied Calculus). Intended to strengthen algebra skills. The study of functions and their inverses; polynomial, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Credit not allowed for both M 121 and M 151. Co-Requisite Support sections of M 121 are 4 credits; they are offered autumn and spring. Co-requisite support section prerequisites as follows: EdReady placement level 2.5; M01-Maplesoft Arithmetic score >=16; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >=10; or ACT score of 22; or SAT score of 540 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.4; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.4; if the student is fresh out of high school, completion of Algebra II or beyond; or consent of instructor.
courses.prereq: M 095; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.4; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.4

courses.subject: M
courses.title: College Trigonometry
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., M 121. Preparation for calculus based on college algebra. Review of functions and their inverses. Trigonometric functions and identities, polar coordinates and an optional topic such as complex numbers, vectors or parametric equations. Credit not allowed for both M 122 and M 151.

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Numbers and Operations for Elementary School Teachers
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., M 095; or M 115; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.5; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.5. The study of number and operations for prospective elementary and middle school teachers, including whole numbers, decimals, fractions, percent, integers, operations, numeration systems, and problem solving.
courses.prereq: M 095; or M 115; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.5; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.5

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Geometry and Measurement for Elementary School Teachers
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., M 132. The study of geometry and geometric measurement for prospective elementary and middle school teachers, including synthetic, transformational, and coordinate geometry, constructions, congruence and similarity, 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional measurement, and problem solving.

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Precalculus
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., EdReady placement level 4; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 17; or M03-Maplesoft Calculus score >=10; or ACT score of 25; or SAT score of 590 (with the new test); or ACT score of 23 and HS GPA 3.6 and HS Precalc or Calculus with a B- or better; or SAT score of 560 and HS GPA 3.5 and HS Precalc or Calculus with a B- or better. A one semester preparation for calculus (as an alternative to M 121 - M 122. Functions of one real variable are introduced in general and then applied to the usual elementary functions, namely polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, trigonometric functions, and miscellaneous others. Inverse functions, polar coordinates and trigonometric identities are included. Credit not allowed for both M 151 and M 121 or M 122.

Topics include combinatorics and graph theory, including enumeration, graph algorithms, matching problems, and networks.

courses.title: Partial Differential Equations
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., M 274. Fourier series, Sturm-Liouville and boundary value problems. Partial differential equations: Cauchy problems and the method of characteristics, separation of variables and Laplace transform methods. Numerical methods and selected topics. M 418 computer lab recommended. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Deterministic Models
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., M 263 or M 274. Linear and nonlinear difference and differential equations: stability, phase-plane analysis, oscillatory behavior, limit cycles, and chaos. Eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Emphasis on models in biology. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: History of Mathematics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., M 307. Historical study of the development of mathematics from the Egyptian and Babylonian eras to the 20th century. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Abstract Algebra I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., M 221 and M 307. An introduction to modern ideas of algebra through the study of groups, rings, and fields. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Abstract Algebra II
courses.desc: Offered intermittently in spring. Prereq., M 431. Continues the investigation of groups, rings, and fields begun in M 431. Further topics include vector spaces and field extensions. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Euclidean and NonEuclidean Geometry
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., M 307. Euclidean geometry from a rigorous, axiomatic viewpoint and Non–Euclidean geometries chosen from Lobachevskian, projective, finite and Riemannian. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Numerical Analysis
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., M 221 and M 274. Some experience with computer programming is expected. Topics include: error analysis, approximation and interpolation, numerical solution of linear and non-linear equations, numerical optimization, numerical integration of ordinary and partial differential equations, and applications. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Data Science Analytics
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., STAT 342 or STAT 421; and M 221 or M 273. This is a methods course supporting the Big Data Certificate Program. The course provides the students with the essential tools of data analytics. The content consists of data dictionaries and data mappings, distributed computing, and related methods. Other topics may include data visualization, regression, and cluster analysis. This course may be used to satisfy the course requirements of the Big Data Certificate Program. Level: Undergraduate. Co-convenes with M 561.
courses.prereq: STAT 342 or STAT 421; and M 221 or M 273

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Theoretical Basics of Big Data Analytics and Real Time Computation Algorithms
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., M 221. The main goal of this course is to provide students with a unique opportunity to acquire conceptual knowledge and theoretical background behind mathematical tools applicable to Big Data Analytics and Real Time Computations. Specific challenges of Big Data Analytics, e.g., problems of extracting, unifying, updating, and merging information, and processing of highly parallel and distributed data, will be reviewed. The tools for Big Data Analytics, such as regression analysis, linear estimation, calibration problems, real time processing of incoming (potentially infinite) data, will be studied in more detail. It will be shown how these approaches can be transformed to conform to the Big Data demands. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Data Science Projects
courses.desc: Offered spring. This course is a practicum course aimed at developing skills needed to solve data science problems facing industry and academics. Problems are brought to the class by local technology-oriented businesses and university researchers. Lecture topics include project management, interacting with clients, and written and oral presentation of results. Additional lecture topics will be selected to address the specific problems brought to the class and may cover data reduction methods, algorithm design and predictive analytics. Level: Undergraduate. Co-convenes with M 567.

courses.title: Introduction to Complex Analysis

courses.subject: M
courses.title: Advanced Big Data Analytics Projects
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., STAT 341 and M 221 or M 273 and one of M 461 or M 462. In this course, local businesses and University researchers will contribute practical problems from data science to the class. Students will learn how to work in teams to develop solutions to the contributed problems, graduate students will serve as lead investigators on these teams. Learning outcomes include: Develop data reduction algorithms for complex problems and varied data. Apply mathematical, statistical, and computational methods used in solving big data problems. Extend and adapt core algorithms to specific problems. Work with a client towards understanding client objectives and meeting the objectives. Propose alternative paths towards the solution when necessary. Plan a project (determine what is realistic and achievable within a time frame). Document progress and elicit feedback from clients. Write concise and focused progress reports. Efficiently allocate workload among team members. Effectively communicate and participate as a team member. Level: Graduate. Co-convenes with M 467.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Fundamentals of Esports
courses.desc: (R-4) Offered every term. Class meets on Mountain Campus in the U.C. Game Room. Explore the basics of various esports including rules, concepts, strategies, and mechanics. Semester concludes with a gaming tournament. Students must bring their own headset for team play. Graded Credit/No Credit based on participation and attendance policy. Students may include up to, but not more than, 4 credits earned in MART 100 and all other ACT 100-179 activity courses in the total number of credits required for graduation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Intro to Media Arts
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. How do narrative and literary techniques manifest themselves in the media arts? Using the language of film as a starting point, students analyze storytelling through various media, including movies, television, the Internet, animation and video games.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: History of Games and Play
courses.desc: This course explores the cultural, political, and social histories of games from antiquity to the present. Students will investigate how games function as primary sources and cultural artifacts across a range of historical and contemporary contexts, from ancient board games, sporting tournaments, and medieval carnival to modern video games and tabletop RPGs. By considering games as both texts and lived experiences, students will learn how playful pursuits have shaped culture, society, and the course of history itself. Through weekly case studies, hands-on playful experiences, and reflective writing, this course encourages critical inquiry and reflection on history through examining one of the most enduring and revealing forms of human expression: play.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Introduction to Film Editing
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Study of the history, process and philosophy of narrative ﬁlm/video editing.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creative Coding I
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. This course focuses on the fundamentals of programming and its connection to the creative and expressive possibilities of media art. Visual and scripting languages provide the foundation by which stories and games are created.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Jams
courses.desc: Game Jams are rapid iterative development sessions used to inspire creativity in the gaming industry sometimes conducted in as little as 24 hours. Although this course will not require the student to work quite as quickly, we will be completing roughly one game every week, sometimes every two weeks depending on the project. Through this rapid creation, limited and often simplified tools will draw out creative ideation and conceptualization. Every project will focus on a certain aspect or genre of game design. The aim in these methods is to allow a space for experimentation and to promote creativity, weirdness, and even failure. Through this process of prototyping, playtesting, and theory, students will learn and develop the core principles of game design and development.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Esports Team
courses.desc: (R-4) Students may include up to but not more than 4 credits earned in ACT/ACTV/HHP 100-299 or MART 100/189 activity courses in the total number of credits required for graduation. Students graded Credit/No Credit based on participation and a strict attendance policy.

courses.subject: MART

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: History of Digital Arts & Culture
courses.desc: Offered every term. This course places current digital technologies within a historical context in order to understand and articulate how the digital world in which we live, and the tools with which we create, are connected to people, cultures and times before the latest innovations were even conceived. This knowledge will prepare students to engage with creative professionals across areas of expertise and to have a broader sense of their lives as citizens in a globally and historically connected world.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creation of Media Story
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Preparatory to writing in visual story forms (screenplay, animation, games) students immerse themselves in writing and drawing improvisations through journaling and short project creation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Digital Publishing & Design
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. A comprehensive foundation of layout and design principles to integrate digital media essential for effective print-based and web-based business publications.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Tabletop Game Design: Card Games, Board Games, and TTRPGs
courses.desc: This course covers the design of tabletop games of all kinds—board games, card games, and tabletop roleplaying games. It introduces the foundational principles of game design through analog games, offering an accessible, no-code way to approach game design and development for beginners. The principles covered in this class—including rule systems and mechanics, narrative and theming, visual and component design, playtesting, and technical documentation—are all transferable skills and concepts that can inform future work in digital game design and development. Working in teams, students will conceive, prototype, test, and refine their own tabletop games over the course of the semester, culminating in a final presentation and play session. By analyzing classic games, engaging in regular playtests, and applying design theory in practice, students will gain a deep understanding of how to create compelling, balanced, and immersive analog experiences.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creative Coding II
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., MART 120. Building on the techniques, theory, and skills acquired in Creative Coding I, students create artworks and experiences focusing on physical computing. These include, but not limited to: Raspberry Pi, Arduino, Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creating for Social Media: From Concept to Final Cut
courses.desc: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the creative and technical process of producing content for social media platforms. Students will learn to translate ideas into effective visual narratives by planning, filming, and editing short-form video with attention to platform conventions and audience engagement. Through project-based learning, peer critique, and critical reflection, students will develop practical skills in storytelling, production workflows, and digital editing, preparing them to create purposeful, high-impact media for contemporary platforms.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Interactive Web II
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Offered at Missoula College. Provides a background and foundation skills required for designing and implementing Web sites for public and private organizations. Marketing and design techniques are applied using state-of-the-art software.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Sound Production & Design Fundamentals
courses.desc: Offered every semester. Sound Production & Design Fundamentals introduces students to the fields of sound production, sound design, audio technology, and sonic art. This course is intended as a foundation course to create shared terminology, skill sets, aesthetics, and techniques for students to utilize as they take additional sound design, sonic art, or audio courses within the School of Visual and Media Arts (SVMA) or larger College of the Arts and Media (CAM). This course includes the study of notable examples in sound art/design, music, intermedia, and installation. Starting with listening, students will examine the practices and innovations that led to the most current ideas about sound art and sound design and from there develop contemporary analytical methods for exploring sound as a creative medium. Additionally, students will apply this knowledge to the creation of their own sonic art works.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Photoshop: Art and Design
courses.desc: Offered spring. This project-based course explores a variety of design principles and techniques through Adobe Photoshop.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Illustrator: Vector and Layout Design
courses.desc: Offered every term. An introduction to the basic principles and techniques of still image design and manipulation using Adobe Illustrator, the industry leading application for creating vector-based content. This project-based course demystifies the powerful Illustrator toolsets and workspace and enables students to actualize their ideas by helping them to develop an efficient production process. No prerequisites required.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: 2D Game Art
courses.desc: This course introduces students to the various forms and workflows in the creation of art and assets in two-dimensional video games. We will look at the various styles and aspects of 2D games such as pixel art, side-scrollers, top down, isometric, character design, environment design, concept art, animation, and user interfaces. This course is project based and centers around developing the students' own creative concepts and portfolios. This course acts as a foundation for the various pathways in game art.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Visions of Film
courses.desc: Offered spring. Study of major ﬁlm theories that led to the constitution of visual ﬁlm language and their application in contemporary ﬁlm narrative and direction.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Intro to Motion Design
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. This project-oriented course will introduce students to the basic technical and aesthetic components of digital motion design and 2D animation using the industry standard software programs Photoshop and After Effects.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: 3D Modeling for Game Design
courses.desc: This course is an introduction to theories and skills in developing 3D assets and environments for game design and interactive media. 3D modeling covers the fundamentals and workflows from concepts to creation in covering 3D design, modeling, lighting, texturing, rendering, character creation, rigging and leading up to animation. 3D modeling acts as a foundation for many forms of digital image creation and courses offered at the University of Montana such as animation, game development, and other media arts courses. The goals of this course is to develop the conceptual and cultural theories as well as the technical skills of 3D modeling. The course primarily focuses on Blender, it will also overlap with game engines such as Unreal and Unity and touch upon other various industry software, workflows and topics such as UV mapping, texturing, AI, technical art, procedural and parametric design.
courses.offered: at the University of Montana such as animation, game development, and other media arts courses

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Modern Horror Film
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. This class explores the changing landscape of the horror ﬁlm since 1960, studying the genre and its sociological importance through the language of cinema.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: 3D Animation I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. This course is an introduction to fundamental concepts, principles, and practices of 3D digital modeling with Maya. Students will develop 3D modeling techniques, including production of geometric and organic objects. Through lectures, tutorials, in-class exercises, and projects, students will be exposed to various techniques that may be used for innovative and artistic content such as filmic animation and compositing.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: 3D Sculpting for Games: Characters and Soft Surface Techniques
courses.desc: With an emphasis on 3D character development, this course covers concepts for creation in digital 3D sculpting techniques and applications. This course works in conjunction with the 3D-modeling course and acts as a foundation for hard surface modeling and environments. This course teaches soft surface modeling and emphasizes character design through a specific 3D workflow known as sculpting. The goals of this course is to develop the skills and workflow in soft surface, from sculpting, to retopology, texture painting, rigging, animation, and integration with a game engine.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Introduction to Animation
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Introduction to two-dimensional digital animation, focusing on character and motion design animation fundamentals including: cell animation (frame by frame), motion-tweening, working with keyframes and motion paths, moving elements on a 2D stage, object choreography, and text animation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Intro to Cinematography
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Study of digital cinematography including color theory, composition, lens choice, continuity, camera movement/support, lighting for film and video, and grip in both studio and location situations.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Edconic: Digital Futures in Contemporary Art
courses.desc: Offered every semester. Restricted to students in the Edconic program. Taught at Sotheby's Institute in London by Edconic instructors. This course explores the dynamic discourse at the intersection of contemporary art and digital technologies, equipping students with a practical and contextual knowledge of how these technologies are reimagining the landscape of contemporary art practice.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Analog Sound Design
courses.desc: Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Introduction to fundamental concepts, principles and practices of acoustic sound to establish a common aesthetic and technical language necessary to develop quality, audio-based Art.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Directing the Fiction Film
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., MAR 251. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Developing, directing and editing a five to seven minute fiction movie. In depth work on creation of shooting script, casting, work with actors and location work. Emphasis on collaborative process and diligence and preparation in all levels of production.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Principles of Interactive Media
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., MART 120. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Introduction to interactive theory and art. This course is designed to help students gain the skill sets necessary to successfully create work in the constantly evolving arts environment. Installation-based works. Uses code and material.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Introduction to Web Design
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., MART 120. Students will gain necessary skills in this introduction to the fundamentals of website structure, content design and navigation. Areas of focus will be directory structure, visual design, user navigation, audio/video integration and domain management. This course is open to all university students and geared to non-majors.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Art & Science of Interactive Games
courses.desc: Offer every term. Online course. This class is an introduction to the technological achievements and artistic and social impacts involved with the development of interactive games. It will cover the evolution of the gaming profile and the advanced visual, sonic and narrative properties that make interactive games the explosive growth industry that is today.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Sound for Film
courses.desc: Offered spring. This course is targeted at the Digital Filmmaking student and introduces fundamental concepts, principles and practices of digital location sound recording and post-production editing to picture in order to establish a common aesthetic and technical language.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Writing for TV
courses.desc: Writing for TV builds on the principles, theory, and practice of dramatic writing to engage in the specific techniques of screenwriting for television. Students will learn the unique format of writing for TV, analyze professional examples, develop original concepts, refine characters, write an original pilot episode, workshop their script pages in class, and practice pitching their series.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Ethics
courses.desc: Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. This course explores the ethical debates surrounding both analog and digital games. As a seminar course, students will actively engage in ethical argumentation with one another and explore ethical issues faced by both game developers and players. Students will gain an understanding of both applied ethics and normative theories as they relate to the development and analysis of digital games through case studies, games research, and current issues in the games industry.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Serious Games
courses.desc: This theoretically based course explores a different aspect of gaming as it pertains to serious games. As a seminar course, students gain an understanding of the serious gaming environment used in professional education and simulations. Students will also gain experience examining the most current research in this area.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Development
courses.desc: Offered fall. This is a fully online class with an optional synchronous component where students share ideas, collaborate, and create a fully functioning game throughout the semester with the potential of creating something for a full year with the intent of deploying it to a store. This course includes presentations from industry experts, game design principles, software engineering best practices, project management, and testing. Teams will work through hackathon challenges together and create projects for distribution.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Level Design
courses.desc: Prereq., MART 342; and MART 460 or MART 465. Level design is all about crafting interactive, evocative digital spaces for entertainment games, serious and training games, and museum exhibits. A level designer is responsible for creating immersive gameplay experiences for players and designing how a player flows through a digital environment. Exploring principles from a variety of disciplines, ranging from game design to architecture and urban planning, this course teaches students how to design engaging gameplay experiences and provides students with a generalized level design toolkit usable in all game genres. Students finish the semester by putting theory into practice to design and build working prototype levels.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Introduction to Immersive Media - Augmented and Virtual Reality
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Students will be introduced to immersive media through developing their own augmented and virtual reality experiences.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Esports Leadership
courses.desc: (R-3) Esports Leadership is a course focusing on leadership theories and skills specific to esports. Using scientifically backed research will empower leaders to work through many different situations. This course will also provide many growth opportunities using in-person and generative AI tools.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Practicum I
courses.desc: Offered every term. This course offers the student the opportunity to apply their media arts skill sets and techniques to a variety of professional level projects that include movies, web site design, and still image design.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Thriller Cinema: No Safe Place
courses.desc: This course explores the evolution and technique of the thriller genre in modern cinema. Through close examination of narrative structures, stylistic strategies, and thematic concerns, students learn how thrillers engage with questions of truth, identity, and power in ways that are deeply relevant to contemporary media and society. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Analysis
courses.desc: Prereq., WRIT 101 or WRIT 201. This course explores how to formally analyze games and interactive media. Students engage in a variety of analytic writing styles within game studies, from journalistic reviews to feature reports and interpretative analyses, and construct written arguments for both academic and professional audiences. Through close reading and critical play, analytic writing, and iterative revision, students develop a methodological toolkit they can employ to conduct formal analyses of games and interactive media. Emphasizing games as complex and interactive texts, this course covers topics such as narrative design, mechanics, spatial storytelling, interface, and intertextuality. By the end of the semester, students will have a critical vocabulary they can employ when writing and talking about games, insight into how analytical frameworks can inform their own game design work, and gain a deeper understanding of games as a form of interactive art. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Production Studio I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in Art and Media Arts. Students create storyboards/previsuals, idea sketches, and writing synopses, as well as identity and promotion of what will become ﬁnished works. Projects begun here will be continued in MART 457. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Sonic Programming
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., MART 120. This course merges skills and technique of creative coding with the creation of sonic art works. The majority of the class is focused on the creation of dynamic sound-based art works, and the application of concepts from interactive theory and interactive systems. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creative Improvisation in Sound and Visual Art
courses.desc: (R-9) This course explores the practice of creative improvisation as a collaborative and interdisciplinary art form. Students will form an ensemble dedicated to creating spontaneous sound, music, and visual media works, emphasizing process over product. Through experiential sessions, students will practice improvisation techniques, develop individual expressive vocabularies, and engage in collective creation without preconceived outcomes. While the majority of class time will be spent in active improvisation, students will also pursue outside work in the form of solo and small-group practice, development of technical proficiency in their chosen mediums (instruments, technologies, or expressive means), experiential engagement with contemporary improvisatory work (listening, viewing, attending), and short reflective/conceptual assignments. The course culminates in an ensemble presentation of improvised works, highlighting the integration of sound, music, and visual media.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Advanced Sound Arts Studio
courses.desc: (R-9) Prereq., MART 245. This is an advanced critique-based studio course focused on the exploration and creation of sound-based artworks. Students will design and propose their own projects while also responding to guided assignments that address contemporary sound art practices. Emphasis is placed on technical refinement, conceptual development, and the integration of sound within broader artistic, cultural, and social contexts. Through studio work, readings, presentations, and critiques, students will develop a personal vocabulary in sound while engaging in critical dialogue about their work and the field at large. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Producing
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Students take on the creative role of the producer in making narrative films. The class covers everything from script choice and analysis through hiring, casting, budgeting, and all of the steps from pre-production to post-production in the delivery of a completed project. Included are guest lectures from industry professionals in key areas of the filmmaking profession. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Browser-Based Games
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. This online advanced web technologies course explores client-side scripting using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JQuery. By creating complex interactive functions and user experiences, students understand the overall environment of web design technologies and a more integrated set of web design skills while building games for the browser. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Professional Development in Games
courses.desc: This course prepares students for finding and applying to jobs in the games industry and related sectors. Students will learn how to successfully network in-person and virtually, prepare resumes and cover letters specific to games jobs, build a supporting portfolio, create a professional online presence using social media, and connect with current industry professionals. This class also covers legal issues pertaining to the games industry, such as NDAs or IP ownership, and how to negotiate contracts. Finally, students will learn how to overcome challenges awaiting them after hire in the games industry, such as cross-cultural communication, discrimination, and layoffs. They will leave this course with all the necessary materials and skills for applying to games industry jobs. Level: Undergraduate & Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Sound for Digital Media
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to majors in Art and Media Arts. This course is targeted at the Integrated Digital Media student and introduces fundamental concepts, principles and practices of digital sound recording and editing. This will enable students to expand their aesthetic by integrating their sonic and visual creative work. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Topics in Film & Media Studies
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Research and exploration of contemporary ﬁlm, video, digital art and design. Focus on areas of student research both in commercial and non-commercial venues and styles. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Visions of Documentary Film
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. Class focuses on the study of different works of documentary filmmaking as well as the processes needed to succeed in the world on non-fiction storytelling. While studying films students will prepare and complete a short documentary film piece of their own. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Production Studio II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Art, Media Arts, Game Design and Interactive Media, and Sound Design and Media Technology. This course covers the principles and techniques of finishing projects. Students will focus on advanced rendering tools, prototype testing, installation and final performances, refined editing/titles/credits, enabling students to leave with a well polished finished project. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Fundamentals of the Unity Game Engine
courses.desc: Prereq., MART 120 and MART 220. This game programming course explores different game engines including but not limited to the Unity and Unreal Game Engines. Through multiple design and programmatic experiences, students gain an understanding of the overall game programming environment and their technologies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Multiplayer Games
courses.desc: Prereq., MART 120, MART 220, and MART 460 or MART 465. This class is designed to give the student a general understanding of programming server-side code and databases and interacting with APIs to create multiplayer games. Knowing game programming is highly recommended but not a requirement. We will focus primarily on connecting the server side to the client side. This class is a programming class; however, it is assumed that the student has a good understanding of programming concepts. This course focuses on C# and database development. Although this platform is used, it will not prevent the student from leveraging other tools provided by different vendors. The concepts covered in this course are generic and should translate to any language/platform. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate
courses.prereq: MART 120, MART 220, and MART 460 or MART 465

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Mobile Game Programming
courses.desc: Prereq., MART 120 and MART 220. This mobile game programming course explores different mobile game platforms and languages including but not limited to Android Studio with Java and Kotlin, XCode with Swift and Objective-C, and Visual Studio with Xamarin. Through many design and programmatic experiences, students gain an understanding of the mobile game programming environment and their technologies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Studio
courses.desc: Offered spring. Game Studio is a fully online class with an optional synchronous component where students share ideas, collaborate, and create a fully functioning game throughout the semester with the potential of creating something for a full year with the intent of deploying it to a store. This course includes presentations from industry experts, game design principles, software engineering best practices, project management, and testing. Teams will work through hackathon challenges together and create projects for distribution. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Creatively Exploring Artificial Intelligence: An Interdisciplinary Approach
courses.desc: This highly experiential artificial intelligence course is offered and open to any major. The course's primary objective will be to help students understand what Generative AI is and how to use it effectively while thinking about the ethical and moral aspects of this technology. By bringing several experts into the class with diverse perspectives, students will gain a broad understanding of Generative AI and how it will affect their lives in various ways. The class will ask students to think holistically through writing reflections, exploring creative possibilities in their disciplines, and generate projects that can affect the world around them. Level: Undergraduate/Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Fundamentals of the Unreal Game Engine
courses.desc: Prereq., MART 120 and MART 220. This game programming course explores the Unreal Game Engine. Through multiple design and programmatic experiences, students understand the overall game programming environment and their technologies. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Advanced Acting for Film I
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 320. This studio class builds on the techniques of basic realistic acting, adding processes that prepare students to work in the world of filmmaking. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Human-Centered Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
courses.desc: This is an interdisciplinary course that explores leadership theories, frameworks, and practical skills for guiding individuals, teams, and organizations in an AI-driven world. Based on scientifically backed research from leadership studies, cognitive science, ethics, and technology studies, this course emphasizes the human necessity of decision-making, responsibility, creativity, and equity in the world of artificial intelligence. Students will examine how AI systems shape work, learning, power, and culture across disciplines, and how leaders can thoughtfully integrate these technologies while maintaining human agency and values. Attention is given to ethical considerations, bias identification, transparent communication, governance, and the societal impacts of using generative AI systems. Through an experiential approach, students will actively explore modern generative AI tools to explore real-world leadership challenges, experiment with AI-assisted workflows, and reflect critically on the limits and risks of automation. By combining theory, applied practice, and reflection, this course will empower the next generation of leaders to understand the complexity, uncertainty, and technological challenges with confidence, responsibility, and a human-centered methodology. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Professional Portfolio
courses.desc: Offered spring semester. This course focuses on preparing students for the transition between academic and professional environments in the media industry. Students have spent the past few years building a robust body of work, which they will now polish and package through creative branding and design. Guest lectures and interviews will provide insight into current industry standards, professional workflow, and entering the creative workforce. Students should leave this course with all the materials they need to enter the professional world. Level: Undergraduate

courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.title: Practicum II
courses.desc: Offered every term. This course offers the student the opportunity to apply their media arts skill sets and techniques to a variety of professional level projects that include movies, web site design, and still image design. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Senior Project
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered spring and fall. Restricted to students in the Arts and Media Arts majors. This capstone course gives the student an opportunity to create an integrated senior project which brings together all of the elements of their course of study. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Core Research: Practice-Led Research in Arts and Technology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. This course explores the relationship between aesthetics and the emerging capabilities of arts and technology. This relationship will be explored through consideration of the reciprocal relationship between research and art. Students will be pushed to explore how practice-led research, research-led practice, and practice-based research methods may influence their own creative practice. They will also consider how creative practice and associated research methods create new novel knowledge and how this may contribute individual communities and the world at large. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Core Research: Creative Process and Story
courses.desc: Offered fall. This course breaks apart creative process models through exercises in writing and drawing. Students also critically engage with essays on the narrative processes of different writers, filmmakers and artists. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Game Analysis & Theory
courses.desc: This class explores how to formally analyze games as an artistic medium. Students will develop a methodological toolkit they can employ to conduct formal analyses of games and interactive media, informed by methods and theories from within game studies. This course also explores relevant theories from adjacent disciplines such as film and literature, but within the context of how these concepts can be applied to deepen our understanding of interactive games as an artistic medium. Students will leave this class with an informed vocabulary they can use to talk and write about games academically, knowledge of theories they can apply to improve the design of their own games, and a deeper appreciation of games as interactive art.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Professional Presentation in Games
courses.desc: In this course students will publish and present themselves in a professional capacity in game design and interactive media. This course creates a framework for students to assess and develop their own industry practice, set goals, and gain experience in the professional environment. Such examples may include producing a game, presenting at a conference, or publishing a research paper.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Graduate Studio
courses.desc: (R-18) Offered every semester. Each semester students work on individual projects under the supervision of a faculty mentor. Each year begins and ends with a faculty and peer review of projects in progress. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Graduate Game Seminar
courses.desc: (R-18) This course centers on students' work in developing a game project leading up to a thesis. This course will cover the theoretical and physical elements of game design and development. There will be playtests for feedback supported by readings, theories and discussions. This seminar aims to equip masters-level students with both the theoretical background and practical skills needed to thrive in game design. By the end of the course, students will have a portfolio piece to showcase their collaborative project and a deeper understanding of the complexities of creating engaging games. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Graduate Studio in Game Design and Interactive Media
courses.desc: (R-6) In this course students will work together with their team of MFA students to research and develop a project. This student cohort will work together to research a concept, design gameplay, create a timeline, assign rolls, organize playtests, and publish.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Research in Multi-plot and Serial Screenwriting
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered fall and spring. Development of screenplays for game design or serial writing for television.

courses.subject: MART
courses.title: Research
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered intermittently. Directed individual research and study appropriate to the back ground and objectives of the student. Level: Graduate
