courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Statistics
courses.desc: Offered every term. Prereq., M 105 or higher or a score of 3 or higher on the EdReady math placement exam. Application of descriptive and inferential statistical techniques to sociological data. Required for all Sociology majors.
courses.prereq: M 105 or higher or a score of 3 or higher on the EdReady math placement exam

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Introduction to Criminology
courses.desc: Offered autumn. A critical examination of crime in society: how crime is defined, the extent and distribution of crime, theoretical explanations of criminal behavior, and crime control efforts.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Race, Gender & Class
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Analysis of the intersecting structure and dynamics of race, gender and class. Focus on power relationships, intergroup conflict and minority-group status.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Criminal Justice System
courses.desc: Offered spring. A systematic survey of crime and the administration of justice in the United States, including the organizational structures, processes, and dynamics of law enforcement, criminal adjudication, and corrections.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Careers in Criminology
courses.desc: Offered spring. Overview of criminology-focused career paths with an emphasis on learning from professionals in the field and development of career planning competencies.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-24) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Criminal Justice Ethics
courses.desc: Offered spring. This course will be an examination of competing moral philosophies and their application to ethical dilemmas within the criminal justice system.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Work
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., WRIT 101. Restricted to students in the Sociology and Criminology majors and minors and Communication Studies majors in the Organizational & Strategic Communication concentration. An introduction to contemporary sociological debates on work including overwork, working poor, housework, globalization, mechanization, routinization, surveillance, and unions. Special focus on gender and class impacts on working life.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociological Research Methods
courses.desc: Offered every term. SOCI 202 or STAT 216 or PSYX 222 recommended. Restricted to students in the Sociology and Criminology majors and minors. Methods of research in the social sciences including naturalistic observation, interviewing, measurement, experiments, surveys, content analysis, and basic data analysis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Stratification
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. The origins, institutionalization and change of class, status, prestige, power and other forms of social inequality. Special attention to the effects of stratification on individuals.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Green Criminology
courses.desc: Green criminology explores the intersection of environmental issues with criminal activity and behavior, examining how environmental harms are defined as criminal (versus legal) acts, and evaluating the criminal justice system’s response to these issues. It considers the diverse range of victims affected by environmental offenses, including ecological systems, species health, and human behavior. In essence, green criminology aims to create a critical space within its parent discipline for analyzing crimes committed against humanity through environmental destruction.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of the Family
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Historical, cross-cultural, and analytical study of the family. Emphasis on ideology, social structures, and agency affecting family composition and roles.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Education
courses.desc: Restricted to students with at least junior standing in the Sociology and Criminology majors. Why do some students succeed while others struggle? How do schools reproduce—or challenge—social inequalities? This course explores the social forces shaping education, from classrooms to policy debates. We examine how factors like race, class, gender, and culture influence learning, teacher expectations, and access to opportunity. Through theory, research, and real-world examples, students will investigate how education both reflects and transforms society.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Juvenile Justice System
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. An analysis of the juvenile justice system in the United States, including the historical development of policies and practices. The role of various social agencies in defining, preventing, and responding to delinquency.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Rural Sociology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Demographic, economic and sociocultural change in rural communities with an emphasis on global economy, political structure, urbanization, and economic and social infrastructure. Special attention given to the rural west and Montana.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Crime, Justice, and Media
courses.desc: A critical analysis of portrayals of crime and justice in politics, news, and entertainment media, including comparisons between historical and contemporary portrayals.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Law Enforcement
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. An examination of policing in society, with emphasis on the cultural context in which it occurs, its structural characteristics, and social psychological processes.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Guns in America
courses.desc: This course explores the historical, cultural, legal, and political significance of firearms in the United States from the colonial era to the present. Through a sociological lens, students will examine how guns function as both tools of safety and objects of danger, shaped by political, legal, and cultural narratives. The course considers the role of firearms in shaping American identity, public policy, and debates over self-defense, regulation, and state power. Topics include the intersections of gun ownership, violence, and social identity, as well as the broader societal impacts of gun-related trauma.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Comparative Criminology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. An overview of macro-criminology, including an examination of macro-theoretical perspectives, cross-national variation in crime, and a comparative analysis of criminal justice systems around the world.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Health & Medicine
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to students with at least junior standing in the Sociology and Criminology majors and minors . This course examines the healthcare system, the social determinants of health, the historical epidemiological transition(s), medicalization, and changes in medical profession. Broadly, this course assists students in analyzing issues related to medicine, health, and healthcare from a sociological perspective.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Mental Illness
courses.desc: This course examines mental health and mental illness through a sociological lens, focusing on the ways that social, cultural, and institutional contexts shape our understanding of and responses to psychological distress. Students will explore the social construction of mental illness, the role of stigma and medicalization, and social determinants of mental health. Topics include historical and contemporary treatment approaches, the intersections of mental health with race, class, gender, sexuality, and immigration, the criminalization of mental illness and the role of the criminal justice system, and the broader social consequences of mental illness for individuals, families, and communities.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-24) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to students in the Sociology and Criminology majors. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Crime and the Life Course
courses.desc: This course examines how crime, deviance, and justice unfold across the span of human life. Drawing on the life course perspective, the course considers why individuals begin offending, persist in criminal behavior or desist from crime, and how these processes are shaped by key developmental stages, social contexts, and turning points such as school, work, marriage, and incarceration. Students will engage with major theories and research on the onset, persistence, and desistance of offending, exploring how social structures, inequalities, and institutions shape criminal trajectories over time. Special emphasis will be placed on the ways that age, race, class, gender, and broader social change intersect with individual lives as well as on the implications of life course criminology for policy and practice. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Rural Crime and Justice
courses.desc: This course examines crime, criminal justice, and social control in rural settings. While rural crime is often overshadowed by urban crime in media and research, it presents unique causes, challenges, and characteristics. The course explores topics such as the nature and prevalence of crime, law enforcement and justice system responses, the role of community and informal social control, victimization, and the intersections of race, class, and geography in rural settings. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Family Violence
courses.desc: This course is an advanced seminar on domestic violence/family violence examining the nature of domestic violence, causes of family violence, and potential solutions. We discuss specific forms of family violence, including intimate partner violence, child abuse and neglect, and elder abuse. We also examine societal reactions to family violence in the form of police, legal, and community responses. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Violence in America
courses.desc: This course surveys the trends, nature, patterns, and causes of violence in the United States of America. Blending criminological, sociological, and psychological perspectives on violent behavior, the course reviews various types of violence, including serial and mass murder, youth and school violence, violence among intimates and family members, as well as the role of firearms. The effectiveness of various criminal justice responses is also examined, including intervention strategies, gun control, incarceration, and capital punishment. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Punishment
courses.desc: Prereq., SOCI 101S. An examination of variation in punishment across societal contexts which addresses sociological theory and research on mass incarceration, capital punishment, and corporal punishment among other sanctions. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Corrections
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. An examination of the purposes, structures, and processes of jails, prisons, and community corrections, including probation and parole. Emphasis on historical development and current trends and issues in corrections. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Victims and Society
courses.desc: Restricted to students with at least junior standing in the Sociology and Criminology majors.This course surveys the field of victimology, addressing the extent of victimization in the U.S. It examines the dominant theoretical explanations for victimization, and it discusses the causes and consequences of victimization, including the behavioral and psychological reactions to being a victim of crime. It examines victimization in a wide range of contexts and a wide range of victims. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Immigration
courses.desc: This course examines theories of immigration, immigration experiences and adaptation, and social, political, and legal responses to immigration. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Communities and Crime
courses.desc: This course examines sociological theories and research on communities and crime, including spatial variation in crime rates and the impact of efforts to control crime on the structure and well-being of communities. The class takes a holistic approach to understanding how crime comes “bundled together” with other social problems at the community level. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Advanced Criminological Theory
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted students with at least junior standing in the Sociology and Criminology majors and minors. This course surveys the field of criminological theory, which attempts to understand and explain crime. It examines a range of major theories, including classic theories and their modern revisions. It also focuses on recent research testing and expanding criminological theories. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Deviant and Criminal Behavior
courses.desc: An analysis of the causes and theoretical perspectives of deviance, crime, and antisocial behavior. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Gender, Crime, and Justice
courses.desc: This course will examine the role of gender throughout the criminal justice system. Focus will be placed on victimization, incarceration, and the reentry of female offenders. Moreover, this course will examine women professionals in the criminal justice system such as police officers, corrections staff, and court service providers. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Race, Crime, and Criminal Justice
courses.desc: This course addresses the empirical relationship between race and crime and its theoretical explanations. This course addresses offending and victimization patterns and trends and introduces the major theories used to make sense of these trends. This includes providing an overview of existing research which examines how race influences criminal justice outcomes. Finally, the course addresses public attitudes about race and crime, including how race motivates attitudes and policies about crime and justice in the United States. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Classical Sociological Theory
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., SOCI 101S. Exploration of the classical foundations of sociological theories, emphasizing Marx, Durkheim, and Weber. Required of all sociology majors. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Media & Research
courses.desc: Restricted to students in the Sociology and Criminology majors with at least junior standing. This course introduces students to the emerging field of computational social science, focusing on using social media data to examine pressing sociological questions. Social media platforms offer complex, dynamic data that provide valuable insight into human behavior and social life in the digital age. In this class, students will learn the technical skills needed to collect, structure, and analyze social media data using Python, including data collection, data wrangling, and basic data visualization. Alongside skill development, we will critically examine how digital data and methods are being used across academia and industry, with attention to ethical considerations and the sociological insights they can offer. Students will evaluate and synthesize course readings, formulate theoretically grounded research questions, and develop an original research paper using computational methods. Topics covered include text analysis, network analysis, and an introduction to machine learning. No prior programming experience is required; students will gain hands-on experience and leave the course with a foundation in computational tools and sociological writing. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Homicide
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted students with at least junior standing in the Sociology and Criminology majors. This course is a specialized introduction and overview of homicide as a societal and criminological phenomenon. The course focuses broadly on criminological, interdisciplinary, and psychiatric perspectives about homicide offending and victimization. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Environmental Sociology
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Introduction to environmental sociology and the social dimensions of environmental change. Case studies of major environmental problems as applications of environmental sociological perspectives. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Race, Politics, and Public Opinion
courses.desc: This course critically examines the role of race and ethnicity in shaping politics and public opinion in the United States. We will explore how racial identities, attitudes, and group interests influence political beliefs, policy preferences, and electoral behavior. Central questions include: How do racial attitudes shape political ideologies and voting patterns? What role does racial prejudice play in shaping public opinion? How do politicians leverage or respond to racial divisions in their campaigns and policymaking? The course learning objectives include: 1) examining theories of racial prejudice, 2) comparing various theories of racial attitudes, 3) examining the historical and contemporary impact of racialized political strategies (e.g., the Southern Strategy, dog-whistle politics), and 4) critically analyzing the evolving role of race in shaping partisanship and political polarization. We will also examine how race intersects with issues such as criminal justice, immigration, and social movements, considering how racialized narratives influence policy debates and media framing. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Work, Labor, and the Criminal Justice System
courses.desc: This course explores the intersection of work and the criminal justice system in the U.S. by examining the experiences of unpaid (incarcerated) and paid workers (corrections/probation/police officers, etc) in the system. We’ll also investigate the influence of the criminal justice system on the American labor market and solutions to problems with work in the system such as collective action, regulations, and legislation. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Crime & Deviance
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered every term. Restricted to graduate students in Sociology. Graduate-level studies of a specific criminological topic or issue with special emphasis on theory, research, policy, and practice. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Qualitative Methods
courses.desc: Offered spring even-numbered years. Restricted to graduate students in Sociology. Introduction to the basic methods used to conduct qualitative studies including ethnography, interviewing, observation and/or focus group. Includes hands-on fieldwork projects, data coding and analysis, and research ethics. Draws on examples and literature from sociology. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Quantitative Methods
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to graduate students in Sociology. Introduction to the basic methods used to conduct quantitative sociological research and program evaluation including proposal development, survey design, sampling techniques, data analysis, and dissemination of findings. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Data Analysis
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Restricted to graduate students in Sociology. Introduction to basic techniques of quantitative data analysis emphasizing multivariate regression analysis. Students will learn how to prepare a dataset, assure that basic statistical assumptions are met, correctly estimate and interpret regression coefficients, estimate regression models using data analysis software (SPSS). Level: Graduate

courses.title: Graduate Research
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered every term. Directed individual research and study appropriate to the background and objectives of the student. Those students electing the professional paper option in Sociology may apply three credits of this course toward the master's degree. Level: Graduate

This course, taught in Spanish, is designed to facilitate rapid immersion in host-family activities, the academic and social cultures of the local universities in which students might be taking classes, and the daily life of the student's surroundings in Seville and Spain.

This course, taught in Spanish, offers intensive conversation, culture, grammar, and writing within the classroom with linguistic and cultural skills reinforced outside the classroom through immersion in the daily life of a Sevillian host family and engagement in the life of the city.

courses.title: Spanish: Oral and Written Expression

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Spanish Phonetics
courses.desc: Offered once each academic year. Prereq., SPNS 202. A practical and theoretical exploration of the Spanish sound system.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Intensive Spanish Abroad
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered spring. Prereq., SPNS 202. Intensive Spanish language course to coincide with intensive language course given at an institute or college during the Spanish Study Abroad Program. Credits vary according to the hours and intensity of the course and are determined by the director of the program.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Topics in Hispanic Culture
courses.desc: Prereq., WRIT 101. This course offers a rigorous and comprehensive study of a major author, work, cultural phenomena, or relevant issue in the Spanish-speaking world.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Advanced Conversations
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., SPNS 202. Intensive practice in oral Spanish through individual presentations, vocabulary and grammar work, and film discussion and analysis.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Contemporary Spanish Literature
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., SPNS 202. The study of contemporary works by peninsular authors, including an introduction to literary genres.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Cultures and Societies of Latin America
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., SPNS 202. An interdisciplinary introduction to Latin American culture, society, and history with emphasis on contemporary aspects.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Bilingualism in the Spanish-Speaking World
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., SPNS 202. Spanish, one of the most widely spoken languages in the world, is often found in contact with other languages in a variety of social and linguistic landscapes. These contact situations allow us to examine the types, characteristics, and outcomes of bilingualism. This course will delve into many important aspects of bilingualism, such as language maintenance and loss, characteristics of bilingual speech, cognitive aspects of bilingualism, and language acquisition.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: SIGE: The City and The Image
courses.desc: Offered every semester. Prereq., SPNS 202. Restricted to students in the Spanish Institute for Global Education (SIGE) program. Taught at SIGE in Seville, Spain, by SIGE instructor. This course, taught in Spanish, enriches Spanish comprehension and expression skills through applied use of language in the context of learning technical skills, planning and completing a creative project, and discussing work of professional photographers.

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: SIGE: History Through Spanish Gastronomy
courses.desc: Offered every semester. Prereq., SPNS 202. Restricted to students in the Spanish Institute for Global Education (SIGE) program. Taught at SIGE in Seville, Spain, by SIGE instructors. This course, taught in Spanish, is a combination of history, culture, and gastronomy and teaches the relationship between Spanish food and culture and, thereby, socio-cultural aspects of Spain.

courses.subject: SPNS

courses.desc: Offered every semester. Prereq., SPNS 202. Restricted to students in the Spanish Institute for Global Education (SIGE) program. Taught at SIGE in Seville, Spain, by SIGE instructors. This course, taught in Spanish, expands knowledge of Spanish literature, links classical and contemporary Spanish writing to historical and contemporary social, political, and economic phenomena, and deepens understanding of the place of literature in the contemporary life of Seville.

courses.subject: SPNS

courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn even-numbered years. Prereq., SPNS 326 or 331. Emphasis on major works of the Renaissance and the Spanish Golden Age. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Spanish Literature: Modern & Contemporary
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered spring even-numbered years. Prereq., SPNS 326 or SPNS 331. Emphasis on major works of modern and contemporary Spanish literature. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-12) Prereq., SPNS 326 or SPNS 331. A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Senior Thesis/Capstone
courses.desc: Offered in both the fall and spring. This course is designed to be a culminating experience in which the student will demonstrate skills and knowledge garnered from his/her experience within the Spanish Option. We will offer two possibilities for the Capstone: 1) The student can research, write and revise an extensive research paper under the supervision of a Spanish faculty member. The capstone topic selected will directly relate to the language, literature, culture, history and/or civilization of the Spanish-speaking peoples of the world. 2) The student can fulfill a high impact field experience or internship experience as the culminating activity in the program. In this case, students can demonstrate their knowledge, skills, and values in a wide variety of ways. Field experiences and internships may be evaluated by both a faculty member and a field supervisor under whom the student is working. Evaluations may consist of check sheets and evaluation forms that the supervisor and faculty complete both during and at the end of the experience, notes from advisory meetings with the student during the experience, and materials that the student produces during the experience, perhaps gathered into a portfolio. Level: Undergraduate
courses.offered: in both the fall and spring

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R–24) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one–time offerings of current topics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SPNS
courses.title: Graduate Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Counseling in Speech-Language Pathology
courses.desc: Theoretical perspectives on counseling clients with communication and swallowing disorders with an emphasis on counseling strategies, grief and loss, and working with family members. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Speech Sound Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Theoretical perspectives on phonological and articulation disorders with emphasis on application to clinical management including evaluation, assessment techniques, and intervention strategies. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Voice & Resonance Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Study of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of voice. Neural bases of normal and disordered voice and resonance. Diagnosis and management of voice and resonance disorders. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Motor Speech Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Study of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of the speech mechanism. Neural bases of normal and disordered speech motor control. Assessment and treatment of motor speech disorders. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Fluency Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. This course focuses on the nature, diagnosis, and treatment of developmental stuttering and cluttering and acquired neurogenic and psychogenic stuttering. Students examine assessments of historic and current literature and trends in stuttering research and treatment. Culturally responsive assessment and intervention as well as the multidimensional nature of stuttering are addressed. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Social Communication Skills, Behavior, and Neurodiversity
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. This course explores and integrates social aspects of communication (e.g., behavioral and social skills/competence), communication accommodations, adaptations, and strategies for functional communication and independent living skills. Topics include foundational information on autism as well as assessment and treatment using evidence-based practices for autism spectrum disorder and related disorders. Co-convenes with CSD 445. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Augmentative & Alternative Communication
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. This course explores and integrates communication accommodations, adaptations, and links to functional and daily-living in individuals with severe to complex communication disorders. This includes a focus on assessment and treatment processes and practices for individuals requiring alternative and augmentative communication needs across the lifespan, cultures, and abilities. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Language Assessment and Intervention for Children Infants through Preschool
courses.desc: Students learn language assessment and intervention for children with language delays and disorders from birth to preschool including language sampling and analysis procedures, interpreting formal and informal testing, facilitating language through strategies and corresponding theories, planning clinical management and intervention, and enhancing emergent literacy. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Dx /Tx School-Age Lang
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. This course examines various approaches to working with children and adolescents with language and learning disabilities. Practical application of language assessment procedures, individualized planning, and language-literacy intervention strategies will be discussed. Language-literacy interventions in the classroom and collaborative strategies will also be covered. Culturally responsive assessment and intervention, as well as the multidimensional nature of language in the classroom will be addressed. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Evidence Based Practice in Rehabilitation and Education
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Students should have a framework for understanding, using, and applying the evidence-based practice trilogy (client values, clinical expertise, research) in rehabilitation and Education practice. Students will gain exposure to writing style in research, ethics, and evaluating evidence in clinical application. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Aphasia
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Neural bases and medical etiologies of aphasia in adult populations. Evaluation and treatment of aphasia in persons with acquired neurologic disorders across successive stages of recovery. Incorporates models of rehabilitation across prevention, assessment, and treatment, with a focus on the WHO-ICF and aspects of disability across diverse populations. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Acquired Cognitive-Communication Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Assessment, treatment, and prevention of acquired cognitive-communication disorders including pediatric and adult traumatic brain injury (TBI) and mild traumatic brain injury (MTBI), right hemisphere syndrome (RHS), and dementia. Emphasis on neurobiological principles of rehabilitations, differential diagnosis and theories, and evidence-based research pertaining to clinical management. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Clinic Proc/Pro Pract I
courses.desc: (R-3) Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. This course provides content focused on the professional practices, processes, attributes, and abilities associated with professional accountability, ethics, integrity, effective communication skills, clinical reasoning, evidence-based practice, and collaborative practice. In addition clinical consideration of multicultural aspects of communication are considered of clients from all ages, backgrounds, and abilities. Links to clinical application in associated applied classes are made. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Found Applied Clinic Srv/Lrn
courses.desc: (R-9) Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Foundational Application of professional skills associated with the UM DeWit RiteCare Clinic. Assignment of cases and area of specialization will vary with clinical educator assignment. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Advanced Clinic Proc II
courses.desc: (R-3) Prereq., SLP 570. Coreq., SLP 576. This course provides content focused on continued development of topics related to professional development as a speech-language pathologist and will support the clinical externship experience. Emphasis on professional practices and processes, ASHA and state compliance, clinical problem solving, evidence based practice, employment settings considerations, self-advocacy, communication, and multicultural considerations. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Advanced Applied Clinic II
courses.desc: (R-18) Prereq., SLP 570. Advanced application of professional skills in the UM RiteCare Clinic or off-campus. Assignment of cases and area of specialization will vary with the clients needs and availability. Out of state placement by approval of clinical director. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Diagnostics
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Students will develop the following skills: using case history information to form a diagnostic plan; administering various standardized and non-standardized diagnostic tools; interpreting assessment results; writing diagnostic reports; and sharing diagnostic results with clients, caregivers and other professionals. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Master of Science Capstone Portfolio
courses.desc: Prereq., or corequisite, SLP 600. An integration evidence-based practice foundations in Speech-Language Pathology. This course requires comprehensive portfolios that include a best-evidence systematic literature review, a clinical philosophy reflecting current learning theory, and evidence of application of current best practices. Level: Graduate.

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Graduate

courses.desc: (R-12) A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Practicum
courses.desc: Supervised, practical experience in a professional setting relevant to the student's field of study. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Thesis
courses.desc: (R-9) Prereq., SLP 600. The primary purpose of the thesis is to allow a student to conduct a research project in a particular field of study related to speech and language pathology. Course graded only on CR/NCR basis. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Research Methods
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Research methodologies appropriate for quantitative and qualitative studies in communication sciences and disorders. Focuses on critical reading of research papers, design, and implementation of experiments. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Swallowing Disorders
courses.desc: Restricted to graduate students in Speech-Language Pathology. Study of anatomy, physiology, and pathology of swallowing. Diagnosis and treatment of swallowing disorders. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Clinical Externship & Advanced Practicum
courses.desc: (R-12) Prereq., SLP 570, SLP 571, SLP 575, and SLP 576. The course is an externship completed during a student’s final semester of graduate school requiring 30-40 hours a week participation. Out of state placements approved by the clinical externship coordinator. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Topics in Language Science
courses.desc: Restricted to doctoral students in Speech, Language, and Hearing Sciences. This course will explore techniques used to scientifically investigate language development, language function/processing, and language disorders.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Topics in Speech Science
courses.desc: Restricted to doctoral students in Speech, Language, and Hearing Science. This course will explore techniques used to scientifically investigate speech development and speech disorders.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Topics in Hearing Science
courses.desc: Restricted to doctoral students in Speech, Language, and Hearing Science. This course will explore techniques used to scientifically investigate hearing development and disorders.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Professional Seminar
courses.desc: (R-9) This doctoral level seminar is designed to help develop research, teaching, and professional skills required for post-doctoral employment. Sessions will be conducted in a face-to-face (on-campus or via synchronous web-based videoconferencing) format. Each week invites active student engagement in several types of activities, including: reading, writing, reviewing/editing, engaging in discussions, and presenting research and/or teaching modules.

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Research
courses.desc: (R-30) Research including scholarly inquiry, investigation, or creative activity that follows appropriate conventions, is guided by an academic mentor, and produces original intellectual or creative work. Offered CR/NCR only. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) This course it an intensive exploration of a discipline, interdisciplinary practice, or theory not available through regularly scheduled courses. A student performs coursework in consultation with and supervised by a faculty member. The course of study is aligned with the needs and learning objectives of the individual student. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-12) A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Practicum
courses.desc: (R-9) Supervised, practical experience in a professional setting relevant to the student's field of study. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Service Learning: Professional Serivce
courses.desc: This course is a collaboration between students, faculty, and community partners to enhance student learning by applying academic knowledge in a community service context. Student service addresses community identified needs and meets learning objectives through faculty/community-structured service. It incorporates critical reflection to prepare students to be civically engaged members of the community. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) This internship is an opportunity for practical application of classroom learning through professional, career-related work experiences. All interns have a set of learning objectives, a faculty advisor, and site supervisor. There is opportunity for performance feedback from faculty and/or supervisor. The interns’ work benefits a business, nonprofit, or government agency. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SLP
courses.title: Dissertation
courses.desc: (R-9) Dissertation research activities. Graded only on CR/NCR basis. Level: Graduate.

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Introduction to Statistics
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., M 115 (preferred); or one of M 121, M 132, M 140, M 151, M 162 or M 171; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.5; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.5. Introduction to major ideas of statistical inference. Emphasis is on statistical reasoning and uses of statistics.
courses.prereq: M 115 (preferred); or one of M 121, M 132, M 140, M 151, M 162 or M 171; or EdReady placement level 3; or M02-Maplesoft Algebra score >= 14; or ACT score of 23; or SAT score of 560 (with the new test); or ACT score of 21 and HS GPA 3.5; or SAT score of 530 and HS GPA 3.5

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Probability and Simulation
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., M 162 or M 172. Probability, probability models and simulation, random variables, density functions, special distributions, and an introduction to statistical inference. Computer use integrated throughout.

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Probability Theory
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., M 273. STAT 342 is recommended. Fundamentals of probability; discrete and continuous random variables; expected value; variance; joint, marginal, and conditional distributions; conditional expectations; applications; simulation; central limit theorem; order statistics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Mathematical Statistics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., STAT 421. Introduction to the theory of point estimation, interval estimation, and hypothesis testing. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Statistical Methods I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. May not be counted toward a major in mathematics except toward the mathematics education concentration. Intended primarily for non-mathematics majors who will be analyzing data. Graphical and numerical summaries of data, elementary sampling, designing experiments, probability as a model for random phenomena and as a tool for making statistical inferences, random variables, basic ideas of inference and hypothesis testing. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Statistical Methods II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., STAT 451. Continuation of STAT 451. Multiple regression, experimental design, analysis of variance, other statistical models. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Computer Data Analysis I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Coreq., STAT 451. An introduction to software for doing statistical analyses. Intended primarily for students in STAT 451. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Computer Data Analysis II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Coreq., STAT 452. Continuation of STAT 457. Intended primarily for students in STAT 452. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered autumn and spring. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one time offerings of current topics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: STAT
courses.title: Graduate Seminar in Probability and Statistics
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. A review and discussion of current research. Level: Graduate

courses.subject: SRVY
courses.title: Construction Surveying
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Offered at Missoula College. Basic principles of surveying and the use of surveying equipment. Calculation of angles and distances to determine grade elevations. Introduction to Global Positioning Systems, lasers and their relationship to the heavy equipment operator.

courses.subject: SRVY
courses.title: Intro to Surveying for Engineers
courses.desc: Offered spring. Offered at Missoula College. Basic principles of civil surveying and the use of surveying equipment. Surveying introduces students to the link between field (construction) and office (design) practices. Students will become familiar with Global Positioning Systems (GPS), levels, level rods, total stations, basic survey computations, and their relationship to Computer Design Systems.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Introduction to Theatre
courses.desc: The various elements of play production and dance. The basic artistic principles underlying dance, theatre and all of the arts.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Introduction to Theatre Design
courses.desc: Basic understanding of the principles of design for the theatre and television, including the production elements of scenery, costumes and lighting.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Introduction to House Management
courses.desc: (R-3) Offered autumn and spring. Introduction to the skills and experience of the front-of-house staff for a theatrical production.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre Production I: Run Crew
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Operation and running a show backstage on a scenery, costume, or prop crew for a major school production.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre Production I: Construction Crew
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered autumn and spring. The construction and completion of scenery/props, costumes, and/or lighting under supervision. Most assignments involve very basic construction techniques and/or maintenance duties found in professional shop. Involves minimum of two 4-hour labs a week.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Introduction to Voice Acting
courses.desc: This course introduces foundational techniques of voice acting, emphasizing the development of articulate, responsive, and expressive vocal skills. Students will explore various genres from animation to video games while learning to optimize technology to create engaging voice performances. Additionally, students will analyze and critique voice acting work, enhancing both their creative and technical abilities.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Introduction to Acting I
courses.desc: An introduction to the skills and techniques required of the actor to be effective in communication with others on stage and off stage.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Drawing Fundamentals for Theatre
courses.desc: Students will begin to develop skills in drawing the human form, perspective, and architecture.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Special Topics/Experimental Courses
courses.desc: (R-6) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Seminar: First Year
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered autumn. Provides incoming majors with fundamental academic skills and an overview of campus student support services, as well as an introduction to policies and procedures specific to the School of Theatre and Dance and the professional options available in the performing arts.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stagecraft I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Fundamental theories and hands-on application in the areas of costuming, lighting, scenery, and properties.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stagecraft II: Scenery & Props
courses.desc: Fundamental theories and hands-on application in the areas of scenery, properties, and rigging.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre Production II: Run Crew
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., THTR 106. Operation and running a show backstage, as in scenery, costumes, or props for a major school production.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Voice & Speech I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Voice production, phonetics, and speech for the stage.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Voice & Speech II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 210. Character voices, which broadly encompass dialects and accents.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Acting I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Studio class intended to cultivate skill sets necessary for those with a background or interest in the craft of acting, especially those considering a career in the performing arts (theatre, music, dance, film, broadcasting): observation, imagination, concentration, improvisation, and character.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Acting II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 220. Continuation of THTR 220. Scene study and characterization, utilizing modern and contemporary scripts.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Dramatic Literature
courses.desc: The study of representative theatre texts as a foundation for play analysis.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Creative Drama/Dance: K-8
courses.desc: Offered autumn and spring. Restricted to majors in Elementary Education and Early Childhood Education: P-3. Focus on the use of creative drama and dance as types of educational tools. Students will explore, experience, and implement creative teaching methods in order to promote scholarship through kinesthetic teaching in elementary education.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Intermediate Costume Construction
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 202. Intermediate costume construction focusing on the development of skills needed to function as a stitcher.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Makeup I
courses.desc: Principles of and practice in makeup for the stage.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Drafting for Theatre I
courses.desc: Offered spring. Drawing techniques for the theatre with an emphasis on drafting as utilized by technicians, designers, stage managers and directors.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Intermediate Scenery Construction
courses.desc: Prereqs., THTR 107A, THTR 202, and THTR 255 or 355. Advances students' skills in scenic carpentry through practical application of construction drafting, construction planning, project management, advanced layout processes, advanced tool usage, and team management. Students will realize projects to be used in current and future School of Theatre and Dance productions.
courses.prereq: s., THTR 107A, THTR 202, and THTR 255 or 355

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Electrics
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 202. Training for the position of Lead Electrician. Practical application of production planning, lighting paperwork, overseeing lighting crews, advanced electrical theory, power distribution, and creative problem solving. Students will work on major school productions.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Summer Theatre
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered summer. Practicum in school-approved summer theatre companies in the capacity of actor, designer, director, stage manager and/or technician.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Construction I
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., THTR 107A. Students serve as the construction/maintenance crew in a shop (sound, light, costume, or scenery) for university productions.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Team I
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Students function as part of the production team in a role of responsibility (i.e., assistant designer, designer, lead electrician, cutter, first hand, head carpenter, etc.) for a school production. These assignments and duties often serve as part of the required junior project.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Design I
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Students function as a member of the production team in a role of responsibility (i.e., scenic designer, costume designer, light designer, etc.) for a school production. These assignments and duties may serve also as part of the required junior project.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Voice and Speech III
courses.desc: Offered autumn. An advanced exploration of voice acting skills and techniques culminating in the application of industry standards and best practices to recorded and live performances.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Movement for the Actor I
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 221. Basics of physical performance: collaboration, concentration, centering, balance, agility, and body awareness through a variety of stage movement techniques.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Acting III
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 221. Process-based and systematic approach to scene work, character development and rehearsal, focusing on new and emerging playwrights of the contemporary era (21st century).

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Practitioners
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Theatre. This course will introduce a variety of contemporary theatre and actor-training methods to interrogate contemporary scripts. Students perform selected scenes using chosen strategies from the methodologies studied.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Musical Theatre Audition Techniques
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 320. A foundational studio course which focuses on the development and practice of musical-theatre audition skills. The course will comprise specialized training in requisite areas of singing, acting, dancing and materials preparation pertaining to the format, demands and performance of musical-theatre auditions.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Auditioning
courses.desc: Offered fall. Prereq., THTR 120A or 220. A studio course focusing on the development and practice of audition skills, including material selection and techniques. The course will also offer practice in a variety of auditioning circumstances, including monologue delivery, callbacks, and auditioning with a reader.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre History I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. A survey of the major developments of the theatre from ritual beginnings to the 19th century, including various cultures and their representative plays and performances throughout the world.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre History II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., WRIT 101 or equivalent and THTR 330H. Continuation of THTR 330H. The many and varied periods since the 19th century as reflected in the theatre of the times in America, Europe and throughout the world.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Dramaturgy
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 330H. Introduction to the work of the dramaturg; to literary, historical, and contextual analysis of play scripts and performance pieces intended for production; and to building study guides and/or other resources.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Costume History
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. History of costume from prehistory to the present day.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Costume Design I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 102A and THTR 202. Introduction to principles and practices of stage costume design.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Pattern Making I
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 245. Pattern design using the flat pattern and draping method of basic pattern shapes to create basic costume and clothing patterns, gaining advanced principles of fitting.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Textile Selection & Manipulation
courses.desc: Analysis of fibers, yarns, structures and finishes, as related to selection and use for the theatre. Basic dyeing, distressing and painting.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Scenic Design I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 102A and THTR 202. Introduction to the problems encountered in designing scenery, analyzing of script, research and practical demands of theatre conventions. Projects include those for theatre, musicals, opera, and dance.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Design for Film and Television
courses.desc: Introduction to the basic elements of production design for film and television. Students will be exposed to the basics of visual storytelling, including script analysis for production design, storyboards, shot composition, visual research, drafting, and pre-production planning. Students will also gain an understanding of location versus studio work and film versus television design.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Technical Direction
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Prereq., THTR 255. Training for position of technical director. The role and scope of technical direction, production scheduling, design analysis, budgets and bookkeeping, and methods of construction.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Computer Aid Draft & Applications
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 255. Computer drafting for scenery, costumes, lighting, and sound design drawings, including 2-D and 3-D plans, layouts and renderings. Work with CAD, photo manipulation, spreadsheet, database, and word processing programs.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Scenic Painting
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered spring. Introduction to the basic skills needed as a scenic artist. Emphasis on the varied materials and techniques used in the scenic studio, color mixing, and interpretation of the designer's work.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Properties Management
courses.desc: (R-8) Offered autumn and spring. Provides students with the necessary skills and training to serve as a properties manager for a theatrical production. Students participate in the production process, learning through hands on activities and practical training and guidance in the acquisition and/or construction of all props for a given production/show.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre Lighting I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 102A, 202. Introduction to principles and practices of theatre lighting design. Training for position of lighting designer for theatre. Design requirements and decisions, color, development of stage picture; concentration on proscenium theatre design concepts.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Lighting Programming
courses.desc: Training for students to serve as programmers in the professional world of live performance. Computer systems for control of lighting will be covered in depth as well as additional exposure to systems for sound and projection. Exploration of networking systems together to control a combination of the areas.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Sound for Performance I
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 202. Training in the engineering and design of sound systems used in performance venues. Practical exploration of microphones and speakers for recording and public address. Equipment and methods of operation for supporting the needs of sound in a production.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Management I
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 202. Beginning study of the duties of the stage manager concentrating on the rehearsal process in the non-professional theatre situation.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Management Practicum I
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., THTR 370. Stage management practicum involving stage managing a showcase production or assistant stage managing a major show. Involves evening work.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Directing I
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 120A or THTR 220; THTR 235L; THTR 330H. Introduction to the analytical skills, staging, and conceptual techniques of the director; includes some practical application in scene work.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Special Topics/Experimental Courses
courses.desc: (R-15) Offered intermittently. Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Seminar
courses.desc: (R-6) A review and discussion of current research. Topics vary.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Practicum
courses.desc: (R-24) Offered autumn and spring. Service learning experience in theatre in a setting compatible with the students major and interests.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: (R-6) Offered intermittently. Extended classroom experience that provides practical application of classroom learning during placements off campus. Prior approval must be obtained from the faculty supervisor. A maximum of 6 credits of Internship (198, 298, 398, 498) may count toward graduation.

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Professional Theatre
courses.desc: (R-18) Laboratory experience in total play production through participation in state, regional, national and international touring production programs. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Professional Technology and Production
courses.desc: (R-18) Students experience the rigors and develop the skills required of technicians in touring theatre, maintaining integrity of all production elements through three months of intensive travel and varying venues. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Construction II
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Students serve as construction crew in one of the shops for productions. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Team II
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Students serve as a member of the production team in a role of responsibility (i.e., assistant designer, designer, lead electrician, cutter, first hand, head carpenter, etc.) for major productions. These assignments and duties often serve as part of the required senior project. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Production Design II
courses.desc: (R-12) Offered autumn and spring. Students serve as a member of the production team in a role of designer (i.e., set designer, costume designer, light designer, etc.) for major productions. These assignments and duties may serve also as part of the required senior project. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Musical Theatre
courses.desc: (R-4) Offered spring. Requires an audition. Development and presentation of musical numbers in a dramatic context. A broad-based acquaintance with music theatre literature is acquired, and techniques for approaching songs are explored with an eye toward developing competency in music theatre forms. Co-convenes with THTR 510. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Combat
courses.desc: Topics include unarmed stage combat, basic armed combat, and physical performance safety methods and procedures. Students will present the skills learned in the performance of scenes including fight choreography. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Comedy Styles
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in Theatre. Scenes and projects from specific historical and contemporary comedy styles. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Classics
courses.desc: Offered spring. Restricted to students in Theatre. Selected speeches, scenes and projects from verse drama, especially Shakespeare. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Professional Performance
courses.desc: (R-18) Students experience the rigors and develop the skills required for actors in touring theatre; creating characters and maintaining consistent performances through three months of intensive travel and varying venues. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Devising
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Restricted to students in Theatre. Performance and scene work in contemporary practice and theory, using devising techniques across performance disciplines. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Special Skills
courses.desc: Restricted to students in Theatre. Developing actors' skills in specialized areas such as acting for new media, genre-specific performance, clowning, commedia, improvisation, classical repertoire, or other specialized topics dependent upon faculty and/or guest faculty areas of expertise. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Methods of Teaching Theatre
courses.desc: (R-6) Building and addressing specific curriculum in theatre arts. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Pattern Making
courses.desc: Prereq., THTR 345. Pattern design using the flat pattern and draping method of advanced costume and clothing patterns, gaining advanced principles of fitting. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Tailoring
courses.desc: Offered spring alternate years. Principles used in the construction of tailored garments. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Scene Design II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 350. A continuation of the techniques and projects in THTR 350. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Scene Painting
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 356. Students will explore advanced scene painting techniques. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Theatre Lighting II
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 360. Advanced study of principles and practices of theatre lighting design. Training for position of light designer for theatre. Design requirements and decisions, color, development of stage picture; thrust and arena theatre. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Management II
courses.desc: Offered intermittently. Prereq., THTR 370. Additional study of stage management concentrating on pre-rehearsal duties, aspects of maintaining a show's integrity as established by the director, inter-production relationships, supervision of crews and union contracts. Understanding a stage manager's need for paperwork and writing skills. Students encouraged to enroll in THTR 472 to use skills in a living situation. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Stage Management Practicum II
courses.desc: (R-9) Offered autumn and spring. Prereq., THTR 470. Stage managing a major show in the drama season in the Montana or Masquer Theatres or assistant stage managing for an Equity stage manager on a Montana Repertory Theatre production. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Directing II
courses.desc: Offered autumn. Prereq., THTR 375. Directing skills for the advanced student; extensive scene work. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Directing III
courses.desc: Offered spring. Prereq., THTR 475. Continuation of THTR 475. Course material coordinated with laboratory projects. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Advanced Acting: Professional Skills
courses.desc: Offered spring. Developing professional skills, material for the actor, professional portfolio, resume audition material, commercial acting, performance market research. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: (R-12) Independent research under the direction of a faculty member. Level: Undergraduate

courses.subject: THTR
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc: (R-18) Experimental offerings of visiting professors, experimental offerings of new courses, or one-time offerings of current topics. Level: Undergraduate-Graduate

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: (R-24) Course material appropriate to the needs and objectives of the individual student. Level: Undergraduate
